[Survivors of the Balaclava Charge were found in a work- house recently. Public subscriptions for their relief were opened ; the total result was a few pounds.] Half a life, half a life, Half a life backward. All in the valley of death Rode the Six Hundred. Half a life, half a life, Half a life onward, All that is left to us OE the Six Hundred. How have we honoured them, Those hoary-headed men, All that is left to us Of the Six Hundred? Those glory-covered heads Laid low on workhouse beds I All that is left to us Of the Six Hundred. Oh, God! forbid such shame Should tarnish England's fame. Can our blood be the same That runs in these heroes? • Shame on all England's sons, From her mighty ones down Thus to neglect tile bright Jewels of her crown, Those of the Light Brigade, Of whom the Laureate said— ' " Ne'er shall their glory fade, Noble Six Hundred." . Forward, ye Britons brave, Succour the Light Brigade! All that is left to us Of the Six Hundred. Let them not live to say 'Would life had ebbed away On that far distant day, At Balaclava." —Otago Witness.

Be brief; for it is with words as with sunbeams—the more they are condensed the deeper they burn. We find flags used as far back as the days of ancient Egyptians, and ensigns and standards are observable on their monuments and tombs. A writer on small things says that he always takes notice of even a straw, especially if there happens to be a lemon squash at the end of it. A girl sued a man for breach of promise, and proved him such a scoundrel that the jury were of opinion that she ought to pay him something for not marrying her. A young lady sent to a newspaper a poem, entitled "I cannot make him smile." The editor ventured to ex- press an opinion that she would have succeeded had she shown him the poem. Hollingsworth: "You say you are an experienced driver?" Pat: "Tie, sorr." Hollingsworth: " Where did you get your experience?" Pat: "Oi was a pile- droiver in th' Boshtan Back bay for two years, sorr." A: "You have heard. I suppose, that I am married again ?" B: "Yes; and they say you married your de- ceased wife's sister." A: " Yes,l did." B: "Why did you dose ?" A "Simply to avoid two mothers-in-law." Lady: "I can't stand this any more. You have a different soldier here in the kitchen every week." Ser- vant: " That's not my fault. In a house where the table is as poor as it is in this, you can't expect the same soldier to stand it more than a week."

CHARACTER THE BEST SECURITY.—"I owe my success in business chiefly to you." said a stationer to a paper- maker, as they were settling a large account; "but let me ask how a man of your caution came to give credit so readily to a beginner of my slender means?" "Be- cause," replied the paper-maker. "at whatever hour in the morning I passed to my- business I always observed you without your coat at yours." AN ODD MARRTAGE.—Many years ago, a gentleman whose first wife was dead rose one morning with the whimsical resolution of marrying any one of his maid- servants who should first appear on his ringing the belL He rang, and the chambermaid came up, to whom he abruptly said, "Get yourself ready, and go with me to be married." The girl, treating the affair as a joke, re- fused, and withdrew. He rang the bell a second time, when the cook appeared, to whom be said, "Well my girl. I intend this day to make you my wife; go and dress yourself in the beat you have, and order the coach to be got ready immediately." She took him at his word, dressed herself, and on coming downstairs was met by the chambermaid, who asked her, "Where are . „ . _ .
• 66 you going. Abroad," she said. "I have my master's leave." She had scarce uttered the words when her

master came down, and took her by the hand to the le•ge -hie, &aye to St uoent's Church in London, ecatrci - • - • - . **where theY Were 'Pitt uwon, it said, was singularly happy. Bow TO SAVE DOCTORS' BlLLS.—Never go to bed *kb I cold or damp feet. Never lean with the back upon anything that is cold. Never begin a journey until the breakfastt, has been eaten. Never omit regular bathing, I for unless the skin is in regular condition, the cold will I close the pores and favour congestion or other diseases. , When hoarse speak as little as possible until the hoarse- ness is *recovered from, else the voice may be per- manently lost, or difficulties of the throat be produced. Merely warm the back by the tire, and never continue keeping the back exposed to the heat after it has become , comfortably warm; to do otherwise is debilitating. Keep the back, especially between the shoulder-blades. ' well covered. The chest should also be well protected. In sleeping in a cold room establish the habit of breathing through the nose, and never with the mouth open. Never stand still in cold weather, es- pecially after taking a slight degree of exercise. When going from a warm atmosphere into a cooler one, keep the mouth almost closed, so that the air may be warmed . by its passage through the nose ere It reaches the lungs How A ROBBRR WAS CAUGHT.—There WAS a young woman left in charge of a house during the absence of ' her master and mistress in the country. One night on her going to bed she took a good look in the Making- glass and said to herself, smiling complacently, "How handsome I look in this cap !" When she rose in the morning she found the house robbed. She was taken into custody on suspicion of being concerned in the rob- bery, but on being tried was acquitted. Some time afterwards, as she was walking in company with another servant girl, a man in passing said softly to her, " How handsome I look in this cap !" This expression forcibly struck her mind, and she at once concluded that he must he the man who had robbed the house. She seized hold of him with the utmost courage, and assisted by bey companion held him fast till he was taken charge of bf the police. The man confessed that he was, indeed, the robber, and that he had heard her use the expression when he was hiding under the bed previous to his rob- bing the house. Lobbing was a hanging matter in those days, and the man subsequently paid the penalty ol his misdeeds on the scaffold. NERVE.—A number of Englishmen were on a tiger- hunt in India. The beaters hail been at work for some time when a shut was heard which meant that a man- eater was making towards the sportsmen. All hands

put themselves into psition to rec'eiye the attack. One of the company describes the ineetinT, which ended ' with an adventure which no one was expecting,. Lieu- tenant Farrington was on my right, in lino with the mouth of the gully. and not more than 20 feet from my elbow. He had a double-barrelled rifle of heavy calibre, while I had a repeater. In three or four minutes after the cry of warning the tiger appearecl in the mouth of the gully, head on to Farrington, and looking him straight in the face. " Bold on! De's my meat r shouted the lieutenant, as he brought his gun up, and it became a point of honour with the rest of us to hold our fire. He took cool and careful aim, but the bullet simply touched the skin between the tiger's ears. The beast dropped 'like a Stone, tut was up in an instant, and with a roar to shake any man's nerve be sprang forward at the lieutenant. In the tenth of a second I turned my eyes to the oflicer, and what was my hosror to see a serpent twining itself about his! legs and rearing its head to a level with his shoulder. I. forgot all about the tiger, and for the:first time in my life nay blood seemed turned ,to ice. Farrington stood with his left foot ahead and his right foot braced, and as the tiger touched the ground ph- his last spring the rifle spoke again, and the beast calieci pver with a ball through his brain. Then, while we all kept our places like so many blocks of stone, he .dropped his rifle, Seized the snake "just below the head with his right hand, and cared walking towards us. The serpent writhed and twisted ia its rage, and as it un- coiled itself from the man's leg, he flung it thirty feet away. It was rushing back at hint, when one of the party with a shotgun blew its head off. 000 d shot!" 'remarked Farrington, as he walked back and piked up this rifle. We ran after him, and shookhis head, and lhowered unstinted praise on him for his nerve, but he itot be, a hero. It was the presence of the ;serpent which ha 4 disturbed his first aim. The Pope has opened the library of the Vatican to the public. The library contains one of the most valuable collections of old MSS. in existence.

The Prince of Wales is to go to Hungary in September, when he will he entertained by Counts Festetics and Kalnoky. After shooting for a few days on their estates, he will go on to Bucharest, to invest King Charles with the Order of the Garter.

Sir Edwin Arnold will not leave Japan until Sep- tember, though he may possibly visit Honolulu next month. It is said of him by one who knows that `. the truth and earnestness of his study into Japanese institutions during his brief sojourn, is really marvellous."

The arrangements for Mr. Gladstone's visit to Midlothian are now complete. He will arrive in Edinburgh on 20 Oct., and on the Saturday follow- ing will address two meetings—one in Dalkeith and another at West Calder. The people of Glasgow also want Mr. Gladstone to pay them a visit.

Nothing could exceed ,the German Emperor's amiability while on his visit to the Queen, and his evident desire to be very gracious and pleased has delighted his grandmother. The Prince of Wales surpassed himself in his attempts to make every, thing go off well, and he succeeded marvellously.

The authorities of Christ Church, Oxford, have rudely shocked the hopes of a number of Etonians of birth and title, who went up for matriculation, and thought they would get in as a matter of course. The eldest sons of peers and baronets and even an ambassador's son have been informed, that unless they can do better in October, there will be no rooms for them in Christ Church. Eton is astonished and disgusted, but Dean Liddell is firm.

"Why," " P.N." asks, "do railway magnates and hotel managers persist in labelling certain carriages and rooms thus: 'Smoking room," smoking car- riage,' and lately smoke room,' instead of the simple and true description smokers' room,' smokers' carriage?'" We do not know, any more than we know why people generally—" F.N." pro- bably included—prefer" dining room " to " diners' room," "reading room" to "readers' room," and so forth.

The New York Central Railway, the scene of the great strike in America, is the leading highway westward from the American metropolis. It is one of the richest railways in the States, and is owned by the richest men in the country—to wit, the Vanderbilts. Mr. Chauncey M. Depew, who was recently in London, and is now on his way home to help to fight the strikers, is the manager of the line, and is also a millionaire. The stoppage of the traffic on the "great four-line track" will be a very heavy loss to the company.

Mr.Duncan,the editor of the "Matrimonial is a tall, rather good looking. mat], with A white beà and moustache, which give him a patriarchal air. His office at the " Matrimonial News" is a set of miserable, scantily furnished rooms, furnished— save the mark—with a bed, a table, and a chair or two ; in fact, they look as if Mr. Duncan slept there. The editor of the " Matrimonial News "is in the habit of talking of his wealth to his clients, but it is doubtful whether he is anything like as rich as the jury seemed to think him.

Here is the specimen of the way in which we are educating our masters in the year 1890, twenty years after the passing of the Education Act ; it is a correspondent of the "Standard " who supplies it;—" The 'School Board man' called at my place of business, and requested that a certain boy should be 'paid off,' so that he might return to school, as he was not of the full age, nor had he passed the required standard. The boy sauntered up to the timekeeper's office this morning for his 'pay off ticket' coolly smoking a cigar."

M. Chaudoin, a Frenchman who, has recently been a captive in Dahomey, give&- this picture of the cruel king. He is about 40 years of age, and an admirable type of the negro. With a good figure, though only of medium stature, he has an open and intelligent face, a frank expression, and does not wear ally of the tawdry finery generally associated with negro sovereigns. We feel that we are in the presence of a man, and not of a grotesque monkey, and lie is dressed in the plain and sensible costume of his warrlOhz, while hie attitude is proud and digni- fied. He has a clear, deep voice, and articulates his words distinctly.

Young Mr. Arthur Walter, the manager of the "Times," evidently intends to put some life into the all but moribund paper. It was he who had the foresight to send a special correspondent to Buenos Ayres to await the result of the financial crisis. The " Times " got thus ahead of all its con- temporaries, and its graphic descriptions of the revolution were copied by every paper in Europe. The difficulties of telepraphing were enormous, and so was the cost. The tariff was seven shillings per word, so that a column of eighteen hundred words would have cost the " Times " six hundred and thiity pounds.

Mr. and Mrs. Stanley are enjoying a short stay in Paris, on their way to Lucerne. A Paris Correspon- dent says that Mr. Stanley is not looking unwell. He had the other day the satisfaction of seeing his book on the Dark Continent in the windows of all the booksellers he passed. Some French geogra- phers called upon him. The explorer told them that, whatever • might be thought of the Anglo- French Agreement, it was better for France to have England for a neighbour in Africa than Germany. Mr. and Mrs. Stanley also received calls from the gentlemen of the British Embassy.

Mr. Patrick O'Brien is bent on making the poet Swinburne's life a burden to him. On Tuesday he made the Attorney-General say that it was an in- dictable offence to incite to the murder of foreigners, and quote the cases of trials—including that of Most--under the Acts. Unfortunately, the Speaker —who seems to have the poet Swinburne under his especial charge—would not allow the .obvious ap- plication of this ruling to the Tyrannicide Ode. So Mr. Swinburne is balked of his martyr's crown again. Mr. Smith won't read him—will only pub- lish him—and the Attorney-General won't prose- cute him. Is a poet's life worth living at this rate?

Sir Edward Watkin is evidently bent on "improv- ing" his property on Snowdon; but the improvement is not to take the form of a railway. His offer of a Site for an observatory has been declined by the Royal Astronomical Society, on account of the scarcity of the Society's funds: Sir Edward, how- ever, not to be daunted, is going to build an hotel in a commanding situation, and intends to convert the present path to the summit into as much of a road as is practicable. These improvements will perhaps restore to Snowdon some of the glories which have departed from it since the terrible rumour was started, after the recent survey, that I Cardinal Llewelyn overtop it by a few feet,

Sir Chatles Edward Pollock forms the subject Of the cartoon in 'the last "Vanity Fair." The writer of the accompanying sketch says :—" The Pollocks are a large family, and most of its members Having shown that they know how to take care of them- selves, they are supposed to be a clever family also. Two generations ago, one David came from Scotland to Piccadilly, where he sold his wares to the South- ron, accumulating much money and many children. of whom two were sent to law, with the result that one became a Chief Justice in Bombay, and another a Chief Baron of the Exchequer. To this Chief Baron were born some score of young Pollocks, who are known by their severely legal faces and by their legal and other successes.

The lists of the intermediate examinations in medicine at the London University afford further demonstration of the ability of women in this brunch of study. Miss Ann Francis Piercy, of the London School of Medicine for Women, occupies the most prominent place in the honours list. She has obtained a first-class in the three divisions of (1) anatomy, (2) physiology and histology, (3) materia medics and pharmaceutical chemistcy„ VI the former of these divisions there ari."ordftWO first- classes taken, and Miss Piercß, (pjacedAlcond, i awarded a gold medal; in the secautl.divisban she i bracketed with two other succes,ful candidates and in the third she is the first of six c9ndi4ates taking an exhibition and, a goldimedal. TM§ iv remarkable record.

John Boyle O'Reilly, whose death is announced this week, was born at Douth Castle, Comity Meath, and he bad a very remarkable career. At eighteen he was a soldier in the Hussars ; in 1866 be was sentenced to twenty years' penal servitude for Fenianisni. When in Millbank Prison, he spent his time in working out geometrical problems on the

floor of his cell. He was sent to West Australia te• complete his term of imprisonment, but escaped and went to America. His first position was sub-editor of the" Boston Pilot," of which paper he afterwards became editor and proprietor. He latterly became best known by his poetry. He had unquestion- able poetic genius, and some of his smaller poems— known all over the English-speaking world—are perfect gems. He is one of the most picturesque and poetic figures in modern Irish history.

Lord Granville is looking forward to an angling holiday in Bulgaria. It is a country not much known to English wielders of the rod; but it has plenty of good sport to offer, for all that, both in lake and river. There is a particularly fine salmon- trout to be taken in some of tributaries of the Danube which has been likened to the " sewin," well-known to those who have fished South Wales waters. I have heard in my time wonderful stories of the size of the fish taken in the Bulgarian rivers. The " hoochan," the " shill," and the " forgoache," which range from forty to seventy pounds, ought Ito give the Waltonian's right arm some work to do. But what do our trout and salmon fishers think of the Bulgarian" deek "and " shaden," which—when they happened to be blest witrt a constitution like that of the English peer who is now preparing to tackle them at the ripe age of threescore and fifteen —will, It is said, often attain to three hundred and jifty pounds weight in the scale, . _— There is more than a touch of affectation in a good many of the obituary notices of Cardinal Newman. Very few, comparatively, of those who are talking and writing so fervently about him to-day ever read a line of his writings or have more than the most shadowy acquaintance with the facts of his life. A brilliant and accomplished politician asked me not long ago if I recommended him to read Newman's works, and if I thought he would like them. It was a question which, with all the will in the world to be civil, it was difficult to answer politely. The members of a college which produced the late Cardinal, the present Dean of St. Paul's, and Mat- thew Arnold are not without justification when they boast of "the Oriel style." It is a style pre- eminently hard to characterise, or define, or even describe; but perhaps its chief "notes" are perfect clearness, absolute ease, an entire freedom from pomposity, and a courageous use of colloquial Eng- lish, so homely as to be almost slang.

RUBY V.O. CHAPTER It was a dull October morning, chilly and grey. A mist hung as a white shroud over hill and vale. A few yellow lea es'—Nature's tears—fluttered sor- rowfully from the almost skeleton trees. Nature was mourning, for the year was dying—dying. It was a morning made for partings, and partings were abundant in Monkford. There was scarcely a home in that barrack town but was saddened at the departure of a father, brother, or lover. Many were the tears, few the smiles, in. poor dwellings as in great; and with good reason too, for the gallant —th was to march that day for Plymouth, thence to embark for Africa. On the steps of Monkford Hall, a slim, fair girl stood gazing sorrowfully down the drive. Her fingers were tightly clasped as she neived herself for the coming wrench, which was to part her from him whom she loved best on earth. But one short week ago she had promised to be Arthur Penmore's wife, and now—ab, it was ter- rible! Her mournful reverie was soon interrupted by the sound of approaching footsteps, and a groom came in sight leading a high-spirited horse, whose trappings and g•meral appearance marked it out as every inch a soldier's. It was a splendid creature, perfect in wind and limb ; its red-brown glossy coat shone and glis- tened, its sensitive nostrils quivered with excite- ment as the distant sound of the drum smote upon the ear; it marched in perfect time as though un- consciously to the strains of music. At the sight of the horse the girl ran down the steps and stood at his head. " Ruby," she said sadly, "Ruby." He turned to look at her with his soft, brown eyes, and then put his nose comfortingly and confi- dingly in her hand. A dumb sympathy, but far more effective than words at such a moment. As by a sudden impulse she threw her arms round his neck (they were very old playmates) and laid her cheek wearily against his, while with a stilled sob she whispered— "Take take care of him, for Whinnied, by way of a promise, a step Do"stauhkytieb's csraek him' was heard behind them, a strong arm was thrown around Dorothy, and a passionate kiss imprinted on her brow. There the three stood—the horse, the soldier, and the girl. They were well accustomed to each other's company ; they had walked, ridden, almost talked together—for Ruby's eyes were ex- pressive even to speech—and now they stood toge- ther for the last time, while the sad autumnal wind blew round them, and the mist grew thicker. Eager words were spoken; for one moment Dorothy clung to her lover's embrace, then mock- ingly up the drive floated the strains of "The Girl I left behind me," and the moment of parting had come. "I must go, my darlie- " 'This-at-A arthur, pas- "°P. ft stave s'heart for my sake and, emumstety ; II iheeans e lieC4 tood; e e oarnwae nbtaoc kr e t ut or n yfoot ag rt one last kiss. A moment after and he was gone. The tramp of horses and men died away, and all was still with the silence of despair. Stunned with grief, Dorothy stood rooted to the spot; and the wind moaned sadly around, tossing the dead leaves pettishly, seeming to chant one gloomy refrain, "Gone, gone, gone !" Which is the harder part—to go forth to tight, to win a glorious name, perhaps to die a noble death ; or to stay be- -I:jtid, to wait, to watch, to pray, maybe to bear a lifelong sorrow? CHAPTER II,—" TWO." What a blessing it was when the sun at last sank, and a light breeze sprang up. The day had been hot, breathless, and in South Africa the heat was almost unbearable. Those two solitary riders, though still far from the British camp, sighed with relief as the sun set, and it grew darker and slightly cooler. If I remember rightly, I have not described Cap- tain Arthur Penmore, or you would hardly have failed to recognise him in one of those two horse- men. lie was a tall, well-built man, dark and handsome, with the kindest, bravest eyes it has ever been my lot to see. Dauntless in courage, courteous in voice and manner, he was a soldier, and a geatleman. His companion, a brother officer, was handsome also, but in a "fair' way, with true Saxon hair and merry blue eyes. They had ridden far that day on an important missiun to a distant part of the British camp, and now three miles of dangerous country lay between them and their journey's end. The men were fagged and the horse's jaded, but they kept up bravely, cheered by the thought of rest. "Soon home now, Maxwell," said Arthur cheerily, as they neared the top of a slight hill. Even as he spoke, from a cluster of trees, about two hundred yards away, came a puff of smoke and a sharp report, followed by another—and another. At the second shot Ruby stopped still and shivered, the ball had struck his leg. At the third Arthur reeled in his saddle, for his arm was shot through. Another bullet forced Ruby, writhing with pain, to gallop on a few paces; but a touch and a word from Arthur soon brought him to a standstill. Biting his lips to keep down a groan of agony, Arthur wheeled his horse to look for his companion. The first bullet had done its work well. Maxwell lay stretched on the ground, while his horse in wild career was fast disappearing in the darkness. Ruby saw it all in a moment, and a touch of his master's spur was hardly needed to send him tearing back to the wounded man. Sick with pain, increased by the motion of riding. Arthur slipped from his horse's back. "Are you hurt, Maxwell?" "Shot through the leg: don't mind me—save yourself." "Nonsense," said Arthur, helping him to rise; "Ruby can carry us both." Slowly and painfully Maxwell was dragging him- self on to the saddle, when a well-aimed bullet struck the horse in the neck—the Boers had started in pursuit. • "Ruby," whispered Arthur, patting the horse's neck, "try, old fellow, for Dorothy's sake." Then he pulled himself up behind Maxwell. Two wounded men on a wounded horse! what are they against unwearied, fleet-footed enemies? Still there was hope it Ruby kept up, though who could expect it, wounded as he was in three places? But he trotted ,bravely on in the gathering gloom, , with a jolting motion almost unbearable to Arthur, who supported on his arm Maxwell's unconscious form. And now darkness came to their aid, while their pursuers shot at random. One more report and Ruby stopped with a groan. "Cowards' muttered Arthur, longing for a free arm and a well-loaded pistol. Then the 'firing ceased, and Ruby stumbled on, now almost falling, then recovering himself at the sound of his master's cheering voice; and may one think that the thought of Dorothy helped him to keep up nobly to the end? How they managed the last few yards Arthur never knew. I think he must have fainted, for when he opened his eyes they were holding brandy to his lips, and Ruby's head lay on his knee. Arthur seized the flask and poured the rest down the horse's mouth. The dying creature opened those soft brown eves of his. A last farewell he could not give, it word of love he could not speak; but his last look was one of perfect trust, saying—to Arthur if to no one else—" I did it for love of her." It was not pain that made Arthur's eyes grow dim and his lips quiver as he was supported into the ambulance tent. Men are brave to bear great pain, they are tender-hearted at the sight of a noble devotion.

div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

"He would be a Gentleman. or Treasure Trove" is the title of one of Samuel Lover's novels which has been published by Messrs. F. Warne and Co. en their Crown Library series. It is needless to say that the novel of such an eminent hand is not only readable, but racy from beginning to end. No- body better understands the Irish character the* the author of "Handy Andy," and nobody has a happier way of bringing out its humorous features, The story gurtipp cic4l. with the rNne of 17A and is al VA aaveniure lent; DAIL' ;ea. It is a book of 450 pages, handsomely bound in cloth, and is published at the price of 2s. "Musical Groundwork" (2s. 6d.) is also published by Messrs., F. Warne and Co. It is a "First manual of musical form and history for students and readers." It is from the pen of Mr. Frederick J. Crowest, author of "The Great Tone Poets " ; "Phases of Musical England " ; "Advice to Singers," Sze. It is not a large work, and still it covers a great deal of ground, as may be gathered from the following heads of chapters—" Ancient Music" ; " Notation" ; " Scales, clefts, and bars " ; "Time and Accent" ; " Melody "; " Harmony " ; "VoCa; ;Music"; 'lnstruments and Instrumentation ' ; " Musical Form" ; and "Schools of Music." Mr. Crowest has something thoughtful, pertinent, and authoritative to say upon all these matters, and he has the art of putting things in a clear and intelligible style. No person who is interested in music can fail to benefit by a perusal of this important work. There is an index of unusual fulness, and the book becomes further valuable for reference by contain- ing a chronology of the principal events in musical his- tory, and an alphabetically arranged list of eminent musicians, with their birth and death rates. _ .

I In the Great Writers" series, published by Mr. Waiter Sete, we have "The Life of Lord Byron," by the Hon. Roden Noel. There have been many lives of the great poet, from Moore's downwards, but it is due to say of the present issue that no more interesting one has been presented to the public. Every detail cannot, of course, be given in a shilling volume of 200 and odd pages, but nothing of moment is omitted, and all the points and stories, both for and against Lord Byron, are fairly stated. The life is followed by a biography by Mr. J. P. Anderson, of the British Museum, with a chronological list of the poet's works. The reader is pre- sented, too, with an hitherto unpublished poem by Lord Byron, called "The Monks of Athos." The current work in the Camelot series, also published by Mr. Walter Scott, is" The Ethics of Aristotle ; Chase's translation, newly revised, with an introductory essay by George Henry Lewes." The translation, it should be stated, is accompanied by explanatory notes which are given at the bottom of the pages, and are thus especi- ally handy for reference. The introductory article by Mr. Lewes admirably prepares the reader for a right consideration of the "Ethics." Distinguishing between

Bacon and Aristotle, Mr. Lewes says "Ban endea- voured in particular facts to trace the general laws; Aristotle endeavoured in particular facts to trace the general ideas." The student of the " Ethics " will be struck throughout with the carefulness of statement, and what may be called the modernness of the sense. The rule which Aristotle laid down may be well observed to-day, when he remarks on an occasion of doubt—" We must wait for further phenomena, since phenomena are more to be trusted than the conclusions of reason."

_ The August issue of the "Westminster -Review " abounds in good things. The first article is on Mr. Stanley's new book, and proves to be careful in sum- mary and pointed in criticism. Speaking of the cruelty and murder which result from ivory hunting in Africa, Stanley says—" Every tusk, piece' and scrap in the possession of an Arab trader has been steeped and dyed in blood. Every pound weight has cost the life of a man, woman, or child." The subjects of the other papers are--" Lunacy Law Reform, "Life in Achill and Aran," "Cremation at Milan," "Divorce, does Scripture forbid it ?" "The Nevr Educational Code, will it work ?" and" Home affairs."

The current issue of" The Century " is published as the Midsummer holiday number for 1890. The frontis- piece is a charming re-production of "Madonna and Child," by Bottieelli, and in the magazine itself there is an article on this Italian master by Mr.J. Stillman. The paper by John Muir on "The treasures of the Yosemite" is fully and splendidly illustrated. It sets one longing to see scenery which is truly sublime. The delightful autobiography of Joseph Jefferson is continued, with its striking portraits of eminent men, and there is a further instalment of " An artist's letters from Japan," illustrat- ed. Other illustrated papers, &c., are—" A Provencal Pilgrimage,"" The women of the French Salons," " The perils and romance of Whaling,"" Anglo-Maniacs," and "A Yankee in Andersonville."

Lippincott's" commences, as usual, with a complete I novel, the one in the present issue being "What gold cannot buy." It is from the pen of Mrs. Alexander, authoress of the " Wooing o't." Amongst other con- tents may be mentioned papers on " Lawn tennis for women," "Harriet Beecher Stowe," " Thorold's anti- slavery and reform papers ;" "My Aunt's Cat," &c., concluding with " With the Wits," which is, as usual, cleverly illustrated. In " Scribner's " the leading paper, which is capitally illustrated, is " The Paris of the three Musketeers," by ,E. H. and E. W. Blashfield. It is preceded bya carefully I finished frontispiece of " The Exquisites of D'Artagnan's Lime," as Seen in the Gardens of the Luxembourg. "How Stanley wrote his book "is a well written article from the pen of Mr. Edward Marston, publisher. It is appropriately illustrated, and accompanied with fac- similes of Mr. Stanley's notes and drawings. " Gal- legher "Is the title of a racy and brilliant newspaper story by Mr. Richard Harding Davies, and it is followed by another excellent complete story, entitled "Sergeant Gore." • Other papers and verse are up to the high aver- age of this high-class magazine. " The English Illustrated Magazine" has for frontis- piece a portrait of an Italian Nobleman, from a picture by Moroni, in the National Gallery. There is a capitally illustrated paper on" Heligoland, from which we re- cently gave a number of extracts. "An August Ramble down the tipper Thames," is from the pen of Mr. Regi- nald Blunt, with numerous illustrations engraved from photographs taken by the writer. Lady Fairley Cunning- ham contributes an illustrated article on Cowes Castle, and Mr. William Morris continues his singular story of " The Glittering Plain ; or the land of living men." " Horncastle's Manual," written by Mr. W. R. Horn- castle, is a useful book for all connected with companies. It may, in fact, be regarded as a standard work of refer- ence for anything relating to companies and the forma- tion of companies. It contains a chronological list of last year's companies, and a paper on joint-stock enterprise of 1889. " Walks in the Ardennes' is admirably edited by Mr. Percy Lindley, and contains valuable information re- lating to cycling, driving, boating, or travelling by rail and on foot, with fishing and shooting notes, and some capital pen and ink sketches by Mr. J. F. Weden.

One of the greatest trials of patience is a stammering barrister examining a stuttering witness in the presence of a deaf judge.
A loving act'does more good than a fiery exhortation. What mankind needs is not more good talkers, but more good Samaritans. .

div.head: CHAPTER 111.-" UNITED."
div.p: CHAPTER 111.-" UNITED."

It is spring again, the birds are singing, the trees are fresh and green, a sunny smile spreads over the whole earth. Again we stand at Monkford hall; but bow different now are circumstances and sur- roundings! Then it was cold, bleak, mournful—now it is warm, sunny, gay. Then, we wept at partings—now all is bright a ith the joy of meeting. Let us follow Arthur and Dorothy as they first pace the nut-walk, and then seat themselves beneath the spreading elm. Who cannot guess what loving words were breathed, what tender looks exchanged, in that first blessed time together! But see, at last she half draws herself from his arms, and looking up— "l should like to hear about the Victoria Cross," she says gently. "I do not call it mine," he answers, "it was Ruby who deserved and won it, and I always call it his.' So he tells her the simple story of the horse who died doing his duty, and as he tells she lets a bright drop fall upon his hand, and it glistens and sparkles there.
his a tear for Ruby's sake.—By AMY WILSON, in "The Newbery house Magazine."

"YOU'RE not going to turn your back upon me, George?" It was a heart appeal to his old love and tender- ness which she had betrayed; and yet Lucy did not seem to think of the injury she had done. She wanted help, and did not hesitate to stoop to ob- tain it. But Collier turned away from her, and sat in silence looking over the railway. "George," she continued, approaching, but not touching him, "George, don't scorn me, for I cannot bear it. I'd rather lie down upon the rails there and be killed than think you despised me. For bld times, the happy, days—" "Old times! Ain't ye ashamed to come hero talking of old times and happy days? Who made them unhappy to remember? Who but yoursell turned my love to bitterness and ran away? And now you come back-- Well, never mind how. Who can tell whether you are married or not ? "
"I was—l am marired. Oh, George, don't be so hard! You are the only person I would come to. My husband—" A violent expression rose tci George's lips, but he controlled himself.

"My husband took me to India. He, I thou,ght, deceived me; and when I found he was not an officer as I fancied, I rebelled. He is—dead I be- lieve—killed b e• and now I have come backxt(o4lePoyOur paidon, and die most likely." (~orge looked at her as she spoke, and she per. ceivPd she had made an impression upon him. She was pretty and neat, and her figure, moreire;dll`.al and matronly than of yore, would have been con- sidered good by competent judges. There was a caressing look in her eyes as they met his, and his stern gaze softened as it rested upon her, for had he not loved—did he not still love, this woman, and here she was again by his side, almost touching hi He stood up beside her for a moment, and then with a sudden movement put his arm around her. She was startled but made no sign. Correctly :ha had es imatcd Collier. She had played upon the old strings—his devotion and his former passion. She had created sympathy for herself, and might yet obtain his assistance in her views and plans. So she did not shrink from his embrace.

He clasped her tightly to his side and felt his heart beating fast against ter boson. What if she were free she rrlightin iime be his wife, so pretty as she )I and so much better in her manner-; I quite a lady. Lucy made no reslstanc i e., S-;vas I passive in his clasp, but her pretty head . just-as t were unecrscio,usly-,droppecl a little to his broad shoulder's, -ant. nereteey they, es met his pleadingly. So pleading that George understood - appeared to ask him not to them at once. They -,ntance, but to treat her take act-raptage of her rep.. if he chose. He was well because be might vitt but, • as if to do so- sorely tempted fo kiss her, and tla4, -ot venture, she never-preventing him; but he class. and hedet her go. • She was disappointed, and a shade of AnnoYMICO crossed her face. She had counted on that, for she knew George Collier's nature, and felt That she might win him by permitting a caress, for Nslich she did not care the least, except inasmuch as \he might be attracted by it, and do as she required him to do. A pupil of the Syren Vivien was Lucy Layton. Collier released her with a jerk; and, as a man of his temperament might be expected to do, he kept at a distance now. He would not trust himself within reach of the woman he still loved, for he felt he might offend. But he did not know how much she wished he would offend, so that he might he made submissive; but all of course within most proper bounds.

"I suppose I'd better go. I don't know what people will say if they knew I was here. I can, perhaps, get a bed at the inn, though it is late." "Yes, the house is pretty well closed up by now," replied George, standing helplessly aloof, wishing to be, but not daring to go, near her. "Ye can't remain hero, Lucy." "No, and the child wants looking after," sho answered.
The child !—Layton's child. George had quite forgotten that. She was a wife and mother; what business had he to kiss her or to love her now?

The mention of the child brought all his manhood back to its proper channel, and George Collier was himself again. He had been very nearly carried away, but the old love had been put aside. Lucy perceived what was passing in his mind, and her better instincts recognised the restraint which he put upon himself, though it was no part of her tortuous policy to permit him to go scot free. His care and protection—his assistance at any rate—was necessary for her, and she determined to make use of him.
"Whore am I to ga, then ?" she asked simply. 'Of course I can't go to your house, but father—"

"No, I suppose not,. he answered, scarcely heeding what he said, as his attention was taken up by his duties. "No, ye can't go to my horse," he added, more steadily; "there would be fine gossip." "What do I care for gossip," she said. "And now, George Collier, I've something to ask of you; nobody tells me truth about it. Where's father ?" "Your father? Jack Raymond, d'ye mean? Why, don't ye know, Mrs. Layton ?" "Know—what? Don't call me Mrs. Layton. George. I don't know anything-. I went to find him, and ho wasn't at home."' " Yes; he is at home," repned George, solemnly. "Be is at home. He'll never come back here again. He's dead." " Dead ! Dead! Oh, George Collier, ye don't mean that? Tell me now-- at once?"

She was greatly excited and perplexed. He remained silent, and in the few moments which elapsed, the whirring noise of tho blazing gas was distinctly heard by both. "Yes, he was killed on the railway the very night you ran away with that soldier." "Yes. Go on; go on. God help me!" "Well, that fight—three years ago, nearly, I suppose it saw a ghost—an appearance." "A ghost!" gasped the woman. "Go on." "Yes, two ghosts," he sail. "One was a femaTo figure; the other a man, or the appearance of a man; and they paseed the line yonder by the tunneL What's the matter?" Lucy had turn( d as white as a sheet, and sank down upon the bench in terrified silence, After a minute or two she again locked up. Her face was ashy pale; her eyes were starihg into vacancy. The child she held in hr arms uttered a plaintive, exy, and sho.ronsed her:self to quiet it.

"Well ?" she said, hoarsely.. "Ye frightened me, that ye did," said the signalman. "I never thought ye believed in ghosts any more than ze. Howsomdever, poor old Jack he sees them, and he makes across the line to find out whether they were the appearances he had seen before, ye remember?" "Yes, yes, I see it all now. Oh, father, father, I've killed you! It's a judgment on me." "You're off your head a bit to-night, I believe," remarked the signalman, not very sympathetically. "What had ynu to do with it Ho never knew ye runned away. Bill told me. Be saw ye. All, he did."

"And told father? It kill& him_ Oh, father —poor father !" "Killed hint! No. Mc train killed him. He was huntin' for those 'appeanancee and the fast goods '—that very one as is a, comin' up presently— Joe Brown was drivin' it—come out of the tunnel and knocked poor Jack over. He didn't suffer, poor chap. It was all done in &wink like. It wasn't your fault, Lucy."

'The honest guileless man even then attempted to console the woman who had so reuthlessiy wrecked his life, and who had caused her father's death. " Don't touch me," she alm.st screamed. "I tell you I killed him. There was DCP ghost. Frank and I crossed the lino many a time, and we did it that night too." This fact took time to, penetrate to George's brain. Stubborn things, like facts did, as a rule, take time to reach his mind if they were unconnected with the railway bud. its signals.

But in a moment or two ho perceived that the " appearances " were due to Lucy and her lover. George Collier turned away, and looked out at the door of the signal-box.. He was not in a mood for love now.

It was a lovely night, nearing the witching hour. The stars glittered overhead, and winked through the gathering moisture. The moon was setting already, and only a faint gleam was in the sky. All was blue—a beautiful sapphire blue—and not a breath of air was stirring. There was a noise of some kind borne to the signalman upon the air. It came from the direction of the " shops " some distance away, 801 had not Collier been certain that nobody was 1110.01 y tg. bring

out a locomotive at that hour,. he would have fancied that an engine was. slowly coming up the line. He listened for a second or two longer, and the noise increased in ever-rising loudness. Ho hurried down the steps to the metals, and lay down upon the permanent way, with his ear upon the rail. "Good God !"' he muttered, "there's something coming up, and I've had no warning. It's not a. special; it isn't fast enough. It ain't a 'goods;' it's not heavy enough. It's an empty engine, I'll bound !•" An empty engine! There was nothing very alarming iman engine without a train; such engines are known on the railway as "empty," but th& time and the mysterious manner of its slow approach, quite unannounced, puzzled the man. "It's curious, by Jingo!" he said, as he rose and ascended the steps. Then taking his lamp he left his signal at danger, and leaned out as far as 10 could to get. a look at the intruder, and hail the driver. There was no mistake about it. 'An engine was coming along the lino, tender first, at a slow speed, but increasing its pace as it proceeded, as the signalman's practised ear detected as soon as the locomotive came round the curve.

"Whatever is the matter ?" inquired Lucy. ik Anything wrong, George l'" He made no answer, and she relapsed into silence and distressful thoughts. Collier was hanging out his lamp. The engine came on, unheeding the red danger signal in the lanthom and on the semaphore.

It approached with a gliding,. ghostly motion; the great wheels revoli ing almost noiselessly it seemed. No steam issued from the valves; no whistle sounded through the trees and awoke the echoes from the hill behind them. A thin stream of smoke and steam rose from the funnel, and the Phantom Engine glided on. "I never saw the like of this," said the terrified signalman. "It doesn't look natural. Who's below ?" he shouted, as the engine approached, the) beat of the huge connecting rods being imperfectly audible,

No answer was returned. The huge mathirie, glided on majestically, and never slackened alai:ea)). er was any whistle sounded. The signals Yew) dead against the driver. "Hullo !" shoUted Collier, leaning,. %at of the window. "Pull up, man. Stop !" There was no reply. With unetb•jted, even with increasing speed, the engine ll' ed on dark and weird in the starlight, and. 'disappeared in the shadow of the tunnel.
There was a lad lying onA;:he footplate. The engine was a runaway from the s 7 ,ed. So much George Coils.er saw—no more.
V..tAPTER XIV. TERRIBLE RIDE

Hz had scarely time to warn the next box, when he heard tlr.i fast "goods " approaching. A sudden thought occurred to him. Ho wq eve that the goods lar,d two engines attached, rindtlipifor,4a.rg know, went no farther than N—. If ho could get t det d, the runaway might be caught before y mischief was done. ianor:l; He blocked the line at once and called Lucy. "Can ye stand by the instruments for a bit ?" asked. "Ye used to know them."

"I remember them well," she answered, seeing that something was wrong and she might help. "Yes I can signal well enough." "Then wait there till I come back," he said. "Mind the child; put him on the floor." "It's a girl, George," she said, as she laid the infant in the corner, well wrapped in a shawl. " She's fast asleep now." '-- had she turned when the fast " goods " drew mare4'lot 2 sl tunnel, and pulled up in response out Yr to George's sigfifil, "Here we aro, stopped again," shouted the man who wets clpivinj4 the foremost engine or "pilot." " What' s the matter to-night ? I believe this Cutting's bewitched" "Did ye pass an ?" inquired George. "A big one, tender first, b'c'in' slow. "Aye, and says' to I,IY mate, I says, that's tha 'Watson.' Didn't Ir rml? assented Fred, who did "Yes, we both says it," not wish to be left out of de, question and discovery. "We've no time for taria.lg," replied Collier; "uncouple your pilot 'and le follow him up; thes governor's eon is aboard of it, INsaw the gold band on his cap." "Young Master Ectard on that hi:"; engin", why she'll drag his arms off if he tries to, am, her. Lord A'mighty Fred, take up." "All right," replied the active Fred- 4" Here's a pretty row. Step the trains behind nay..a.t:d we'll pick him up. Ready, mate? " "Aye, aye. Stand clear, Gearge." "I'm goin' with ye. I've got a mate lie the box all right. Now, rim to the cross-ever, and I'll pub ye erross to the up-line." The engine rapidly reached the points, and with the hand-lamp George signalled to the hal:. and Lucy rapidly changed the points from the box. "They've got a pretty bit o' start,'""remarked the driver, as he put on the steam and pulled up his lever. "These goods engines ain't as speedy as they used to be." Scarcely were the words' spoken when the tunnel was gained, and in two minutes the engine had: emerged at the other side, and pulled up) to inguirze whether any warning/had come from the- next box ahead at the station two mires away. "No," replied the man; heard notling pass. I suspect ye're all on a wild goose chase—a phantom engine like the old story rny grandfather told about a ship—" "Tell it to-your grandmother," retorted Tallier. "I saw it with young Master on it." "Go on, then; ye're all clear. I'll protect ye," said the old man, not meaning to usurp the• func- tions of Providence, but intending- to stop alit fol- lowing trains. Again the chase was renewed and this timercon- tinned. The small wheels of the goods engine were revolving at a tremendous, pace—a rate they had never been intended to rum—along the level, rattling and roaring; along the embankment, catilt- ing a glimpse of the dawn, and then plunging into a cutting in which the the was reflected, and seemed to surround the engine as in a conflagration. Then again emerging as the banks on each side sank down with a rapid roar, and gave place tb, fields, the furrows in which leaped, across from side to side, and the fence raced the engine to the end of the field, till it came to a sudden stop, and held ibc breath as the rapid locomotive disappeared again. It was a terrible ride, and none ok the men on the, pursuing engine knew how far or how fast the run- away might have run. A curve was rapidly turned after. about fifteen minutes' racing, and a long piece of straight lino, terminating in a sicepish gradient, led into the Great llamble Station—a busy place, with chimneys and furnaces roaring, wheels whirring, and much clanking of great hammers day aucrnight. "We shall get a glimpse of her now," said the engine-driver. "If we can't catth her up on the level, she'll kill somebody sure as cl atb." "Is the mail due, George?" asked the firdinan. "What has the down mail to do with it," he replied. "We're on the up line" "This much," sontinued the fireman. "There's cross-over points near hero—. By Jove there's the mail, and we can, perhaps, race the Watson.'" "There she is,"-exot4uned George, unheeding the fireman. "Now let us wire in and catch her. up."

"I say no," interposed the fireman. "Look here, mate, you knows as well as me that we can't catch up the runaway on the down grade. We must catch her before that and keep her fast, else she'll run ahead even at her present speed." "What do you mean then—be quick ?" "Let us hurry to the points ahead, where she is about now. Cross over, get the lino blocked, and run in on the down line and, pull her up. There's a whistle, listen!" ,; "Good for you, Fred," was the driver's reply, and, with a rash of steam, the " goods " engine soon covered the intervening ground. The runaway engine was nearing the top of the incline on the up line. The men proposed to cross to the other metals, and ran alongside them to catch the loose engine. George Collier ran up into the box, and told the signalman. Altering the points, and blocking the line between them, these two men waited the result. The engine sped on now at a furious pace, and a regular chase began. The huge locomotivs had all this time been going leisurely„ but, just as it had passed the long curve a somewlaat rude shock had released the break, till then partly on the t,nder wheels, a.nd had awaked the lad lying upon the footplate. He rose stap;gering to his feet, and gazed dreamily around. What did it mean? His first idea was that it was a terrible dream, but the increasing pace, the regular beat of the pistons, the rattle of the tender, soon aroused him to a scnso of his position. The engine had got loose. It was running away with him "What's that! A whistle behind him. The shrill sound thoroughly awoke him to his danger. He had no idea where he was, and expected almost instant death. But the lad had presence of mind enough to blow the whistle and to try to shut off the steam. But the regulator was new and stiff. It would not move. He could not close the valve! The whistle was heard, however, both bv the =suing

engineers and by the men near the Great 11 arab e Station, where some consternation was felt at the already signalled approach of the Phantom. ' Preparations had already been made for turning, the engine into a siding, but the news from the ast box that a boy was en the footplate-, changed these , ideas, and the line was cleared, while an engine wai already moving upon the other line ready to start at speed and grapple it. However, all these precautions were happily un- necessary. The boy was surprised and daighted to hear the goods engine gaining upon him, and though he could not shut the, regulator valve, ho was able by tremendous effort to pull back the lever and so reduce, the steam a little in the cylieders. This effort was almost more than he could :9..c00nl- - plish, but fortunately practice stood him in good stead, and in a few miles more the engines ran side by side. The driver of the " goods " engine thee went fore ward, and, biding his time, leaped upon the broad plate and buffer-beam over the front wheels of the. new engine. In a moment he had gained the foot- plate, and, with a powerful arm, had wrenched, back the regulator valve, and all danger was over. . • • "Thank you," said the lad, firmly enough. • '; will not forget you. What's your name The driver told him, and then as t'ne two engines were brought to Great Hamble as quietly as if nothing had happened, th,e boy, inquired how they had ascertained he had been adrift on the loco- ' motive. "It was George Collier as saw you, sir. Ile noticed it and stopped our train, and then my mate, Fred, here, he said vr) had better run across and , alongside of ye, apP,J. then—" "You risk s&; our life to stop my runaway horse," , 'interrupted t)'e lad. "Give me your hands, friends; / think Lte,e promise you something handsome for , Pabio'sery. Where is Collier?" 413, I'.,y told him, and, then the" young engineer reted upon taking the engine back again, piloted the goods to the shops. They had run full thirty miles in about thirty-five minutes. "Pretty smart going," remarked the young man; the last bit was speedy, eh?" "Yes, sir. Ye went easy at first, but when we got r on the grade it was a mercy as we cau_eht ye up, replied the driver. "But how could you leave your signals, Collier? Won't any harm come of that ? " "I left a person in charge," replied the man, reddening. "Quite accidentally an old friend, who's used to signals, came, and he—ehe I me3a-15 in the box." As soon as the tunnel had boon cleared and the

familiar cutting recained, the signalman and the young man ascended the steps and found Lucy standing at the instrument quite self-possessed. The 'lovely bttle girl was sleeping peacefully beside the great signal levers. Young Watson advanced and thanked her, and

then stiijod gazing at her and th 9 little girl—a 'well- Prwrbarleitth ono year old. As he looked the child awoke, and, opening her tiny arms? Fre at the comely face of the boy, though now his Ikul was not free from dust. "How curious!" he exclaimed. "There is quite a likeness to somebody I know. Who is it, I wonder? Thank you," he continued, turning to Lucy. "I am much obliged to you all. Good- night. I will see you again. Good-night." Lucy's heart fell when she heard him speak of the likeness. The boy had seen it, too. The child was like her father, Colonel Deane, and Edward Watson knew it. This was the first fruit of her deception ! (To 14 continued.)

BRUTAL MURDER IN MINCHESTER.

The Manchester police have in custody a labourer named Thomas Cosgrove, charged with the murder of s young man, aged 21, named James Ashton. It seemS that on Saturday night, between eight and nine o'clock, the accused, with other men, was in a beerhouse at the corner of Oswald-st. and Tame-st., Ancoats. The house was kept by Ashton's mother, and a game of dominoes was being played in the tapvoom. A dispute arose be- tween Cosgrove and Ashton as to the payment of a quart of beer. Shortly afterwards Cosgrove, at the doo.t of the beerhcAise, drew a large clasp knife from WS pocket and stabbed Ashton in the chest. The latter felt to, the ground, bleeding profusely, and was conveyed 00 a. litter to the Alienate Hospital, where it was found NY had already bled to death througit the severance of a' main artery. Cosgrove was at once arrested, and after, [wards charged wits the. crime, but the police will not istate the nature of hisreply. A verdict of wilful mar- !der was returned bya coroner's jury at Manchester, on, 3lbnday, against Ccegrove.

LORD. HARTINGTON ON THE GOVERN-- RENT' FAILURE: The Liberal Unionists-in. the Rossendale diviAbn ou Tuesday held a picnic at Chatsworth. Daring tho-mord-' ing meeting; was held, and was addrelsed by Lord Hartibgton and Sir Ffenry James. Lord Harting,ten, iw accepting an illuminated address presented to him hY Mr. Thomas Brooks, expressed regret at the delay thet. has taken place in the passing of the Tithes Bill, thel Irish Laud Pirrchase Bill andla, Local Govestiment Dal for Irefamd„ but said thit that delay was not ducto: any fault on the part of the Government, but to the obstructive tactics of the Opposition. It was for tne electors to insist that the Opposition in the House of Commons should be fairly conducted. The failure . to legislate did not prove any incompetence on the part of the Government, for,. apart from legislatiwn, the Government had a great deal of work to do, and tlle/: had accomplished it successfUlly. The Government that maintained peace abroad,, and at the same time protected the interests of the Empire in every part of t.h,,.° world, and maintained our great establishments with , efficiency and economy, deserved more credit than the ,Government which, neglected these important administra- ,tive matters, even if it succeeded in placing on the statute book measures which would long be spoken of and remembered. The failure to Imes the princiP!,l measures of this-session did not arise from any defect IC the principle of those measures, and he did not despair of them being ultimately passed into law. Sir lienrY James spoke hopefully of the position of the Liberal -Unionist party, and said that whenever the time of danger came again, an. it would come, then fresh strength would accrue to their party:

In the House-of Commons, on Tuesday, Mr. Caleb Wright said :I beg to ask the Secretary of State tor the Home Department whether he has now received from the incumbent of the parish. of Holy Trinity Ashton-in-Makerfield, an acknowledgment that it has been notifiedlo the inhabitants that breadths or graves are appropriated in the churchyard " °DIY on condition that, no other than the Church of England service is ever used," and whether the in- cumbent has been informed that such an intimation is opposed to the intention of the Legislature as - indicated by theZturial Act of 1880.—Mr. MattheWs: - The Rector does not deny that the condition 1.?,q ot• ed is attached to certain charges. made for particu- Tar interments, but in all the cases where sucliA condition is appended the burial, would be accorce• ing to the rites of the Church of England, and in none of them was the Rector asked to apply the provisions of the Act of 1880. The Rector holds that he has an absolute power to order the positiont of every interment, and moreover that he canno be compelled to sell or appropriate a grave to Or' one. These are questions of law as to which it tis not my duty to offer an opinion. I have written .0 the rector-to say that in my opinion to stipulate beforehand that a grave where the Church ssrvieva is used shall be in any respect superior to a gras where the Church service is not used aPPears• cop_ trary to the spirit of the Act of 1880. In replY tc! Rector assures me that in his. church yard all graves are alike as to position, and no one grave is- in auj sense superior to another, whether the Church England service is used or is not used.

div.head: INDIAN BUDGET.
div.p: THE INDIAN BUDGET.

The House w;sii-itTo-comm-itiee on-the East India Revenue accounts.—Sir J. Gostor *aid he had nothing but a dull and prosaic tale of prosperity to unfold. The surplus which was estimated in the Budget in March, 188 D, was RxloB,ooo. Although the -salt-tex was 'no doubt one which ought to be removed as-soon as it was financially possible to do so, he thought the increased consumption would encourage the• Government to give thetirst place to the restoration of the famine insurance grant. The enhancement of 'the Fan duty ,eught only to he regarded as a temporary measure. 'He thought thaton the whole the finances of ffndia were in an en- couraging condition, and that theyenight •contemplate the ,future of that country with hope antkiheerfulness. (Hear, hear.) Mr. BRADLAUGH, who had the followinponstion on the paper, "That the late date of presentatiom'of the ac- counts and papers relative to the revenues of India, renders it impossible to satisfactorilvevmmine and discuss the Inclan financial statement," said it seemed to be the desire cf the Government to lessen year bryear the time at the disposal of the House for the investigation of the affairs of 270 millions of people. lie thoughtit positively disgnaseful that the Indian Budget, which -in the year 1873 was considered important enough to occupy three days' time of Parliament, should be brought forward at a timelike this. _ _ . .

div.head: SHOWER OF FROGS.
div.p: A SHOWER OF FROGS.

An extraordinary phenomenon has taken place in Holywell. During the heavy rain on Wednesday,morfi- ing tens of thousands of small frogs descended t from the clouds on Holway-road just outside the town. For a distance of 200 yards the road is completely. covered with the little creatures. The incident is causing 'much interest and speculation in the neighbourhood.
THE 3.IILITARY INSUBORDINATION AT

CHATHAM. • fVhe insuborditnatioi manifested among the men of the.army servieecorps at Chatham last week was fol- lowed on Saturday by a serious outrage. On the har- ness room being esamined on Saturday evening, it was found that every particle of harness had been out to shreds. The men were confined to the barracks, when it was found that time men harl deserted. The outrage is supposed to be intended as a protest against the alleged excessive Sunday duties. The outrape was discovered at sunrise on Sunday by a patrol. The premises which were forced were in full view of the sentry on duty iu the Batrack-square. It was soon afterwards found that a number of men had deserted, some taking their kits and accoutrements. Three of them, Thomas Smith, W. Runacres, and W. T. Williams, all drivers, are under suspicion of being concerned in the outrage, and a full description of them has been circulated throughout the country.

• SHOCKING TRAGEDY IN LINCOLN- SHIRE 'DOUBLE CHILD MURDER AND SUICIDE. At'Thurlby, near Bourne, Lincolnshire, on Monday evening, Charles Holliday, a labourer, who had been i away from home engaged n harvest work, returned to his house and found the body of the woman who lived with him as his wife hanging to a beam in the kitchen. He searched for his two children, aged respectively eight years, and six months,and found them in bed with their throats cat. Use coroner for the Spalding division of Lincolnshire on Tuesday investigated the circumstances of the tragedy. The woman, Hannah Hall, was, it appeared, much addicted to drink. She was left on Saturday night because of her drunken habits. At an early hour on Monday morning she murdered the two children., and then hung herself. The house was not entered until Monday night. Holliday waS overcome With grief when he found his children had been mur- dered. The suicide was 33 years of age, and had children living in London. The verdict was one of " Wilful murder "against the mother.

div.head: LIBERAL CONFERENCES IN WALES.
div.p: LIBERAL CONFERENCES IN WALES.

, The South Wiles Liberal Federation held two confe- rences on Wednesday, at Builth, Breconshire. At the morning meeting resolutions were passed in favour of Home Rule for England. f3cotland, and Wales as well as Ireland,and supporting reform of the land laws. At the afternoon conference the principal question discussed was Disestablishment in Wales, and a resolution on the subject, which was carried, was vigorously supported I by, among others. Mr. Osborne Morgan M.P. I Speaking at Builth, Brecon, on Wednesday night, at a meeting of the South Wales Liberal Federation, Mr. Mun- della said that Wales would now have £lOO,OOO for educational purposes, and it would be the fault of her people if they did not raise her to the highest educational pinnacle. Disestablishment, which involved the solution of all other Welsh questions, would be effected after the Irish question had been disposed of. (Applause). Mr. T. Crompton seconded the resolution, which was supported by Mr. T. B. Royden, M.P., who also congrat- ulated Lady Gerard upon the largeness of the attendance. He said it showed conclusively that the old spirit which had in the past animated South-west Lancashire still remained, and that the inhabitants were true as they were of yore to the great Conservative party. (Hear, hear). Speaking to the resolution he said they could point with pride to the many acts which had been placed upon the statute book during the last five years by her Majesty's Government, acts which must tend, and which have been admitted in most instances by their opponents would tend, to the happiness of all classes of their fellow subjects. (Hear, hear.) (Applause.)—The resolution was put to the meeting and carried unanimously.—Air. W. Valiant next proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. T.W.Legh, for his services as member of the division in Parliament. He referred to the popularity of Mr.Legh in the division, and assured them that he had not heard a single indivi- dual make a complaint against him since he had been their member. He was warmly respected by his own people, and esteemed by his opponents. (Applause.)— Mr. Naylor, a workingman, seconded the resolution, which was carried with acclamation. Mr. T. W. Legh M.P., on rising to respond, was -received with loud cheers. He said he thought the gathering that afternoon went far to disprove the asser- tion that the Unionists represented a broken and discre- dited cause. They were told that they did so on the authority of no less a person than Sir William Harcourt. (Laughter.) Of course they all knew that everything he said was invariably correct. (Laughter.) If they repre- sented a broken and discredited cause he was proud to represent a discredited cause—(hear, hear)--because he considered that the career of the Government, of which he happened to be a humble supporter, would bear favourable comparison with that of almost previous Government in this country. They were elected, as he supposed even their opponents would admit, upon the question of the Union. What was the case now? Did they hear much about Home-rule? They heard next to nothing about it, because the question had been practi- cally settled; but they heard a good deal about temper- ance legislation and about eight hours' bills and various other subjects which were of no particular moment. They, however, heard uncommonly little about Horne-rule. In fact it appeared to him there was only one man in the country who showed any keenness for Home Rule at the present moment, and that was the Grand Old Man him- self.' If they were to ask Mr. Gladstone what he meant by Procne Rule, to save his life he did not think he could tell them. But he had got Home Rule permeated in his system, and to every query that was propounded to him, he answered, "Home Rule." (Laughter.) He thought even Mr. Gladstone must be getting tired of being obliged to preach Home Rule to an unwilling audience. Home Rule was certainly no nearer than when Mr. Gladstone first took up the idea; in all probability it was further off. He claimed that the present Government had up to now done remarkably well. They had experi- enced checks; there had been checks at by-elections, as was invariably the case, and there had been checks in the House of Commons. But what did a check in the House of Commons prove? It merely broved that their opponents by an elaborate system of obstruction were able to impede their legislation; but was that a reason for putting them into office? According to their own views it lwas their duty :to turn the present Government out and put Mr. Gladstone in. It was true the Government found themselves in difficulties because they were unable to pass their licen- sing proposals, and the origin of their difficulties was that the Government, through the ability of Mr. Goschen, found itself in possession of a large surplus which he did not know how to apply. He (the speaaer) was quite certain Mr. Gladstone and his party would never be in a similar difficulty, because they were not in the habit of finding themselves in possession of a surplus. (Laughter and applause.) Before very long the voters would be called upon to make their choice' aid he asked them as -fair-minded men to forget the aright difficulties the Government had experienced, and on the other hand to remember the good they had done, and to remember the "iincreased prosperity that had attended this eountry dur- ing their tenure of office. If they would bear those , things in mind, they would not, he thought. hesitate as to the verdict they would again give, and their verdict, If he mistook not, would be in favour of the men who were pledged to maintain the unity and integrity of the empire. (Applause.) On the proposition of Mr. M. Rowe, seconded by Major M‘Tear, a vote of thanks was accorded to the speakers, and votes of thanks were also passed to Lord and Lady Gerard for granting the use of the park and grounds, and to the chairman for presiding.

div.head: PRIMME LEAGUE pEIiONSTRA.TION
div.p: PRIMME LEAGUE pEIiONSTRA.TION

AT GARSWOOD. ; A successful demonstration under the auspices of I the Garewood Habitation of the Primrose League ' ' was held in Garswood Park, on Saturday afiernoon. Lord an Lady Gerard had kindly thrown open the rich and extensive Park for the occasion, and, for- ' tunatety, the gathering was favoured with fine I weather. The central meeting place was the , Ashtonin-Makerfleld Conservative Club, and here a procession of Primrose Leaguers and their friendS was 'formed. About S,OOO persons took part in the Idemerettration, including contingents from Wigan, Earlestown; Newton, Golborne, and St. Helens. The processionists were headed by the St. Thomas's (Ashton). Brass Band, and then came the lady- demonstrators. The male contingent were headed by thO Downall Green Brass Band. The procession wended its way along Gerard-st. and Lodge-lane to the •ontrance-gates of Garswood Park, where a Isplelidid large portrait of the late Lord Beaconsfield wassuspended. Lady Gerard, dame president of the 'Habitation, received the processionists at the ,entrance to the Park, and the large concourse of people weetenducted to the portion of the Park where a plat- fornahadteen erected. A public meeting was held, a report of which appears below. Afterwards the crowds dispersed to enjoy various attractions. There were three bands in • 'attendance and they played alternately for dancing—a form of pleasure which seemed to meet with popular favour. An interesting i feature of the demon- stration was a show of flowers n a tent erected for the .purpose. 'Plants and flowers had been kindly lent by Lord Gerard, Dr. Street, Major Walinesley, Mrs. Banks, antlddr. Clarke. Prizes were awarded for the best pro- ductions of amateurs and cottagers, resident in the district, and the winners were Messrs. W. Wood, C. Hayes, C. Houlton, R. Haut, and G. Lowe. The prizes AISO included two for the best boquets of wild flowers, collected by children .under fourteen years of age, and these were won by Misses Ellen Sixsmith and Mary A. Zeitleins. An amusing competition Was the climbingof, a greasy pole, 35 feet high, for a leg of mutton placed on the top. The champion " climbist " proved to be W. Asidey, of Sutton whose feat in taking the mutton from the pole secured Sutton, him the plaudits of the onlookers. Other sports included flat races, and a half-mile donlieb, race.' It was estimated that over 5,000 persons enterea, the`Park during the afternoon,and the entire proceedings' were considered to be an encouraging success. "The public meeting was attended by the vast majority atthese present. The chair was occupied by Major B. 'Reif, the ruling councillor of the Garswood habitation of , thitLeague, and he was supported by the Hon. Lady 'Gerard (Dame President), the Hon. Mrs. Gerard, the Hon. Robert Gerard, Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P. for Newton 'Division,lMr. T. B. Boyden, M.P. (Liverpool), Mr. W. HAL Tomlinson, M.P.' for Preston; Rev. W. .1. Mel-, ville-(rector of DownallGreen) ; Rev. H. Siddall (Ash- ton) -, Major Meteor (St. Helens) ; Captain Walntsley, Captain T. E.Withington, J.P. Messrs. T. H. Pearson, U:r4 (chairman of the Newton Conservative Association); Stapleton-Bretherton, J.P., H. S. Woodcock, T. Cromp- ton; W. Valiant, and M. Rowe (hon. sec.). Letters of , apology for non-attendance were received from the lion. W.,111. Cross, M.P., and Mr. W. C. Jones, the Conserve-, tive candidate for Leigh division. Among those present inithe park were Messrs. Joseph Robinson (St. Helens); G. B. F. Borron, R. H. Wright, J. E. Pardey, G. Clarke and Captain Royse (Newton-le-Willows.)—Major Relft orebehalf of,Lady Gerard, extended a cordial vrelcome •to the representatives present of the various habitations' .of the Southwest Lancashire Association. lie then: called upon Mr. T. U. Pearson, to move the first resole- ction.-aMr. T. H. Pearson, J.P., who was received with i -warm applause, then moved—" That this meeting of the•Garswood and neighbouring habitation of the Prim= rose .League and other Conservatives and Unionists of the Newton .Division of Lancashire, expresses its lin- s.bated cotfldence tin her Majesty's Government, and oongratulates Lord Salisbury and his colleagues on the -isaecess os 'their administration whereby peace has been •maintained, taxation reduced, the defences of ,the -empire increased, contentment and prosperity spreading in Ireland, and trade generally has im- proved throughout the British empire." (Appismse.) 'Ho remarked that success had ttended the present Gov- ernment in every department. (Applause). Owing to 'Lard Saliabeiry's foreign policy, they were now at peace, with all thoworld. He thought they should more par- tionlarlv congratulate his lordship upon the recent settle- mentwith Germany, which was eminently satisfactory, and,had cemented an alliance which was of the greatest importance toiboth nations. (Applause). Then, under thetable administration of Mr. Balfour, the condition of 'lreland was improving day by day, and this was proved by the fact that dewing last year the convic- tions for outrages were only 85, while during the time thatireland's destinies were governed by the Grand Old Man—(laughter)—the number amounted to 14,000 in one .year.
