div.head: BREACH OF PROMISE ACTION.
div.p: BREACH OF PROMISE ACTION.
£lO.OOO DAMAGES.

A breach of promise action, in which Miss Gladys Enemies, 21, sued Mr. Leslie Fraser Duncan. editor of the •"Matrimonial News," for moo damages was de- cided At Lewes, on Tuesday. The plaintiff deposed that on her.visiting the "Matrimonial sews" office the de- fendant offered her marriage. They became engaged, and she visited his house' Gray Court, Ham. A few days before the marriage was fixed to take place, lie entered her room, but she ordered him out, and when he took her to an hotel next day, she declined to stay with him alone. Be renewed his promises to her mother, but he did not carry them out. At the conclusion of her evi- dence the plaintiff fainted. Elizabeth Knowles, the plain- tiff's mother, deposed that Mr. Duncan offered to make a marriage settlement on her daughter of £1,500 a year.— The jury found a verdict for the plaintiff, damages £lO,OOO.

div.head: STRIKE IN WALES.
div.p: THE STRIKE IN WALES.

IThe situation in South Wales continues to increase in gravity, though earnest effmts are being made to bring about a compromise between labour and capital. The I Cardiff Chamber of Commerce passed a resolution, on Tuesday,in favour of establishing a Board of Conciliation, and an intimation was received from Mr. Ben 'Ellett, on behalf of the Dockers' Union, to the effect that co-oper- ation in such an object would be cheerfully given. The mails were, on Tuesday, despatched in brakes by road, and travellers had recoluse to whatever vehicles they could find. Meanwhile, the coal, iron, and tinplate trades in the Welsh valleys are becoming more and more paralysed, and it is estimated that the loss to the com- munity has reached £50,000. An application for the loan of police-constables was on Tuesday submitted to the Watch Committee of the Liverpool City Council, and it was decided to reply that none could be spared. Although no absolute proof is forthcoming that the labour crisis in South Wales is passing away, there seemed to be a more hopeful feeling on Wednesday as to the speedy termination of the dispute between the rail- way men and their employers. Much inconvenience is being caused by railway communication being stopped and supplies at many of the country shops are running short. The signal-box at the junction of the Taff Vafe and Rhymney lines at Cardiff was burnt down on Wed- nesday morning. At first it was supposed that the fire was the work of an incendiary, but investigation showed that it was probably accidental. THE DISPUTE ENDED.—TERMS OF SETTLEMENT. The negotiations for a settlement of the great Welsh railway labour dispute were resumed at Cardiff, on Thursday. The joint directors met early in the fore- noon at the Park Hotel. The Rhymney, harry, and Taff Vale Railways were strongly represented. Mr. Inskip, chairman of the Taff Vale directorate, again presided. The point which the directors had to consider was whether they would give to Mr. Inskip full powers to treat with Mr. Harford, the men's general secretary. A favourable decision on this matter would, it was believed, lead to a settlement, for both negotiating parties were known to be averse to the prolongation of the struggle. At two o'clock a note came from Mr. Inskip to Mr. Hat- ford, in which the writer said "1 am glad to inform you that I have been authorised by the Joint Committee to meet you upon the terms of the workmen's proposal of the 11th inst. and your letters of the 11th and 12th, and I beg to propose that the meeting take place at the Park Hotel at two o'clock this afternoon; and it the notice is too short I will ask you to name the .time as near that hour as practicable." The men received the announcement with much cheering. Mr. Darford ar- ranged that he would meet Mr. Inskip at three o'clock, and the Directors adjourned till after the confer- ence between the two representatives. The con- ference between Mr. Milord and Mr. Inskip lasted three hours, leading railway officials being at hand to assist, if necessary, on disputed points. At five o'clock the official intelligence was spread abroad that terms of settlement had been arranged, and that they would be made public at a later hour. This announce- ment was received with an extraordinary public demon- stration of satisfaction. The agreement provides that the railway companies shall pay for a week of 60 hours, subject to the condition that the men will not be paid overtime for the period lost during the monthly holiday, but as heretofore over- time during the holidays of Easter, Whitsuntide, and Christmas will be paid for. On the Taff Vale Railway the hours of pilot enginemen and shunting men are to be eleven hours per day, with six hours per week allowed ' for meals. This represents a total of 60 hours per week. The time for signalmen is to Le twelve hours per day, with twelve hours in the week for food, which again re- duces the hours to sixty.
WE CAN ONLY SAY THAT HIS INITIALS.
ARE "J. D."
, When a woman travels ten miles merely to ask a few questions, we may assume that her curiosity is excited.

In the year 1883, a story went forth from Leverstock Green, Hemel Hempstead, Herta, which aroused great interest in all the region thereabout. People came from various directions to inquire into the matter; what Wad alleged to have occurred had to do mostly with ene man. If the story turned out to be true, some good was likely- to come of it; if false, it would only put the community more on their guard against all sorts of wild rumours. Among the women who were bound to get at the founda- tion ot it was one from St. Albans and a cook from Langley.

How strangely things work out in this queer world. Seven years have passed and the facts are now to become generally public for the first time. It appears that about the first of January, 1883, an old resident of the place above named was said, and commonly believed to be, in. a dying condition. For five months an able and clever physician had been attending him constantly; no medical man could have done more. His ailment was decided to be gout and rheumatism, which are now held to be practically the same malady differently located.

Well, this began back in July, 1882. As time ran along the patient grew worse. The doctor's ability and experience didn't seem to count. The sufferer's ankles, feet, and hands became badly swollen. We all know this must have been a scary symptom, because that the fluids of his body (and the body is nearly all fluid any way), instead of being carried off as they naturally should be, were flowing over their channels and inundat- ing the parts around them, just as a stream does after - heavy rains.

The doctor said the danger of this state of things lay in the fact that, when the water reached the heart or lungs, it might end in sudden death. The cause of dropsy is the refusal of the kidneys to carry off the water; so much is plain. But what makes the kidney's strike work? We now know the reason of that. It is because they are partially paralysed by a poison in the blood, arising from undigested pod in the stomach. In plain English a chronic state of indigestion and dyspepsia was responsible for results which now threatened our unknown friend's life. It was reported—and of it's truth there isn't a doubt—that his abdomen was blDwn like a bladder on account of the water which soaked all through his flesh. In conversation, a few vieeks ago, he said, "All my friends now looked on me as a dying man." And reasonably enough too ; for what chance is there for a man who is gradually drowning in this way ?—For that is what it was—drowning, and nothing else in the world. Medicine appeared to be of no use, and the phy- sician suggested that possibly the poor man might be benefited if he could go away from home and try the baths, mineral waters, and change of scene and air. But nobody believed in that plan ; and in honest truth, it is hardly likely that the wise physician believed in it himself. At all events the idea wasn't put into practice. About this time the patient's Fife happened to be in the shop of Mr. Bass, the Hemel Hempstead chemist, and he gave her a little book, a sort of small pamphlet, and said she might like to read it. She did read it, and found in it a full description of the very complaint that was fast sending her husband to his grave, and also the name of what was asserted to be a remedy for it. After some trouble she got him to consent to try it, and sent to Mr. Bass for a bottle. He began, and kept it up for four months, taking twenty-six bottles altogether. At the and of that time he was a well, sound man, and is so to-day. The whole neighbourhood was amazed. His recovery, when he had been looked upoci as no better than a dead man, set tongues wagging all round the country. He now says: "I should not have been here now if it had not been for Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup." Our friend requests us not to publish his full name, but says we may print his initials, which are "J. D."' Address: Leverstock Green, Hemel Hempstead, Herts- He will answer letters.

div.head: LONDON OUTRAGES.
div.p: LONDON OUTRAGES.

At Lambeth Police Court, on Wednesday, Harry New- man, son of the proprietor of the Sloan Tavern, Peckham Park-road, was remanded on a charge of discharging a revolver at a customer named Robert Winn, who now lies in a critical condition. At the North London Police Court, Alfred Haigan was remanded on a charge of wil- fully murdering William Lambert and Walter Wheeler, by shooting them 'with a revolver. It wil/ be remem- bered that the affair was the sequel to a quarrel in the Wagon and Horses public-house, the prisoner having interfered to protect he landlady from violence.

div.head: TWO CHILDREN POISONED.
div.p: TWO CHILDREN POISONED.

An extraordinary poisoning mystery, resulting in the deathlof two young children named Corfield, living with, 1 their parents in Ardwick, was the subject of a coroner's. 1 inquiry on Wednesday. The mother, whose husband is- a carter, gave the children some pudding made of rice, obtained from a neighbouring shop, and they were taken violently ill, fatal results ensuing in spite of prompt medical attention. The doctor found in the bottom of ' the pudding dish about a spoonful of a white sediment, which has been ascertained to be arsenic. How it got into the pudding is a mystery, and the inquest has been. adjourned pending further irmestigaVon. „ An inquest was Opened and adjourned at Alanches&; on Wednesday, on the two children of a labourer named Corfield, living at Ardwick, who died after eating rice pudding made by the mother. The pudding was found to contain arsenic.

div.head: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.
NORTHAMPTON.

The Conservatives of Northampton have selected Mr. R. A. Germaine, London County Councillor and barrister, as their candidate to oppose Mr. Labouchere and Mr. Bradlaugh at the next general election. Mr. Germaine twice unsuccessfully contested Hoxton.

YGRK. At a joint meeting of the general executive council of the York Liberal Unionist Association and the central council of the York Conservative Association, held on Wednesday night, a resolution was unanimously passed adopting Mr. John George Butcher, barrister, of London, son of the late Bishop of Meath, as the candidate of the joint parties at the next general election for the city.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.
THE NATIONAL LEAGUE.

Mr. John Dillon, M.P., presided at the weekly meeting of the National League at Dublin on Tuesday, and pro- posed a resolution placing on record the profound grief of the Irish people at the death of Mr. John Boyle O'Reilly, an exiled Fenian. Mr. Dillon bore testimony to the worth of the deceased as a supporter of the national cause.

div.head: ARREST OF TEN MEN.
div.p: ARREST OF TEN MEN.

Early on Tuesday morning, ten men, including some farmers' sons, were arrested at Tratnore, West Clare, in connection with the recent shooting into the house of a boycotted farmer. It is reported that one of the prisoners has turned informer.

.RELEASE OF A PRISQ:NER. Captain Tont IV, a umglstrate, who was undergo- ing SentenCe of two moliths' imprisonment, passed at last Cork Assizes for firing at and wounding a labourer, was on Saturday released on account ot the state of his health.
STRIKE ON THE DUBLIN, WICKLOW, AND WEX-

FORD RAILWAY. The strike on the Dublin, Wicklow, and Wexford Rail- way still continues, and neither side shows any signs of surrender. The directors have succeeded in running a fairly adequate service of local trains,and a complete ser- vice of through trains without any hitch. No disturbance of any kind has taken place in connection with the strike. Some more men came out on Monday, but the company declare their confidence in being able to replace them.

The Teryism of the peers is of.the narrowest and stupidest kincl,„and two instances of its °Teets have during the, week been bringing trouble upon themselves and upon the HOUND of Commons. A private measna&known as the Wain Corpo-ation Bill providedfor the municipality of the capital of Ireland doing what every °then Corporation in, the ' Kingdom do, namely, collecting their Own srates. The- Bill passed the House of Coramons without difficulty, but when it reached, the Upper House— the home of ; the Unionists they struck out the clauses giving power to collect rates. This was mere than the Commons could tear they stuck to their guns.; and on Tuesday) the Lords hadto con- sider whether they or the Commons wore to be ' masters in .the matter. There was considerable debate, inwhich the Tory-peers let it be seem how empty is all the talk aboutrthe Unionist desire to extend local government in Ireland. Extension forsooth,. when they were unwilling that thel largest Corporation in should have power to collect their own rates Illorsl Ssisseenx, who weal present; ,saw that if hia supporters cEdnot beat a retreat the struggle -mould be damaging to the Ministry, particularly as the ham SmonErmtv committed himself to the bill as it left the Com- mons.. Ho therefore appealed to the peers, not—we, may remark, to do what they might think was right, from their owmmuddle-headed point of view, but to agree with the Commons bocause,if they, did nott,." a blow wouldd be struck akthe moral credit of-the Government at a moment when the very heavy task before them required the greatest amount of suppo" This ignoble appeal had its effect; their lcodships climbed down—as they have so often done—and the Corporation of 'Dublin are to be allowed to become possessed of the ordinary powers of a Corporation. The other case in which the peers have gone out of their way tor wrong is, with regard,to the bill for the removal of gates across London streets. There are as many as two hundred of these gates in various parts of the metropolis, chiefly upon the Duke of Banroan's estate, and they have for years, by interfering with traffic, proved a, great nuis- ance. As these streets are maintained by the ratepayers, it is a matter of comse to say that the ratepayers should have control over them. If these barred streets have less than a fair share of the noise and inconvenience a traffic, it is obvious that otherstreets must get more than a fair share, with resulting injustice to the inhabitants. It is to enable the London County Council to right this wrong that the bill has been carried through the House of Commons, But the Lords must meddle

and they have introduced a clause which strikes at the very heart of the measure, for it provides for claims for compensation on the part of the owners and leaseholders. The impertinence of this is obvious when it is stated that the Duke of BED' FORD has not raised the question of compensation', and that the leaseholders ought to be out of court because there is nothing in their leases to say they have any title to the benefit of the bars, the Duke being at liberty to abolish them whenever he nlaY think fit. div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
I,

le Ship Canal contractors are like the navvy's ; they are great at "blowing up." They blew me of the bridges near Moore on Sunday morn- and pretty nearly gave the inhabitants fits. tat next? Their incessant blasting operations e been the terror of weak nerves. They have a to answer for. But it will all come right, say, "when the ship lands." The
wife PP nWh g , have deal they

Newton magistrates have an easy way of dealing with certain offences. They simply "bound over" two men who were so bent on fighting that they had to be separated three times; and in another case, where pokers had been used With marked effect, they dismissed the parties. What do they want? Do they wish to see a limb or a head broken before they inflict a fine?

Hypnotism, which is the new name for Mes- merism, is "all the go" at present in certain scientific circles. Dr. Luys, writing on the subject in "The Fortnightly," says :—" The over-excite- ment of the nervous system is such in the hypno- tized person, that you can bring about the symp- toms of poisoning by strychnine, if a small quan- tity of the poison in a sealed glass tube is placed on the skin in front of the neck."

Dr. Luvs infers that the poison is felt through the skin ; but it is more reasonable to conclude that the symptoms are the outcome of suggestion Passing from the operator to the subject; and the result would be the same if the poison tube con- tained water. As a matter of fact, the old- fashioned mesmerists caused their patients to act aS if they were poisoned without bringing any sort of tube into use. It is not new, either, that hypnotism has curative effects in certain cases. Harriet Martineau was cured by a mesmerist ; but the faculty mocked the suggestion of such a thing in those days.

Electro-Homocpathy is the name of another healing system which is patronised by Lady Paget, and practised by Count Mattei. Lady Paget says of the medicines --" He infuses the electric Spark himself ; that is his secret." A "secret remedy !" That is the essence of quackery. There la this much to be said of orthodox healers all the world ovz,r, that they never keep their discoveries secret. They are above that sort of thing. We shall expect to hear that amongst Count lvlattei's medicines there are" pills against the earthquake" —infused of course, with electric sparks. An American poet writing on the subject of Progress and Pain," says :- 0 God, have pity on Thy world: For man through all these thousand years, Battling against grim want and fears, Holding his banner still unfurled Has won the victory in vain, Since progress means increase of pain. tut is this so? Are we really "advancing," in Paddy's style, "two steps backward?" If we are, it is about time this planet were snuffed out.

That "beggars should not be choosers," is a Proverb which is in danger of being worn out. Two of the ancient fraternity were given food, at Sutton Weaver, the other day; but this did not suit them; they demanded tea in addition. But why tea? Why it insist, as Byron has it, on "lobster salad, and champagne, and chat "—with a little music thrown in ? This is a hard world ; these tramps of the new style have actually been sent to prison.

Mr. Stead, in a sketch of the late Lord Camar- v9n, takes credit for having suggested the inter- view which his lordship, whilst lord-lieutenant of Ireland, had with Mr. Parnell. It confirms the statement previously made that the interview -with the Irish Chief as to the government of Ire- land was held with the knowledge of Lord Salisbury. It is very convenient for the Tories and the -Unionists to forget these things when abusing, the Parnellites, but facts remain when memories fail.

1 An ex-policeman named Stanton has been brought before the St. Helens magistrates for desertion of his wife. It transpired that he went away because "a lodger thrashed him, and his Wife said if the lodger was sent away she would go hard also." This was good for the lodger, but 'lard on the husband. It was evidently a case like that of tlio song: She loved her husband dearly, But another man twice as well. The magistrates, under the circumstances, had regard for the husband; they dismissed the case.

There was a period when it could be said that " a woman will go anywhere, at any time, with any Man—in a gig "; but now it must be a steamboat and the place must be the Isle of Man. But oh! the coming back. Returning excursionists at the end of Bank Holiday week struggled and fought for the gangways of the steamer as if they were the gates of heaven—or, as if they were get- ting away from the other place. Luggage was left t? reach home as it could; and as for separa- tions of wives and husbands—the Divorce Court vasn't in it.

Here is an instance of the way Protection works. The French Government insist on a tax of 2s. 10d. from each visitor from England who spends a few hours on the French coast. Result : the daily 'cheap tickets from Dover and Folkestone to Calais and Boulogne have been suspended by the Railway °olnpanies. Business is thus being spoiled on both aides the Straits' for it is a matter of course to say that visitors to France would, if permitted, spend aomethinp..? besides a few hours in France. Protec- tion in this, as in many other cases, is stupid and suicidal.

Mr. Balfour was the principal performer at Bello Vue, Manchester, on Saturday. As he is merely a dwarf, he gets on Mr. Gladstone's shoulders, when- ever he can, in order to be seen. He did this on Saturday, and smight to make it out, as usual, that the leader of the Liberal party was always wrong. Curiously, however, he added that—" In all matters en which the Government had been attacked in relation to Ireland they had faithfully followed in the footsteps of Mr. Gladstone's own Government." Picture'it ; think of it; the Government faithfully follows Mr. Gladstone! Now is the world grown honest.

Speaking at Garswood Park, on Saturday, the 1 Member for the Newton Division "claimed that the present Government had up to now done remarkably well. They had experienced checks; there had been checks at by-elections, as was invariably the case, and there had been checks in the House of Commons.' He did not add that the final check will come when they pass in their Checks at the General Election. However, we raust congratulate Mr. T. W. Legh on being Well up in the " check " system. When he loses his place as M.P., there will be a chance for him a's manager of a 'Bus Company.

Mr. Leslie Fraser Duncan, editor of "The Matrimonial News," seems to have led the life a mean rather than a" gay Lothario" ; but he Ilas been caught at last. He, an old man of 63 Years, has been making love, under a promise of raarriage, to a young lady of 21, under cireum- tances which are the reverse of creditable to I,Linl. As he did not keep his promise, he was 'rolight into court; and the jury gave damages against him to the tune of £lO,OOO. This is el)ralrig down on him "hot and heavy," but the g9neral opinion will be that it "serves him

There is a clever imposter going about who trades on a real or .a sham illness. His latest ex- plots have been at Egremont and Liverpool; but U I'sl ls believed to be the same rascal who has prac- sed on the inhabitants of Northwich and of Penketh. His plan is to assume sickness High 11.„...11to death whilst on his way to some distant place. zte is taken in by good Samaritans, well-treated, and furnished with money on a hint being given tla at he has not sufficient for his railway journey. t Liverpool a ticket was got for him for Scotland; ,1?,11t, on being left by his benefactors, he got out of 'ale train, and converted the ticket into cash by I'leading to the Station-master that he was too ill
to travel. Let the benevolent beware ; and as soon as possible "run him in " for an arrant imposter.

There is now every reason to believe in the truthfulness of the confession, in America, of a murder in Cheshire some 35 years ago. The evi- dence goes to show that the man Blagg, who was hanged for the murder of a gamekeeper, was inno- cent of the crime. He knew who the guilty man was, for he had lent him his boots ; but it would seem that he determined to die rather than ' "split " upon his friends. It is impossible not to admire this trait of heroism; but what are we to think of the miserable wretch, who, knowing him- self guilty, could see an innocent man hanged? It is just possible that he was out of the country when the trial took place ; and that would alter the situation. But he must have had strange feel- ings when he heard of the execution. The mur- derer is getting on in years; and the thought of death has probably resulted in the confession.
LOCAL • NEWS.
CADETS OF TEMPERANCE, RUNCORN.

The members of the Guide of Youth Lodge were treat- ed to an afternoon's enjoyment at Mersey View Frodsham on Saturday afternoon. Various games were indulged in and ample provision had been made for the wants of the young people.

div.head: PRIMROSE LEAGUE EXCURSION FROM FRODSRAM.
div.p: PRIMROSE LEAGUE EXCURSION FROM FRODSRAM.

On Wednesday morning the members of the Frodsham District Habitation of the Primrose League, to the num- ber of 400 persons, left Frodsham at 7.48 in a special train for Llandudno. The visitors had ample enjoyment in the numerous attractions of this queen of Welsh watering places. The members of the league paid an infinitesimal proportion of the cost of the train fare, the difference being generously made up by Mr. Jas. Rey- nolds, J.P., Chief Ruling Councillor, and Mr. E. A. Wright, J.P. ELECTRO PLATED GOODS.—Garland's oldest established Ironmonger, Warrington.—Adut. BETHESDA SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN._

The anniversary sermons were preached in Bethesda Chapel, on Sunday, by the Rev. Mr. Finn of Stockport. In the afternoon a service of song was rendered by the scholars and choir. The attendance at the services was not so numerous as usual owing to the heavy downfall of rain that continued throughout the greater part of the day. Collections were made in aid of the school funds. On Wednesday afternoon the scholars had their annual treat. They were conveyed by train to Frod- sham at a reduced fare, and spent an enjoyable after- noon at Mersey View. MERSEY MISSION'S TO SEAMEN', RUNCORN% The annual excursion took place on Monday, when about 500 persons had a charming sail down the river in the saloon steamer May Fly. A call was made at the training ship Indefatigable, and ,vere kindly shown over the huge vessel by Captain Bremner. On arriving at Liverpool, the excursionists had an opportunity of in- specting the white Star liner Brittanic, and afterwards they were left to spend the remainder of the day accord- ing to their own ideas. A large number visited New Brighton. The passengers were safely landed at Duke Pierhead at 9 p.m., after a most enjoyable day's outing. SUMMER SALE now on at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt.

WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday under the presidency of Mr. H. Wade Deacon. The Librarian reported that during July 4,221 books had been issued, giving a daily average of 279 in the lending department and 156 in the reference department. The attendance at the Library for the same period were 13,259, or a daily average of 491, compared with 497 for the correspond- ing month last year.—Accounts amounting to £52 10s. were passed for payment.—Dr. O'Keeffe complained that the Selection Committee added too many novels to the Library. He contended that they had a demoralising effect, and that the object of the Library was for the purpose of educating the people and not amusing them. —The Chairman said the list of books was laid on the table for the Committtee to accept or reject. The Selection Committee endeavoured to suit all classes of readers, and they were guided to some extent by others free libraries in which by far the larger proportion of books read were of the fiction class. He hoped they would have the benefit of Dr. O'Keeffe' s criticism when the next list was presented.

WOUNDING AFFRAYS AT WIDNES. On Monday at Widnes Police Court before Mr. T. S. ' Timmis and Lieutenant Col, Gaskell, a youth named I William Glasheen, of 10 Caroline-st., was charged with unlawfully wounding a married woman named Mary Dunn, who lives in the same neighbourhood. It appeared that on Saturday morning the prisoner's sister Ann Glasheen, threw a bucketful of dirty water into Mrs. Dunn's house and subsequently the prisoner's mother dragged Mrs. Dunn's daughter across the street. While , the disturbanee was at its height the prisoner came upon the scene with a rolling pin in his hand and threatening that he would "swing" for one of them, he struck Mrs. Dunn a violent blow on the head. She lost a large quantity of blood, and was taken to Dr. O'Keeffe's sur- • gery to have her wounds dressed. The doctor informed ' the Bench that the woman suffered from a contused • lacerated wound on the left side of the head, and another ' I wound half an inch in length. There was also an artery wound. The woman's clothes were saturated with blood.—Mr. Knowles, for the defence, submitted that the prisoner's sister struck the blow which caused the , wound awl he called witnesses to prove that statement ' and it appeared from the evidence adduced that a general melee took place in which stones, brushes and buckets of water were used with considerable effect by both sides.—The Bench committed the prisoner to the Quarter Sessions for trial.—Felix McConville, of 8 Ann- St. West, was charged with unlawfully wounding Ann Morgan, with intent to do her grievous bodily harm. It was alleged that on Saturday evening the prisoner and the prosecutrix's husband were fighting and Mrs. Mor- gan attempted to separate them. The prisoner knocked her down and while she lay there inflicted a serious wound on the head with some sharp instrument. The prisoner was "in drink" at the time. Dr. O'Keeffe said the woman was weak and would not be able to appear for a week. The prisoner was accordingly remanded. Michael Fitzsimons, ot Greenfell-st., was brough up on Tuesday charged with unlawfully wounding Thomas Fisher Butler, of Lacey-st., on Saturday night. Butler was in an eating house in Victoria-road, kept by his sister, when an altercation took place and the prisoner thre* Butler to the ground and then struck him several times with his fist. His left eye was severely injured and on the advice of Dr. Hutchinson he was taken to Liverpool Infirmary. It is feared he will lose the sight of the eye.—The prisoner was remanded until Monday. --On Wednesday, Thomas Porter, labourer, Pear-st., was charged with unlawfully wounding his wife Mary. —Mary Sutton, widow, Pear-st., said the prisoner and his wife lodged with her. On Monday last the prisoner gave his wife 2s. in order to get some food for break- fast and she went out. In an hour she returned in a state of drunkenness. The prisoner asked her where the breakfast was, and in reply she made use of bad language. The prisoner then struck her on the head with his clog and kicked her.—Dr. Nutchin- son said the woman was suffering from a wound in the throat 2i inches long and two inches deep, clean cut. From the position of the wound it was a strange thing the woman was not killed. He did not believe the pri- soner's clog had done it. The prisoner was remanded. Sr. JOHN'S SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. The annual treat took place on Saturday, the destina- tion on the present occasion being Mersey View, Frod- sham ; where a merry time was spent. A " free tea " was provided.

div.p: THE EXA-MINER, S'A-TtTIIDAt, AUGUST 16, 1890.

A BURTONNY-00D FAMILY AT VARIANCE. • At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, be- fore Messrs. T. J. Gillespie, T. H. Pearson, and W. Mitchell, there were cases down for hearing in which William Warburton and Arthur Warburton, respectably dressed young men, were summoned for using threats to their lather John NVarburton, at I3urtonwood, on the 29th June. They were also summoned for assaulting their father on the 11th July, and there was a summons against the father for assaulting his son William on the 11th July. When the cases were called, Mr. T. Swift, barrister, said he had been instructed to appear on behalf of John Warburton, the father, and his friend Mr. Jen- kins, of Warrington, appeared for the two sons. Upon considering the matter, he found that there was nothing in the case which affected the public, and in the interests ot his client he thought that it was not desirable that the matter should be inves- tigated in public. his client had placed himself entirely in his(Mr. Swift's)hands, and he thought it right on his behalf to say that the summonses taken : out by him would be withdrawn, and Mr. Jenkins, on the other hand, would withdraw the summons taken out by one of his clients. He hoped that the parties might go away from the court and if they did not actually shake hands, that for the future there would be some family affection between them, and that they would live together as father and children ought to do.—Mr. Jenkins remarked that he had done what he felt his duty in trying to bring about an amicable solution, and whatever he might think of the merits of his own case, he was prepared to sink them in the hope that the family relations might not be more embittered, but on the , contrary, might be improved.—The Bench said it was a very satisfactory settlement. 11, you value your wife's health see that she uses SUNLIGHT SOAP.'—Advt

THE NEW NORTH WALES STAMSHIP CO. Now that the season is in full swing at Llandudno and Beaumaris, the New North Wales S.S. Co. have arranged to issue weekly first saloon tickets between Liverpool and North Wales at the low charge of 153 , and these 'tickets are likely to be in large demand amongst those people who have friends staying at these places and whom they wish to see during the holidays. The first saloon monthly tickets, issued at 255. from any date, have been largely applied for during the season, and in many cases invalids who had been ordered a long sea voy- age have taken these tickets, and have derived great benefit from their daily excursions on the "St. Tudno."

div.head: HOME IRON TRADE
div.p: THE HOME IRON TRADE

The improvement in the English iron market, of which the first signs showed themselves last week, has extended. The better tone is due to three prin- cipal causes—the favourable nature of the Board of Trade Returns for July, the prevailing labour diffi- culty and impending further troubles, and the re- vived demand for finished iron and steel. As far as pig-iron is concerned, the higher prices quoted are to be attributed rather to speculative influences than to a better enquiry trade in crude iron being still comparatively small. Scotch warrants are about Is. a ton higher, and some brands of makers' iron are also dearer. Middlesbrough pig has been ad- vanced is. a ton, and Bessemer pig in the north- west 2s. 9d. a ton. Lancashire makers of pig-iron I quote from is. (id. to 2s. per ton more than a few weeks back, and higher rates are asked also in other districts.—lron. AN EARLESTOWN YOUTH REWARDED FOR GALLANTRY. A pleasant ceremony took place in connection with the annual treat to the scholars of St. John's Schools, on Saturday afternoon. This consisted of the presentation of a vellum testimonial from the Royal Humane Society, to James Smith, of 51, Sankey-street, and a member of the Bible Class taught by the Rev. E. W. Whittenbury-Kaye. In the beginning of July Smith succeeded in rescuing a child from drowning in a pond at Wargrave, and as this was the second occasion upon which he had been successful in saving life, Dr. Mouncey, of Earlestown, brought his commendable conduct before the notice of the Royal Humane Society. The result has been that Smith has received the society's testimonial ; inscribed on vellum. This testimonial was presented to Smith before the assembled scholars on Saturday afternoon. The ,Rev. T. R. Matthews (vicar), presided, and explained the object in meeting together. Dr. Mouncey then stated the circumstances under which the presentation was being made to Smith, and said it was an award for physical courage, which meant risking one's life for the sake of another. The testimonial, was enclosed in a neat roll, and read as follows " Royal Humane Society, Instituted 1774. Patron: Her Majesty the Queen, Vice-Patron H.R.H. the Duke of Cambridge K.G., G.C.M.G. ; President, His Grace the Duke of Argyll KG., K.T. At a meeting of the Committee of the Royal Humane Society, held at their office, 4, Trafalgar Square, on the 21st day of July, 1890; present,Sir William Fraser, Bart., in the chair ;it was resolved unanimously that James Smith is justly entitled to the honorary testimonial of this society, inscribed on vellum, which is hereby awarded him for having,on the sth July, 1890, gone to the rescue of Abel Jones, who was in imminent danger of drowning in a pond at Wargrave, Lanca- shire, and whose life he gallantly saved. Argyll, President ; J. W. Horne, secretary; and William Fraser, chairman." SUMMER SALE now on at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.

THE SUPPOSED CHILD MURDER AT WIDNE S The resumed inquest on the body of the newly born male child which was found in an ashpit, at bile rear of the house occupied by Mrs. Clifton. 56, Waterloo-road, was held at Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday morning. Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy- coroner, conducted the inquiry, and Superintendent Noblett was present on behalf of the police. The evidence as to the finding of the body by Saul Mer- cer, on the 20th July, was repeated. Annie Quinn, wife of Samuel Quinn, of 60, Waterloo-road, said about 6 o'clock on the morning in question, she found in the yard of her house a boy's cardigan jacket, a coarse piece of wrappering, and an apron. The articles were saturated.—Dr. O'Keeffe said he had mad a post- in,...rtem examination ef the body, which was that of a male child, newly born. The weight of the body was seven pounds nine and a half ounces. The weight of the lungs was two and three-quarter ounces; the left lung was six drachms heavier than the right. The skull was broken on the top of the head. He was of opinion the child had been born alive, but it had practically bled to death owing to the umbilical cord not having been tied. There was no trace of placenta. The fracture of the skull might have been caused before death. There was no trace of food. The child was full grown and well developed.—The Deputy-Coroner said he had been told before the inquest that the skull was fractured, and he had supposed they would have to return a verdict of wilful murder against some persons unknown, but after hearing the evidence the only course open was to return an open verdict.—Dr. O'Keeife said he had never made a statement with regard to the post-mortem until that day. Therefore, he was not responsible for the idea the Coroner had got.—The Deputy-Coroner accepted this statement, and the jury returned a verdict that the child had died from loss of blood, owing to inattention at birth.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. Colonel Ashton presided at the usual monthly meeting of the Board, on Tuesday, held at the Workhouse, at Dutton, when there were also present—The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Mclntyre, E. Aaron, J. Stokes, Brandreth, Llwis, P. Hall, Bate, Dansey (Government inspector), H. Linaker (clerk), H. G. Linaker (deputy clerk), and J. Farrington (sanitary inspector). THE ALLEGED POLLUTION OF THE KEKEWICK BROOK. The Deputy-Clerk read a letter received from the Local Government Board, acknowledging the receipt of a letter from the Authority with reference to the applica- tion of the Sanitary Authority of the Runcorn Union for , consent to the proceedings under the Rivers Pollution Act, 1876, against Messrs. W. R. Earp and Co., of the Tannery, Preston-e-th'-llill, in respect of the pollution by them at Kekewick Brook, and to state that the Board were in communication with Messrs. Earp and Co. upon the subject.—Mr. Mclntyre asked ',whether there was any further communication. It was a very serious matter.—The Clerk ; We cannot take any proceedings without the sanction of the Local Government Board. INSANITARY STATE OE KINGSLEY. In the course of a conversation, Mr. Dansey drew at- tention to the prevalence of infectious disease in the township of Kingsley, and said he thought it was neces- sary that some steps should be taken in that matter. The Clerk.—There is a great deal of insanitary proper- ty in Kingsley. Mr. is alongside of the brook. Mr. Dansey said he could not sit down without saying that he complained about the sewerage and water supply of Kingsley, and he thought the authority should order that some steps should be taken to remedy the defects. ALLEGED OVERCROWDING AT HALTON. The Inspector reported that he had visited certain pre- mises situate in the township, alleged to be overcrowded, but found that some of the occupants had gone away. NEW HOUSES AT HELSBY AND OVERTON. A certificate of occupation was granted to Mr. Wm. Guest for two new houses erected by him at Helsby, and permission was granted to Mrs. Ann Gorst, of Bradley, to occupy four new houses erected by her at k Overton, the certificate of occupation to be withheld until a satisfactory supply of water had been provided.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday. Mr. E. Carey occupied the chair. There were present Messrs. Wright, Brown, Mid- wood, Cook, Neil, Hargreaves, Liddell, Heyes, Houghton, Sadler, Allen (clerk), Sinclair (sur- veyor). --------

- GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. The Gas and Water Committee minutes contained the report of the Engineer, who stated that the mean rainfall for July was 1.9 inches. The water in stock was 8,937,142 gallons. The illuminating power of the gas during the Month had averaged 1913. csindles. yVater- works : Designs for gates and palings at Pex Hill estimated to cost a further sum of £BO examined and approved. Plans &c. for deepening No. 1 well at an estimated cost of £3OO submitted. It was recommended that tenders for the gates and well deepening be advertised for.:—Mr. T. Duxbury having resigned his position as assistant manager at the Gas Works, it was recommended that Mr. F. Thorpe be appointed in his place at a salary com- mencing at £9O per annum.—Mr. Brown moved the adoption of the minuteS and said the Committee had power to spend about £4O on providing gates &c. for Pex Hill, but they could not carry out the work in a suitable manner, and in a style befitting the town; es- pecially when they got incorporated they would want a little more of this work. If the land was made available for the public, the extensive entrance and palisading would be needed. Alluding to the assistant managership Mr: Brown said the Gas Committee kept losing their assistant manrwers who were promoted to managers at other places,evrdently proving that their office was a very good school for young men.—Mr. Wright seconded the motion, which was carried.

SARCASM AND PERSONALITIES. The minutes of the Highway Committee stated, that the members had inspected the greenhouse lately erected by Mr. Beach, at his residence in Milton-road, and regret to say it is an infringement of the byelaws. It was re- commended that notice to remove the greenhouse be served.—Mr. Sadler moved. and Mr. Houghton seconded the adoption of the minutes.—Dr. O'Keeffe moved that the recommendation be left out without discussion.—Mr. Wright seconded the motion.—The Chairman pointed out that if the motion was defeated, the subject could not be reopened, and Dr. O'Keeffe said he would settle the matter then. He considered it a disgrace to any Board to prevent any individual who wished to improve and beautify his property from doing so. There was still 162 feet of open space in the yard, which was more than sufficient, and he contended that the greenhouse should stand. As to the Committee's "regret," it was the most absurd and ridiculous recommendation he had seen.—Mr. Wright said if this was an infringement, there was a large number of more serious infringements in the town. He alleged that this was a thrust at Mr. Beach, and was also intended for somebody else. But, never mind if it answered for that time, it would not answer for long.—Mr. Neil accused the Surveyor of hav- ing acted in the matter without consulting the Commit- tee or the Board.—Mr. Sadler said, notwithstanding Dr. O'Keeffe's sarcasm, the Committee did regret that they could not see their way to let the greenhouse stand, but this was a new building, and under the new byelaws,and there must be six feet of space between the house and the ashpit, which there was not.—The Chairman con- tended that it was an old building, and in his humble opinion, the building was right. He suggested as an amicable way out of the difficulty. that Mr. Beach should convert the ashpit into a water closet.—Mr. .11argreaves said Mr. Beach would be quite willing to do that.—Mr. Sadler said on that understanding he would withdraw the recommendation. Mr. Wright had insinuated that it was brought forward for a purpose. Mr. Wright ought to withdraw that.—Mr. Wright: I shall withdraw no- thing I said.—Mr. Sadler: I have no feeling—Mr. Wright: I have none either.—The Chairman said he could not allow this irregular discussion. It was not right to impute motives in this fashion. He had always found Mr. Sadler to be upright and honourable, and he d!cl not think Mr. Wright intended to insinuate anything different.—Mr. Sadler: But still you cannot get behind the fact that he ins. The incident then dropped. REALTR OF °THE TOWN. The minutes of the Health Committee contained the report of the Medical Officer of Health, which showed that during July there were 106 births and 43 deaths, being at the respective rates of 41'03 and 18134. Twenty- one deaths occurred amongst children under five years. Zymotic diseases caused four deaths and there were four inquests. 26 cases of infectious disease had been re- ported of which 10 were enteric or typhoid fever and eight were scarlatina.—Miss Downie, matron of the Accident Hospital, tendered her resignation, and the Committee recommended that it be accepted and that a testimonial be given to her. Recommended that a matron be advertised forat a salary to commence at £3O per annum.

div.head: METHODIST FREE CHURCH, RUNCORN.
div.p: METHODIST FREE CHURCH, RUNCORN.

The scholars had their annual treat on Saturday, when about 200 spent a pleasant day on He!shy Hills. Mr. Jeffs catered for the physical wants of the party in a satisfactory manner. SUMMER SALE now on at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adet. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Board was held at the Workhouse at Dutton, on Tuesday, under the presidency of Colonel Ashton, and there were present--The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. Mclntyre, P. Speakman, S. Taylor, E. Aaron, Lewis, P. Hall, J. Stokes, Brandreth, Smith, Dansey (Local Government inspector), H. Linaker (clerk), and H. G. Linaker (deputy clerk.) Mr. Brandreth reported that there was a balance in the hands of the treasurer of £1,942 2s. 9d. The minutes of the Finance Committee were adopted, on the proposition of Mr. Brandreth, seconded by the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi. It was explained that the county rate amounted to £2,552, and the balance in the treasurer's hands was only £1,942 It was also stated,in answer to Mr. Taylor, that the rate was overdue. There was no other business of public interest. BATHS, an kinds.--J. S. Garlands, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge Street, Warrington. Branch—Barlestown.—Adrt.

div.head: }TALTON PtIRLICAN FINED FOR DRUNKENNESS.
div.p: A }TALTON PtIRLICAN FINED FOR DRUNKENNESS.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Thomas Hig- ginson Wolstencroft, landlord of the flalton Castle Hotel, was summoned for having been drunk on his own licensed premises.—The defendant said it was not the , effects of drink, but of the laudanum he had taken.—P.C. Costello deposed that at five minutes to ten on the sth inst. he visited the Hotel, and found the defendant drunk. Witness accused him of being drunk and also stated he was drunk on the previous evening, and he should report the matter. The defendant commenced to swear and on his wife attempting to persuade him to desist, he struck her on the face.—P.C. Fryer gave corro- borative testimony.—Mr. Fletcher, who defended, said the man had been assaulted on the previous night, and was in neat pain with face ache in consequence. He had taken a quantity of laudanum to ease his sufferings, and was not under the influence of drink. To support ' this statement Benjamin Dutton and Henry Howe were , called. A fine of 10s. and costs 12s. 6d. was imposed.
SHOCKING DEATH OF A BOY AT RCWK SAVAGE.

The Deputy Coroner, Mr. R. Dobson, held an inquiry on Saturday, at the farm of Mr. Joseph Stokes, of Rock Savage, into the circumstances attending the death of Robert Bradley, age ten, son of a labourer at Clifton. A school treat was held on Wednesday week, at which the deceased was present, and during the temporary absence of the superintendent, a number of children, amongst whom was the deceased, commenced to play on a thresh- ing machine which was stationed in the field. Bradley made several attempts to climb to the top of the machine, but was eacn time pulled down by the other children. He, however, showed a determination to ac- complish the feat, and climbed up again, the result being that he was caught by the revolving portion of the machine. Deceased's head came in violent contact with the fixed portion at the top, the consequence being that his neck was broken and his head was smashed. The jury returned a verdict pf " Accidental death." It was observed that the children in the neighbourhood were accustomed to play on the horse gear of the roller, and that they thoroughly understood the danger of attempt- ing to climb as the deceased had done. MAIL CARTS for children.—Garland, Ironmonger, Warring- ton and Earlestown.—Advt. CRUELTY TO CALVES AT RUNCORN. Before Mr. Thomas and Mr. Jos. Handley, at Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, Robert Metcalf, a cattle dealer, of Liverpool, was summoned for having, on the 23rd June, caused to be conveyed eleven calves in a certain cart in such a manner as to give the animals unnecessary pain and suffering. rhe defendant pleaded guilty. Mr. Percy Davies, of Warrington, prosecuted on behalf of the R.S.P.C.A., and stated that the defendant pur- Oased the calves at a sale at Moore for £2B, and he arranged with a man named Banner, who is a chapel keeper and coal dealer, Sze., to carry the animals to Run- corn for four shillings. The defendant placed each calf in a bag, only the head being visible and the animals were put in a cart which was only five feet five inches by three feet seven inches. Consequently, they must have been crowded one on the top of the other. On the cart passing through Runcorn, Dr. McDougall recognised the painful position in which the calves were placed, and he followed on to the railway station, where they were un- loaded in the presence of P.C. Woodrow and Mr. Newton, the chief booking clerk. The calves were soaking wet with perspiration and the tongues of most of them were protruding. Mr. Newton thought two of them were dying, and he bathed them with water and gave them some water to drink.—The defendant,who had no excuse to make, was fined £2 and costs £2 6s. 6d. SEQUEL TO NEWTON RACES. At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, S. Swann, of Wigan, was summoned for cruelty to a horse at Earlestown, on the 24th July. Inspector Jowett of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to animals, conducted the prosecution. It appeared that on the date named the Inspector saw the defendant driving the horse from the races. He was beating the animal with the thong and whip- stock, and though the Inspector called out to him he took no notice. A fine of 20s. and costs was in- flicted.—Wm. Carney, Warrington, was also sum- moned for cruelty to a horse by working it in an unfit state, on the 25th July. The defendant was in charge of a horse which had been overdriven and appeared to be completely exhausted.—A fine of 108. and costs was imposed. SUMMER SALE now on at J, & V. DUTTON'S Sankey-at.. Warrington.—Advt.
THE WIRRAL AND BIRKENHEAD AGRICULTURAL

SHOW. The committee of the Wirral and Birkenhead Agricultural Society have resolved not to extend the show yard this year ; therefore all intending exhi- bitors should send their entries to the secretary without the least possible delay, for any received after the advertised time for closing or entries are

liable to -ITe.-ieut4ni;eci,-IT ii7e—ii-timl;er received are sufficient to occupy the space alloted to each de- partment. As already announced, the band and pipers of the Queen's Own Cameron Highlanders, from Edinburgh Castle, have been engaged for both clays of the show, and there are other great attrac- tions ; in fact, fine weather is only required for this year's show, in order that it may eclipse any of the society's previous exhibitions. With so many at- tractions there ought to be a very large entry. SUMMER SALE now on at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adrt.

"A PAIR POKER BOUT" AT EARrEsTowN. At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Catherine Gallagher was charged under a warrant with maliciously wounding Eliza Brannan, at New- ton, on the 6th August. Mr. Knowles (Widnes) ap- peared for the prisoner. The complainant, who gave her evidence somewhat unintelligibly, asserted that the prisoner struck her a violent blow on the head with a poker, and caused a severe wound. She called a witness, who,however, failed to corroborate her statement. Mr. Knowles said his client was on her own door step, when the complainant came up and attempted to strike her with a glass sugar basin. She then brought a poker. and struck the prisoner several times. The ptisoner then went into the kitchen and brought out her own poker, and blows were exchanged. Unfortunately, the com- plainant ran her head against the poker carried by his (Mr. Knowles's) client. It seemed to have been a fair poke' bout between them, and the complain- ant was the aggressor. She was an Irishwoman, and her courage naturally failed her—(laughter)-- and she went home and threw the contents of an article over her. The Bench discharged the pri- soner.
SUMMER SALE Row on at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt. GOOD TEMPLAR. CONVENTION.

Brockbank, P.C.C.T. presided. The report of the C.C.T. (Bro. Devlin, of Warrington) referred to the condition of Good Tem- plary in the district; Bro. E. Newman, C. All the reports were adopted, and and the election of officers of the convention for the ensuing half-year resulted as follows :—C.C.T., Bro. George Clarke (Earlestown); C. Coun., Bro. G. Punshon (St. Helens) ; C.E.S., Bro. R. Skaife (St. Hs eeel .e,Bnsr)o;.Te. I\Slanj:rtie' Sister H. Lindon (St. Helens); C. (Warrington); C.Tres., Bro.T.Train (Warrington), C. Chaplain, Bro. J. Lindon (St. Helens), C. Marshal, Bro. 0. Speakman (Ashton-in- Makerfield), P.C.C.T.. Bro, Colour-sergeant Devlin (Warrington), C,V.T., Sister J. E. Warburton (Earlestown), C.G., Bro. T. Riley (Warrington), C. Sentinel, Bro. J. Blinston (Ashton-in-Makerfleld), B.A. Sec., Bro. Roberts (Warrington), and C.D.M., Sister Sutherland (Ifindley). Bro. J. J. Jakeman, scientific lecturer for the Liverpool Temperance and Band of Hope Union, afterwards gave an address and conveyed•to the meeting hearty and fraternal greetings from the Liverpool Templar Workers Union. A tea party followed, and at a subsequent public meeting the Eev. Mr. Smith presided. Bro. J. J. div.head: MISS DOWNIE RESIGNS.
div.p: MISS DOWNIE RESIGNS.

On moving theWpii-oii-Wtri.;;i:iciites the Chairman said they would all join very heartily in an expression of sincere regret that Miss Downie was leaving the Hospital, and they could not possibly meet with a mat- ron who would perform her !I uties more satisfactorily than she had done for the past twelve years. He pro- posed that some record of their opinion be sent to MiS3 Downie for her acceptance together with a wish that in her future life she may be happy. (Hear, hear).—The motion was tarried unanimously.

div.head: FINANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE FINANCE COMMITTEE.

The Finance Committee recommended that application be made to thn Local Government Board for sanction to borrow £250 for the purpose of providing a laundry and drying room at the Infectious Diseases Hospital and that loans be aolvertised for. That the sum of £2,190 be borrowed froth the Prudential Assurance Company Limited, for the purpose of providing stables, sheds, &c., as per the sanction of the Local Government Board. Instructions given to accept £250 in settlement of account against the British Cement Company.—Accounts amounting to £2,138 11. s. 7d. were passed for payment. —The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Mid- wood.

div.head: TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
div.p: TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

The minutes of the General Purposes Committee con- tained the following :—Technie.al Instruction Act, 1889— Letter, 2nd July, from Mr. J. Morrison, secretary to the Widnes Science and Art Committee, asking the Board to put the Act into operation, and offering to hand over the apparatus. furniture, and library used in the present school, which has cost about £5OO. Recommended that the Act be put into operation as suggested, and that the General Purposes Committee and those members of the present Science and Art Committee who will kindly con- sent to act, be a committee to make the necesFry arrangements.—The Chairman moved, and Mr. Wright seconded, the adoption of the minutes.—ln answer to an appeal for more information, the Chairman said the cost could not exceed a penny in the £, like the Libraries Act, but under this Act they could not carry theirexpenditure over the year in which it occurred. The Board might give assistance to techhical education, or they might supply that technical education. There were two reasons for bringing this matter forward now. One was that the Science and Art School was rather too small for the students, and the other was that some of the subscribers had given notice that they would no longer continue ; and as the members knew there were chances impending which would bring that about. The average expendi- ture of the schools had been from £lOO to £llO a year, and if the Board took over the school it would be con- ducted in the same way as it had been in the past.—Mr. Reyes thought the matter ought to be adjourned for a month, so that the members could consider the question and give an intelligent vote.—The Chairman said the difficulty was that the season commenced at the end of September, and unless they engaged teachers they would not be able to carry on the school.—ln reply to Mr. Brown, the Chairman said the Board could stop the grant to the school at the end of a year.—Dr. 0 'Keefe supported the minute, but suggested that some members of the School Board should be on the Committee.—Mr. Brown said he would prefer to give a stated sum in aid of the school rather than take it over. That was his present impression.—Eventually the question was adjourned for a month, the Chairman observing, without dissent, that it might be taken the Board would help the school in one way or another. WATER DIETERS.

Mr. Hargraves moved that the resolution fixing the minimum price for water supplied by meter at ss. be re- scindcd.—Mr. Neil seconded. A discussion took place, and arguments previously reported were repeated, and finally Mr. Brown, on behalf of the Water Committee, undertook to reconsider the question, and Mr. Hargreaves withdrew his proposition.

div.head: PROPOSED INCORPORATION OF WIDNES.
div.p: PROPOSED INCORPORATION OF WIDNES.

_ Mr. Delaney, secretary to the Widnes branch of the Irish National League, had forwarded the fol- lowing resolution passed by that body :—We, the members of the Widnes branch of the Irish National League, representing a large number Of , the inhabi- tants of Widnes, believe the time has come when the necessary steps should be taken to have the town of Widnes incorporated, and we hereby pledge ourselves to do our utmost to have the same carried as soon as pos- sible."—Mr. D. Wright said the question of incorporation had been under agitation for some time. They wer• told by people who ought to know that it would be bet- ter to leave the question until they saw whether the proposed chemical syndicate was formed or not. If it was formed, they were told there was nothing for it but to obtain a charter of incorporation, but he did not believe in being compelled to do a thing, and he said they ought to have a charter of incorporation whether the Chemical Union was formed or not. Towns smaller than Widnes were incorporated, and he knew some people said it would be better and other's said it would be worse. Perhaps both were right, but there was a danger of Widnes being included in a large electoral area by the County Council, and perhaps , some outsiders would come in and to a certain extent do their business. Ile thought the people of Widnes were well able to manage their own business.—Dr. O'Keeffe quoted II boroughs recently incorporated, which had thus derived benefits, in some cases the rates having been reduced. One great advantage from incorporation was purity of election—voting by ballot, and one man one vote. Then a corporation would be more dignified than a local board, and would not the Chairman rather be called the Mayor, and be really proud to receive the aldermen in their chains of offioe in the banquetting

hall. (Laughter.) As a Corporation they could have their books kept in a much better manner—they would not have so much red tape as they had now. Widnes Local Board was the largest, and had the highest rate- able value of any Locrl Board in the Kingdom. It was the wish of the public at large that the incorporation should emanate from the Local Board, instead of being called for by the ratepayers. There was no reason to hurry the subject, which might be adjourned for a month until Mr. Gossage could be present.—The Chair- man suggested that a Committee should be appointed to present a report on the advantages of incorporation. It was stated that things could be done more cheaply then than now; he should like to know in what manner.— Dr. O'Keeffa said he should oppose the appointment of a Committee,which was shelving the subject sineche.—The discussion was adjourned for a month.

RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held at the Cemetery Office on Wednesday. Mr. S. Taylor presided, and there were present the Bev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. E. Imison, H. Coleburn, W. Mellor, W. Whittaker, • W. F. Salkeld (secretary).

div.head: STATISTICS.
div.p: STATISTICS.

The Secretary reported that during the four months ending July 25, there were 134 interments, last year 128; increase 8. The fees received during the same period amounted to £l3l 2s. 9d. ; last year, £lll ; increase £2O 2s. 9d. Mr. Imison presented the report of the Finance Committee, which stated that the receipts for the month amounted toR46 us. Bd. Accounts amount- ing to £2l Bs. were paid and the balance of £25 3s. Bd. paid into bank. The Committee also recommended the payment of accounts totalling £4 ss. 2d.—The minutes were passed. The Chairman said he had received a letter from Mr. Joseph Stokes with reference to the charge of doublk fees for the burial of a boy who was killed at Roc's Savage. It appeared that the boy had lived with hia brother, who although at present residing at Rock Sav- age, was a ratepayer of RuncArn. The boy was therefore entitled to burial at the usdal fee.—Mr. Mellor moved, and Dr. Gastaldi seconded, the motion that the usual single fee be charged.—Carried.

div.head: LOOKING AHEAD.
div.p: LOOKING AHEAD.

In reply to Mr. Mellor, the Secretary, said the Burial Board owned 11 statute acres of land, 7 of which were enclosed, and 4 remained as agricultural land. This land would meet the requirements of the Board for many years to come—probably for 50 years.—Mr. Mellor said he had mentionel this matter because an important thoroughfare was about to be made in the neighbourhood, and the adjoining land would become enhanced in value and would probably be built upon. Therefore if there would be no enlargement of the cemetery needed for 50 years, it would be a wise proceeding to purchase the land now.—Dr. Gastaldi suggested that cremation would have succeeded the present mode of burial by that time.—Mr. Imison If the present generation pro- vides for itself and 50 years hence they have done their duty.—The Chairman said in the next ten years the whole land adjoining the new road might be built upon and it was well that the matter raised by Mr. Mellor should be considered.—The Secretaryuudertook to obtain full information on the subject and report to the next meeting.

div.head: DESIRABLE IMPROVEMENT.
div.p: A DESIRABLE IMPROVEMENT.

Mr. Mellor said tle property owner on the opposite side to the cemetery had given a corner of his land so that the end of Victoria-road—the new road—could be made in the shape of a bell mouth. The corner of the cemetery was a very acute angle, and providing the Runcorn Commissioners asked the Burial Board to give a portion of that corner so as to make a tound turn there also would the Board agree to do so in order to affect a very great improvement.—The members appeared favourable to the idea thrown out and the Secretary said there were no legal difficulties in the way. It was stated that should the idea be carried out, the Commissioners would bear the expense.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORR' ESPONDENT.

During the past week, a man who passed by the name of Whittaker, has been at Otley, in Yorkshire, posing as a full back of the Runcorn Football Club, and there was only one thing wanting to make this life happy, and that was to act in that capacity for the Otley team. He was received with open arms, and feasted to his heart's content, and the Tykes set about finding him a situation as a stonemason,which the welcome visitor said was his occupation. Be- sides this, a subscription was started, in order to purchase him a set of tools, so that he would not need to return to Runcorn for his own. One or two of the most cautious members of the local club,how- ever, commenced to make some inquiries, and dis- covered that Whittaker had "lied like a gas-meter," , and was altogether an unknown man in football circles at Runcorn or elsewhere; but he bad de- camped before his sins had found him out. A hard and fast definition of drunkenness would be a boon and a blessing to the magistrates, and also to that large class who are engaged in supplying liquor to thirsty mankind. There are so many de- grees of drunkenness, and such a diversity of opinion on the subject,that it is at all times difficult to decide between the conflict of testimony that is adduced when a publican is charged with harbour- ing a drunkard. The Runcorn Bench, on Monday, were engaged for nearly four hours settling two cases of this description. In the first case the super- intendent, inspector, and two constables emphati- cally testified that a man was drunk, and reeled and staggered along the street. The chief witness for the defence was Dr. McDougall ; who had ex- amined the man half an hour after be left the pub- lic-house, and who stated the man had walked a straight line ofils feet, drawn across the waiting- room of his surgery, and had talked clearly and rationally. But even the doctor was com- pelled to admit, in cross-examination, that the man" did not stagger to any extent as he walked through his enclosure to the street," and that "probably he was unsteady." Nevertheless the doctor said that had he been a" boniface " he would have had no hesitation in supplying intoxicants to the man who was "probably in an intermediate state." The Bench in their wisdom dismissed the summons. In the second case the evidence that the man was drunk was equallystrong, but on the other hand, Dr. Beaghan, deputy to Dr. McDougall, de- posed that he was not drunk nor "anything approaching it." Strange to say, in this instance, the magistrates disagreed, and dismissal followed in consequence, but a further summons may be is- sued in order to have a clear verdict. _

In ordinary cases a man may deny that he was under the influence of the "rosy god," and may give reasons and argue the point, but the evidence of two constables will outweigh all his statements, and the fiat will go forth "ss. and costs or seven days." In future any man accused of being "over the line" will, if he is wise, at once, take a "bee line* to Dr. McDougall's, and having walked the doctor's line "pay his ss. and go home happy. Far better to pay a medical man's fee than have the odium of paying a penalty in a police Court. Robert. Moores, sharing in the silly sensation caused by Burns' divine and swimming feats from Runcorn Bridge and excited by drink, attempted to swim from Weston Point to Runcorn, and had to be rescued by a boat after going,half a mile, and died from the effects of his immersion._ It is sad that a man who some years ago, had die courage to dive into the Mersey on a dark night, and rescue a brother from a watery grave, should have had such an end- ing. It is to be hoped his fate will be a warning to the nine "cranks' who have attempted to gain notoriety by jumping from Runcorn Bridge. The discussion on the subject of the incorporation of Widnes, which took 'lace at the meeting of the Local Board on Tuesday, led to no practical result, and the subject will doubtless be more fully in- quired into in a month's time. Mr. Wright was highly indignant at the suggestion that, in the event of the Alkali Union being formed, the manufacturers would leave the town,and there would be a difficulty in finding men to represent the ratepayers. The Union is now stated to be an accomplished fact, and it cannot be denied that it wilt exert a great influ- ence en Widnes for good or evil. Although the Local Board would not go the length of adopting the Technical Instruction Act on Tuesday, there was a pleasing unanimity of opinion that the teaching of science and art in the town should not be allowed to die away for want of funds, which would be an ever- lasting disgrace to those concerned.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS,
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS,

At the fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guardians, held on Thursday at the Workhouse, IVhis- ton, Major Wareing presided. The other members pre- sent were—the Very Rev. Dean Finegan, Rev. A. K. Sylvester, Messrs. C. B. Johnson, W. Middlehurst, J. Burchall, G. Davies, F. Stapleton-Bretherton, J. Golds. worth, G. B. Chadwick, J. Ranson, J. Kenwright, and J. Griffith, with the Clerk (Mr. S. H. Hartley.) MASTER'S REPORT.—The Master reported the number of inmates to be 475, as against 454 in the preceding week, and 470 in the corresponding week last year. Seventy-one vagrants had been relieved, as against 59 in the corresponding week last year. The medical offi- cer had examined the children of oblique vision, and had recommended that one of 'hem be sent to the Eye Infirmary. Two of the children had been taken out of the house by their mothers. IMBECILES.—On the minutes of the Visiting Committee coming up for confirmation, Mr. Middlehurst said it was found that the imbecile ward contained fewer inmates than it did. The inmates had gone regularly out twice a day, and they looked well. He thought, however, that the results were not satisfactory, inasmuch as only two patients out of 80 or 90 had been discharged in three years. He saw no reason why some further improve- ment should not be made. He proposed that a Commit- tee, consisting of Messrs. Dain, Leatherbarrow, and Middlehurst, be appointed to confer with the medical officer on the subject. —The motion was seconded by the Rev. A. K. Sylvester, and carried. THE ANTICS OF A WIDNES Boy. —Mr. Davies drew attention to a case which had come before the Widnes Relief Committee. It was that of a boy who was men- tally affected. He carried on in such a way at home that his parents were in the habit of putting him in the dolly- tub—(laughter)—or tying him to the spouting. He cut all sorts of capers when before the Committee, lay on the floor, and was perfectly unmanageable. The Commit- tee suggested that the lad be sent to the Royal Albert asylum at Lancaster. His parents were willing to con- tribute 3s. a week towards his maintenance. On the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Davies, the Clerk was instructed to do what he could to obtain admission for the boy to the Albert Asylum, the boy to be first examined by the medical officer. NOTICES OF Moriox.—Dean Finegan gave notice that he would, at the next meeting, move the re•appointmant of Dr. Cooper as medical officer for the lower Widnes district.—Mr. Middlehurst gave notice that he would move the re-appointment of Mr. Waterman as assistant- relieving officer for the Woolton district. TOWNSHIP ACCOUNTS.—Dean Finegan observed that in the returns which had been furnished the Board by the Clerk, all the townships were clear with the exception of Eccleston and Sutton. In the case of Eccleston there was a suip of £740 4s. 4d. due, in addition to a balance of £B5 Us. 4d. on school account. He would like to know if there were any explanation why the collectors for those townships were so much in arrears.—The Clerk said it was a fact within the know- ledge of the Guardians that Eccleston had for a number of years been in an unsatisfactory condition. The arrears had from time to time been brought for- ward and included in the new contribution order. It was included in the present order, and he expected that before the expiration of the current half year the whole of the money would be paid up. As to Sutton, the over- seers had all along had ample money to pay, but there had been a dispute as to whether the contribution had been served. MosErs.—The Clerk

TER EcctasTon AND Wixota _ stated that he had not yet been able to re-invest the money belonging to Eccleston and Windle. A power of attorney had to be executed. The document had now to be sealed in the presence of two gentlemen who were not members of the Board. This necessary formality was then gone through in the presence of Messrs. Mann and Hargreaves.—There was no further business of public interest before the Board.
