div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

T,HEFT OF SOAP BY JUVEIMES. On Tuesd,ay, at the Warrington Police Court, Joseph Taylor (15), Vactory--yard,,Elizabeth Ann Grime (14),and Thomas Grinae (12), Cilassbouse-yard, were charged with having, acting in concert, stolen a quantity of bars of soap from the .svarks of Messrs. Crosfield and Sons, Bank Quay. Taylor, it appearedoca,s working at the soapery, and gave the soap to the other youngsters,who,it was al- leged, were acting under the iartigation of theih• mother. Taylor and Elizabeth Ann Grime were each fined 10s. in- cluding costs, and Thomas Gri.ne, on account of his tender age, was disulissed,but a conviction was ecorded against him: _
AVIOLICNT WOMAN SENT W PRISON.

_ Margaret Stokes, a young married woman who aaid, in an answer to a question, that she as separated from her husband, was braught up in custody at the Warring- ton Police Court on Monday.eharged with having been drunk and disorderly in Sl'inwick-road ouSaturday night. and with having assaulted a passer-by named John Platt. The azsault was entirely unprovoked, and the police evi- dence was to the effect that the prisoner was most vio- lent, and had to be carried a portion of the way to the Bridewell. For the drunkenness prisoner was sent to jail for a month, and for the assault she was ordered to undergo imprisonment for another month.
A HUSBAND'S DISAPPEARANCE.

George Dixon, a venetian blind maker, was charged at the Warrington Police Court, on Thursday, with having left his wife and four children chargeable to the Union. Mr. Shearer said that the defendant's wife applied for relief on the 17th April, her husband having suddenly disappeared from the town. They were admitted to the House. where they remained until the 26th April. They then left, and Mr. Shearet said that he had not heard anything of them since. Dixon said that his family were now in Liverpool, and he was willing to pay what coat had beep' incurred. In consideration of this promise, the case was remanded for a week, defendant undertaking to pay the 355. clue 111 the meantime. HUSBAND AND WIFE ACCUSING EACH OTHER.

John Barnes, a married man, who Pretended to cry when in the prisoner's dock, was brought before the Warrington magistrates, on Monday, for drunkenness. That charge was fully proved against him, but his wife stepped forward and made an additional complaint, alleging that her husband was in the constant habit of thrashing her, by reason'of which treatment, she said, she was all over bruised. OD the other hand the prisoner _.Clarecl that big wic!l harl a habit of thrashing him, and that she had "cut him all over." The sympathies of the Court were with the woman: *lnd prisoner was sent to gaol for a month for the drunkennegg. A TnavELLING MUSICIAN " HARD UP."

John Ifock-e-n-hu-ii-,--('4a)i;Werns,--o-i-erTaeavours to earn, a living as a travelling musician, and who plays various instruments, was before the Warrington magis- trates, on Monday, on a charge of theft. He admitted having stolen from a stall in the market a coat that he afterwards pawned, and in explanation of the offence said that he was hard up, and wished to get under the notice of the police. Be told the Bench that his last regular situation was as one of the band of Sanger's circus, and that since he left it he had been wandering about trying to get a living as best he could. According to the police, Hockenhull is a native of Warrington, and was a man of previous good character. He was now sent to prison for ortnight, with hard labour. A PEUSISfinT WIFE nEsP,EITER PROPERLY PUNISHED. On Monday, a middle-aged man named John Edwards was brought before the Warrington ninistrgel on a charge of having deserted his wife, who had become chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union. It was also alleged against him that he had previously been convicted for a similar offence, in Febru- ary of 1885, when he was sent to prison for a month. The Mayor (Alderman Francomb) said that the prisoner began to appear at that Court in 1878, and the present made his twentieth appearance. To this, Edwards re- plied that he had been punished for his previous offences, and pleaded for leniency, but the magistrates considered that he was deserving of imprisonment for the space of two months, with hard labour,and imposed a sentence to that effect.
A FILTHY HOUSE.

Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, al woman named Bridget Dooley was summoned for allow- ing a nuisance to exist at a house occupied by her in Rose and Crown-st. Inspector Norman said that the house was in a most filthy state. Defendant went about the town hawking cooked green peas from public-house to public-house. If the public were to see where the peas were cooked, they would not eat very many.— Alderman Harrison: You think they would be very green indeed .—lnspector Norman said that he believed the house was a brothel, and Mr. Hunt (the Chief Constable) said there was no doubt about that.—The magistrates ordered the defendant to abate the nuisance within 24 hours, and to pay a fine of 20s. and costs, or go to pri- son for a fortnight. If the order is not complied with, defendant is subject to a penalty of 10s. per day for each day on which the nuisance continues to exist. A FAMILY QUARREL IN SHIP YARD.

A young married man of Warrington, named Martin Mitchell, who has for the past twelve months been living in the neighbourhood of Northwich, returned to his native heath on Saturday, accompanied by his wife and child. They visited the house of the husband's mother, and were made welcome, but as evening ad- vanced a quarrel occurred between the old lady and her daughter-in-law. The consequence was that the former tried to forcibly eject her visitors from the house, telling them to get lodgings elsewhere. Evictions of this kind seldom pass off peaceably, and ultimately the result was that Martin was locked up on charges of having assaulted his wife, and also a constable who had been called upon to interfere in the quarrel. Both the wife and the mother of the prisoner now excused his conduct, and denied that any blows were struck, and as the charge of assaulting the officer was not pre.sed, prisoner escaped with a fine of ss. and costs, which was paid by his wife.
THE MUZZLING OF DOGS.

William Savory, newsagent, Church-st., was sum- moned to the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, to answer a charge of having allowed his dog to be at large unmuzzled. He disputed the charge, and said the dog was not at large. It transpired from evidence pro- duced that on the 31st ult. a lad complained at the Police Station that the defendant's dog snapped at him in Church-st., and it was contended that the animal was not muzzled. A witness who was called, however, said that the dog did not leave the shop of the defendant, as she saw it on the door step. The Bench expressed the opinion that even in that case, the shop of the defendant might be taken to be a public place under the Act, but adjourned the hearing in order to obtain the attendance of the lad who made the original complaint, who was not present. Incidentally, Alderman Harrison remarked that the other day the muzzle was taken off his dog, so that it could take some water, and it slipped out into the lane. Although it was only at large a minute or two, a policeman saw it, and he (the Alderman) had half-a- crown to pay. Yesterday mornine, the case was again before the Bench, when the defendant was ordered to pay costs.
THE ESCAPADE OF A TIPSY LOVER; OR BEER A/1D _ _ WHISKEY COMBINED.

Joseph Corbett, WI;;;;;;;;C-r-ed;:;;Mmons at the War- rington Police Court on Monday morning, is a decent looking fellow enough, but it would seem from appear- ances that he has yet something to learn. One lesson that he should take to mind is that beer and whiskey combined is a dangerous beverage, and another lesson is that when he goes forth to serenade the fair object of his affections he should not be so very noisy about it. Corbett had to answOr a charge of having been drunk and disorderly in Knutsford-road, on the sth inst., and he wisely pleaded guilty. It appeared that complaint was made to a Constable of the conduct of the defendant, who was in the grounds of a gentleman's house, throw- ing soil at the windows and ringing the bells. After he had been induced to desist by the intervention of the Constable, he volunt4red the information that he was courting one of the maidservants, and wanted to see her, and he now advanced the excuse that he had "had a drop of whiskey amongst some ale," and was not used to it. It was stated that defendant had since apologised to the head of the household he had disturbed, and under the circumstances he was only called upon to pay a sum of 65., including the costs.

CONFESSION IN AMERICA OF A MURDER IN CHESHIRE. THE WRONG MAN HANGED.

Mr. Henry Churton, the coroner for Birkenhead.xul West Cheshire, is now investigating the circumstabees of an extraordinary confession Made in New Orleans,4of a murder of a gamekeeper, etuploped on Lord Tolle- mache's estate, some 35 years ago. It appears that Mr. James Sawers, who was for many years a well2known Liverpool merchant, and to this day holds a residence at Neston, which he visits occasionally, some years ago went out to New Orleans, and he, being an intimate friend of the Cheshire coroner has been the means of conveying to Mr. Churton the extraordinary confession which has just been made to the rector of St. Paul's, New Orleans. In his letter to Mr. Churton, Mr. Sawers Say:4 Dear Mr. Churton,--The Rector otSt. fads Church, 1 New Orleans, lately wrote me to make some inquiries if I could respecting a man executed in Chester scene 35 years ago. It seems that some man in New Orleans has admitted to Mr. Walters, the Hector of St. Paul's, that he committed the murder. The whole thing might, of course, be pure fiction, but you may be able to throw some light on the subject if you will kindly take the trouble. The circumstances, as reported to me, are as follows :—About the year 1855 there was a man named William Blag,g, who lived in a lonely place in Delamere Forest. Ile was a broom maker by profession ,and was also a poacher. One Friday afternoon,as he was getting ready for market in Chester next day, a friend walked into his hut and asked him to lend him his boots. That night a gamekeeper was shot, and Blagg was arrested. The boots were on him, and, being taken to the place of murder, every nail corresponded with the foot- prints. He was tried and convicted, making, as I under- stand, no defence beyond the statement, 'They were my boots, but not worn by me that night.' One morning in May he was hanged in Chester, the man who killed tho gamekeeper being present at the trial and execution. This is the story, and, if it be true that a man such as Magg was tried and executed for murder 35 years ago, my Friend is disposed to believe he knows the actual mutderer, although for the present no one is disposed to make any official declaration. I shall be glad to hear from you at your convenience. I leave this on Wednes- day, but if you address me at Neston any letter you may favour me with will be forwarded.—Yours truly. "JAMES SAWERS." "H. Churton, Esq.". . . .

A Chester correspondent had an interview with Mr. Churton on Tuesday, and 'found that he is much im- pressed with the strong probability of the story. Singu- gularly enough, though this fact was not known to Mr. Sawers, Mr. Churton himself held the inquest on the body of the gamekeeper, John Bebingrton. He remembers the case distinctly. Blagg did not live in Delamere Forest, as stated in the letter, but near the forest, at Alpraham, and the evidence, though strong, was en- tirely circumstantial, one of the most damning links in the chain being the correspondence of the prisoner's boots with the footprints. Blagg made no statement before the Coroner, and when tried before Judge Crow- der he adopted the same attitude. So strong was the circumstantial evidence at the trial, however, that the jury showed no hesitation in at once coining to the con- clusion that Stagg was the murderer of Bebington, and not a single effort was afterwards made to save Blagg, who, apart from the murder, bore a bad character.

div.head: CONFIRMATION OF THE CONFESSION.
div.p: CONFIRMATION OF THE CONFESSION.

A correspondent residing at Winsford corroborates the truth of the ccnfession as to the wrongful execution of the man Blagg, for the murder of a gamekeeper, in Cheshire, thirty years ago. The correspondent,Mr. Jabez Hulse, who remembers the trial well, and the widespread feeling in Winsford that Blagg was innocent, wrote as follows to a Liverpool paper : Dear Sir.—l happened to be returning home from the Isle of Man, and calling at my brother's in Liverpool, when he showed me the "Liverpool Echo" of to-day's date, with the letter of the Cheshire murder about thirty years ago. lam strongly of the same opinion as the Coroner that the confession is genuine, as I think you will see from the following was acquainted with a man (the name I can give if required), he was much my senior, and he, has now been dead about eight years. Formerly he was a very daring character, but during the time of my most intimate b.cquaintance with him he was a changed man, and often came to my house to talk principally about good things; but several times he referred to the case of Bebbington and Blagg. I remember distinctly his statements to me. He said that Blagg was not out when the murder was committed, and that it was a plot amongst the poachets that night that they should change clothes and also guns. He told me that it was his gun, but that he did not shoot it, but he never would give me the name of the man who did, but said he is far away now. He further said I have never used the gun since. He said much more about the night's fray, but the above statements he made to ethers as well as myself, and also said Blagg was as innocent as I. Liverpool, Aug. 13. LETTER FROM A RELATIVE OF BLAGG.

-. Mr. H. Churton, county coroner, Chester, on Thursday morning received the following letter from a relative of the executed man. William Blagg, respecting whose execution a great sensation has been created in Cheshire since Wednesday morning. Winsford, August 13, 1890. Sir,—l see from this morning's papers that you have received some information respecting the murder of John Bebbington' by which it appears that John Blagg did not commit the murder. This John Blagg was a cousin of my father, andll well remember my father and mother going over to see John Blagg before he was executed, and on his return he told us children that his cousin Jack was an innocent man. John Blagg said to my father, " Bill, I am as innocent as thou art, and I could tell thee something, but I will take it with me." He also told my father he knew who had, and he would see him hanged before he would come and confess. Then John Blagg said, "I will die before I will split." I may say on account of his being a poacher he thought there

would be a possibility of transportation, and he told my father that he would sooner die than be transported. I see from the papers that he was known as a bad charac- ter. I never heard him spoken of as such; but anyhow he had some grit in him to go to the scaffold rather than split on a chum.—Yours truly. W. BLAGG. FURTHER CORROBORATION. Mrs. Bebbington, widow of the gamekeeper murdered in Belamere Forest thirty-five years ago, resides at Crewe, and quite a number of relatives live in the neighbour- hood. The revival of the story of the tragedy has awakened keen interest in the district. Mr. Lewis, a Crewe gentleman, whose father's farm adjoined the estate where the man was murdered, told a correspon- dent on Thursday that a few years ago a well-known poacher named Garner, who, he believed, recently died, volunteered to him the statement that while it was Blagg's gun that shot the keeper, Blagg was innocent, and that the murderer absconded to America. Mr. Lewis says the name of the man who absconded was told to him with further details. The story confirmed in detail the confession made to the Cheshire coroner.

Saturday, on the Unity ground in rather dull but nice cricket weather. The Pearson and Knowles captain winning the toss elected to bat, but owing to one or two of the Unity players not having turned up at the time of commencement it was decided to send the home side in first. This proved to be a very unfortunate move for the Cairoites, as each batsman made an utter failure before the fine bowling of Beaman and A. Shaw, who disposed of the whole team for seven runs. To accom- plish the task of getting this large total the visitors sent in Messrs. Peers and A. Shaw, who soon hit off the required number, the total score being 56, thus leaving the Pearson and •Knowles victors by 49 runs. For the visitors Peers, Beaman, and Thompson played good cricket for their respective scores. Scores :

CRICKET.

Secretaries of Cricket Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
WALKER'S WARRINGTON BREWERY V. WALKER'S Bus- TON BREWERY.—PIayed at Warrington on Saturday. Score :—Warrington, 129; Burton, 27.
CAIRO-STREET UNITY 2ND (WARRINGTON) V. BANK-ST.-- Played on the ground of the latter, and resulted in a victory for the visitors. Score :—Unity, 26; Bank-st., 15.

WARRINGTON v. Serrox.—The return fixture between these clubs was played on the Arpley ground on Saturday, before about 1,000 spectators, and resulted in an easy victory for the home team. Messrs. S. M. and J. J. Crosfield commenced their innings about half-past two, to the deliveries of F. Jones and Oakley. Runs came freely from both men, bringing on Champion in place of F. Jones at 45 and F. Edwards for Oakley at 50. Neither bowler was able to check the run getting for some time. Champion, however, found his way through J. J.'s defence, the first wicket falling for 69. The retiring batsman had played very carefully for his 26. Mr. Smith was bowled for 3. Mr. Lawton gave his captain great assistance, and caused another change of bowling, at 121 F. Jones resuming in place of Champion, and G. C. Rees for F. Edwards. Both bowlers were being played with every confidence, when Lawton was run out for 27, made up of five fours and singles (3 for 42). Mr. Clarke soon got to work, and treated the bowling as it had been by the previous batsmen. Two more changes of bowling were tried, but without effecting a separation. Mr. Crosfield completed his hundred amid loud and pro- longed cheers. One run later, however, he was easily caught by W. A. Morgan, this being the only bad stroke in the innings, which included 13 fours, 4 threes, 6 twos, and singles. It was a treat to see the cuts and drives along the ground. He was an hour and 53 minutes, 81)d is to be congratulated on being the first to get a century either for or against Warrington Ist eleven this sea Son. Without any addition to the score Messrs. Clarke and Jolley were both dismissed, the former for 29, which in- cluded four fours, and the latter without scoring. Messrs. Young and Voisey played carefully for their runs, when at five o'clock the innings was declared closed, the score being 229 for eight wickets. Oakley was by far the best bowler,and met with most success. At 5.15 Messrs. C. L. Jones and T. W. Stubbs commenced the Sefton batting, the Warrington attack being shared by Messrs. Jolley and J. J. Crosfield. With only nine runs scored Me. Jones got his leg before the wicket and had to pay the "laltY. while in Jolley's next over he sent Stubbs p.' back at th 6 same total. Champion and H. Ratcliffe only vre tire latter was bowled by Jolley. G. C. Rees added took the total to 43, when the latter was splendidly caught' and bowled. Rees and E. Rat- cliffe added 13, when thd former Wag bowled by Smith, who had gone on in place of CrOslield. Thret; overs later E. Ratcliffe was bowled by Captain Adam, who re- lieved Jolley. In the samo over he sent H. Fay back, and next over F. Edwards was ',7?y smartly caught by Clarke. W. A. Morgan was soon done with, bat Oakley and F. Jones gave some trouble, and looked like playing out time, but ten minutes before the call of time Smith got a good ball past Oakley, and the innings closing for I 95, left Warrington winners by 134 runs and two wickets. WARRINGTON V. SEFTON r(2ND ELEVENS).—This match was played at Sefton Park, and resulted in a win for the home team. Warrington won the toss, and, of course, elected to bat, and the captain and Adamson commenced, the latter running Jolley out. Muir was grandly caught by Pratt and Brown came in, he and Adamson putting 43 runs, when Adamson was bowled with a beauty. The remainder, with the exception of Spinks and Birtles, offered a very feeble resistance to the bowling. Brown was bowled with the score at 108, after being in a little over an hour, and had played beautiful cricket for his runs. Sefton had a very easy task on such a fast wicket, and coupled with the fact that the visitors were without their regular bowlers, the issue was never in doubt. Overton and Monks soon rattled up their scores, but had plenty of lives granted them. C. Ratcliffe played superb cricket for his 69, and carried out his bat. The ' fielding of the visitors was very bad indeed, and it is to be hoped they will really try to remedy this serious defect in their play. Score : WARRINGTON. SEFTON. CRICK_ET.

The A ustralians played two good matches during last week. One of the most surprising things about the Colonials is their power of endurance. Although they have been almost constantly in the field for three months they show no symptoms of staleness, but play a good and gallant, if too often a losing game, throughout. Their return match with Kent was a reversal of the form shown in the first encounter, only a week before, and they were defeated by upwards of 100 runs. The Kent bowling was excellent; and it may here be mentioned that Martin, who took 4? wickets for 428 runs in July, obtained the "Tit-Bits "twize of £25 for the most successful bowler in that month.

On Thursday the Australians went to Leyton, and began a really sporting match against a Past and Present Eleven of Cambridge University. In the absence of Turner and ;Ferris, the Cantabs had a merry time with the bowlers,,and Mr. Streatfeild bit up 145 before one of Charlton's tearing deliveries hit his wicket. The Austra- lians in their turn made light of Mr. Woods, but their total fell 171 iliort of the adversary's. Then came one of those surprising changes which constitute the enduring charm of cricket, In their second attempt the Austra- lian captain and Trott drove the Cambridge bowling to all parts of the compass. Nobody could stop the run- getting of :Vfurdoch and Trott until a happy catch 9ff c• A. Smith dispowd of the former for 129, and Trott wag bowled for the fine total of 188. The Australians were mvativ t;!dpd by the bad fielding of the Ca.ntabs, and the rnablirty of Mr. W 0905 to bowl fast. Tilts visitors de- clared their inningS Ciosoti at 355 and put the Cantabs in to get 185 runs ; and so welldid Trumble and Charlton bowl that eight wickets were down at the call of time for only 78 runs. A few more minutes and the Colonials would have obtained a thoroughly well-deserved victory,

That magnificent veteran Blackham was the top scorer in the first innings, carrying out his bat for 66 runs. During the present tour Blackham has frequently dis- tinguished himself with the bat. A writer to the Mel- bourne Argus," premising that Bla,ckham is exactly the man to make a stand when it is necessary to "interrupt a procession," says: " No batsman was ever more of a puzzle in this respect than the great Australian wicket keeper. Of nervous and excitable temperament, Black- ham would be considered by most good judges of charac- ter not sufficiently cool for a crisis. All excitement before going in, he appears another man, however, as soon as he steps on to a cricket ground, and evidence of his natural disposition is afforded only by the quickness that marks his every iTovetwlt while batting.'

A writer in the "Manchester Guardian" refers to the enormous difference in the profits of such a match as the England v. Australia, played this week, to the English- men and to the Australians. The latter, who claim the honours of the pavilion and are duly recognised by the "Times" as amateurs—there is really nothing funnier than the " Times' " description of " Mr." Trott and "Mr." Burn as compared with the plain " Shrewsbury " and " Barlow" of the avowed professionals—walk off from a good match with £6O or £7O each ; the English professionals, who have so often shown themselves their masters, are fobbed off with £lO each. In a county match the professionals receive only £5 each—and the money is, to put it mildly, well earned.

There was good cricket at the Oval on Monday in the match England v. The Australians. Much rain had fallen, and the pitch therefore was soft and sticky; accordingly the bowlers had the advantage throughout, and no batsman played with any confidence. Decidedly the best innings of the day was that of Trott, who de- fended his wicket well and hit hard whenever he had an opportunity. In spite of one or two mistakes, the Eng- lish fielding was brilliant, and Lohmann made a wonder- fully tine catch at short slip. Martin thorougltly justified his selection. He kept a good length, and his break at times was very puzzling. The game had an exciting finish on Tuesday when the home team won by two wickets. It was "anybody's game" till pretty well on in the final innings, and had the Australian fielders not missed two or three chances the result might easily have been reversed. M. Read did well for the home side in his second innings, scoring 35. The innings totals were—England, 100 and 95; Australians, 92 and 102.

Cricketers in America are much interested just now in the question of a representative team visiting England next season, and the " Philadelphia Inquirer" strongly supports the project as being feasible andlikely to prove eminently satisfactory to both Englishmen and Ameri- cans. It is suggested that instead of confining such team to amateurs, as hitherto, three or four professional players should be included in any future eleven sent over to this country. Such a combination would certainly enable the American team to meet our players on more equal terms than before, and public interest in the matches would be keener than was the case last year, when the Philadelphians won four and lost three of the twelve contests in which they took part, the remaining five having ended in draws. This season the Americans have given especial attention to bowling, in which, un- like the Australians, their weakness was very apparent, and considerable improvement is claimed for them in this department.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Football, the predominant winter sport, is, undoub- tedly, being anxiously looked for by Warrington's Rugby enthusiasts, but, I understand, that during the coming season there is to be provided a bounteous feast for the lovers of the Association game as well. At the meeting of the Warrington A.F.C., on Wednesday, expectation ran very high ; and freely was the success of the new club speculated upon. I am informed that a splendid ground has been obtained, that the exchequer has a plentitude of "untold gold," and that the members are full of earnestness and zeal. The officials of the club are —" Van" P...rry, captain; C. Onions, sub-captain ;J. Wright, treasurer; J. Mather, secretary; and Messrs. Jones, Phillips, Oyling, Sinapkin, Onions, and Cant, committee. Already the fixtures show that some first- class matches have been arranged for the 'coming season —in all 26—and the club has entered for the Liverpool and District Junior Cup competition.
MISCELLANEOUS. George M'Gregor, champion quoit player of England, died on Wednesday morning, at South Shields. Deceased had been ailing for some time.

Two Warrington athletes and members of the W.F.C. figured as prize-winners on Saturday. H. Rowe secured a rather easy victory in the scratch obstacle race of the Bury Football Club, and Frank Bate came in second in the 220 yards maiden handicap at the Leigh Football Club athletic gathering.
DEATH OF CARDINAL NEWMAN,

We regret to record the death of Cardinal New- man, which occurred at a few minutes to nine o'clock on Monday night, at the Edgbaston Oratory, Birmingham. His Eminence's medical attendants, Dr. Blunt and Dr. Hogg, were present, and his pri- vate secretary (Father Neville) and several Orato- rians were also at the bedside. The Cardinal, whose feebleness had rapidly increased during the last three years, took a chill on Saturday, and during the night symptoms of pneumonia set in. He was comatose during the greater part of Sunday, and on Monday morning he was stated by Dr. Blunt and Dr. Hogg to be sinking. His condition, in fact, was then considered 80 serious that the extreme rite of unction was administered. He remained uncon- scious till he expired. "Men of the Time" says :—His Eminence, John Henry Newman, Cardinal Deacon of the Holy Roman Church, elder brother of Francis William Newman, was born in London in 1801, and educated at Ealing School, whence he proceeded to Trinity College, Oxford, where he gradu- ated B.A. in 1820, taking classical honours, and was elected Fellow of Oriel College. In 1825 he became vice- principal of St. Alban's Hall. then under the late Dr. (afterwards Archbishop) Whatley, and in 1826 tutor of his college, which post he held until 1831. In 1828 lie accepted the incumbency of St. Mary's, Oxford, with the outlying chaplaincy of Littlemore ; and in 1842 he quitted Oxford, and established at Littlemore an ascetic com- munity on a medieval model, over which he presided for three years. He held St. Mary's from 1828 till 1843, where, by his preaching, he gained such influence over the younger members of the university that he became, in conjunction with Dr. Pusey, the recognised leader of the High Church party. He took a leading part in the publication of the "Tracts for the Times," to which he contributed the final tract,No. 90, which was severely cen- sured by the uni versi ty authorities as practically annulling the broad lines of demarcation between the English and I Roman Catholic Churches. In October, 1845, he seceded from the Established Church, was received into the Roman communion, and was, after being ordained priest, appointed head of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri at Birmingham. In 1858 he was appointed rector of the newly founded Catholic University in Dublin, but resigned that post in 1851, and established a school for the sons of Roman Catholic gentry at Edg- baston, near Birmingham. Dr. Newman was elected an honorary Fellow of Trinity College, Oxford, De: cember, 28th, 1877. It has been frequently as- serted that Dr. Newman did not believe in the doc- trine of the infallibility cf the Roman Pontiff when speaking ex cathedra to the Universal Church on ques- tions of faith or morals. In reply to a criticism to this effect made by a Mr. Capes, Dr. Newman wrote as fol- lows (September 13th, 1872) :—" He assumes that I did not hold or profess the doctrine of the Pope's infallibility till the time of the Vatican Council, whereas I have com- mitted myself to it in print again and again from 1845 to 1867. And on the other hand, as it so happens—though I held it, as I ever have done—l have had no occasion to profess it, whether in print or otherwise, since that date. Anyone who knows my writings will recollect that in so saying I state a simple fact." Dr. Newman was created and proclaimed a Cardinal Deacon by Pope Leo XIII. in 1879. His Eminence has written "Lectures on Romanism and Popular Protestantism." 1837 '• " Letter to J. Faussett on Certain Points of Faith," 1838; "Parochial Sermons," 8 vols., 1838-44; "Lectures on Justification," 1840; "Church of the Fathers," 1840 ; "Essay on the Miracles of the Middle Ages," 1843; " Annotated Translation of St. Athanasius," 1842-44 ; " Sermons on the Subjects of the Day," 1844; " Sermons on Theory of Religious Belief," 1844; "Development of Christian Doctrine," 1846; "Discourses addressed to Mixed Congregations," 1850 ; " Life of Apollonius Tyanmus," 1824; " Loss and Gain, or the story of a Convert," 1848 ; "Lectures on the History of the Turks as to Christianity," 1854 ; Ari4Pk4 tht, VTIrt!I coqtur,y," " Callista, Sketch of the Third Centilrv," " DiscourSes on the Nature of Uni- versities," and essays on the "Office and Work of Universities," in 1854-56 ; "Sermons preached on Vari- ous Occasions," 1857 ; "Lectures and Essays on Univerr- ity Subjects," 185 D ; and "Letter to Dr. Pusey on his recent Eirenicon," 1886. Ile published an autobk,igraph- ical record of his life, entitled "Apologia pro Vita Sua," in 1864 ; a " Collection of Poems,' in 1868; an "Essay on Assent," in 1870; and "A Letter addressed to his Grace the Duke of Norfolk, on occasion of Mr. Gladstone's recent Expostulation," 1875.

The " Sear " says :—Cardinal Newman always led a life of extreme simplicity at the Oratory. Until recently he made his bed with his own hands. The rule of total abstinence which he observed for the greater part of his life was more latterly broken by command of his medical adviser. He did not dine with the fathers, but was always present in the evening in the refectory, although he ate nothing but a little soup, which was specially made for him in an adjoining hotel. When the dinner and the "daily lesson " were over the Cardinal used to initiate a brief discussion on the subject treated in the discourse. When this religious discussion was concluded, the Cardinal rose and led the way to the common-room, an adjoining apart- ment, which was supplied with newspapers, and here the affairs of the outside world were discussed. The Cardinal, until his recent illness, conducted his correspondence entirely himself, and until his eighty- eighth year was in the habit of rising at six every morning and when doctors insisted on his taking another hour in bed he was convinced that age was tel- ling on him. His eyesight was remarkably good,although he had to use spectacles when reading small print. His Eminence also hated smoking, and his answer to the man who asked him if he objected to smoking in a railway carriage is historic—" Sir, Ido not mind at all, but I shall shortly be very sick." He was rather aston- ished when, in the middle of his first sitting to Sir John Millais, the painter lit a well-seasoned briar pipe, with the remark, "Hope you don't mind sinoking.Mr.Cardinal ?" In Birmingham the Cardinal was always very popular, and was on the best terms with the municipal authori- ties, and a place was reserved for him at every Musical Festival in the midland capital. He was always invited to civic ceremonies, but the Fathers were somewhat sur- prised when an invitation to a civic conversazione ar- rived at the Oratory addressed to "Cardinal Newman —and lady " ! The Cardinal always held himself aloof from politic, but he was known to entertain general Liberal views. At the election of 18.85 he was the first to record his vote in his polling district. MR. GLADSTONE AND THE LATE CARDINAL. There is one little incident in the life of Cardinal New- man which appears to have escaped notice. Not long ago Mr. Gladstone paid him a visit at the Oratory, and the two old friends had no doubt a very interesting chat on reminiscences. Mr. Gladstone learned that the Cardinal had some difficulty, in moments of wakefulness at night, in getting light sufficient by which to read, and a solution of the difficulty occurred to his eminently practical mind. He went shopping in Birmingham, and soon afterwards left at the Oratory as a present to his friend the very requisite lamp accommodation he

needed. FUNERAL ARRANGEMENTS. The funeral has been fixed for Tuesday next, in the small burial ground connected with the Oratory at Red- nal Hill. The obsequies will be carried out in a manner befitting the rank of a Cardinal of the Roman Catholic Church, and will be attended by many of the bishops and other high dignitaries of the church in England. Several Roman Catholic noblemen, including the Duke of Norfolk, one of the most intimate lay friends of the Car- dinal, will be present, and there will be a large gathering of the clergy and laity. Immediately after death the body was dressed in full pontificals, with the mitre and crozier, and it will be interred with the Whole of the vestments At ten o'clock on Wednesday morning there was solemn High Mass of Requiem, the body being exposed. It is owing to the fact that Friday is a holiday of obligation, and the Feast of the Assumption and the Sunday inter- vening, that the funeral has been postponed till Tuesday. On Monday night, at half-past seven, a solemn dirge will be sung by the Fathers of the Oratory, assisted by the clergy of the town ; and on Tuesday, at eleven, there will be pontifical High Mass sung by the bishop of the diocese, and the usual function of the burial of a Cardi- nal. On this occasion a discourse will be delivered relative to the career and attainments of the great Oratorian by an eminent ecclesiastic. Numberless telegrams of sympathy from all parts of the United Kingdom continue to be received at the Oratory.

div.head: SIR W. HA.RCOURT AT DERBY.
div.p: SIR W. HA.RCOURT AT DERBY.

Sir William Harcourt, speaking at Derby on Wednes- day night, severely criticised the action of the House of Lords in interfering with the Directors' Liability Bill and other useful measures which had passed the House of Commons, the result of their meddling with the first- named bill being to destroy its practical use as a protec- tion to the investing public. As a deliberative assembly the House of Lords, Sir W. Harcourt said, had almost ceased to exist. He went on to defend the Opposition from the charges of obstruction in the House of Com- mons, and instanced useful measures which they had helped to pass. Dealing with Lord Salisbury's foreign policy, he said that if they were able to approve of it it was because it was exactly opposite to that ot Lord Beaconsfield in 1878, and had dealt a fatal blow to what used to be called a "spirited foreign policy." Referring to the existence of the Government, Sir William Har- court said it was practically at an end, and when that , end came it would be the inglorious termination of a misspent life. The Opposition awaited the future =vith patience and confidence. The Government had nothing to lay before the country but a barren programme and coercion, whilst the Opposition would appeal to the nation in the ammo of justice, conciliation, and pro- gress.

THE INQUEST. Some additicnal particulars concerning Mrs. :Pown- send's connection with Birmingham have transpired. Some years ago she was employed in a confectioner's shop in Worcester-st, Birmingham, where her engaging manners and good looks secured for her unlimited atten- tions from the young mashers of the period. At that time Dr. Townsend's brother was living in chambers at the corner of Newhall-st. and Great Charles-st., Birming- ham, and it was here she became acquainted with Mrs. Townsend's sister, Clara Reeve. Lousia Reeve, who afterwards became the wife of Dr. Townsend, was well- known at all the skating rinks as one of the most accomplished skaters of the time. She was also the belle of a dancing-class at the Royal Hotel Assembly-rooms. The adjourned inquest on th 3 bodies of Annie Louisa Townsend and William de la Motte,who were found dead at 14, Park-road, New Cross, on Friday, August Ist, was , held on Monday afternoon, before Mr. E. A. Carttar, the West Kent coroner, at the Brown Bear public-house, High-st., Deptford. Seventeen witnesses were called. The most startling portions of the evidence were found in two letters—one from Mrs. Townsend to de la Motte saying she expected a row, and was very miserable, also asking him to call and see her on the Friday. Another letter was from Mrs. Pearce, a friend of Mrs. Townsend, to the latter, urging her to think better of her purposed action, and go to America with her husband and not sacrifice her honour and all else. It was proved that Mrs. Townsend endeavoured to purchase prussic acid on the afternoon of the occurrence, but it was not shown that she was supplied. The result of the post-mortem examination was that both deaths were due to poisoning with prussic acid, and the jury returned an open ver- dict after nearly an hour's deliberation.

BRUNNER, MOND-, AND COMPANY, LIMITED. ANOTHER LARGE DIVIDEND. The following is a copy of the report and balance sheet to be presented to the half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of Messrs. Brunner, Mond, and Company, Limited, alkali manufacturers, Winning- ton, on Monday next. The report of the directors is as follows :

The balance sheet and profit and loss account, certified by the auditors, and now presented, show a balance to the credit of profit and loss account on the working of the half-year ended on the 30th June, 1890, of £129,691 19s. id., which, with the amount of £13,305 16s. 11d., brought forward from the previous half-year, makes a total of £142,997 16s. The directors propose to deal with the above balance as follows :—Dividend on the prefe- rence capital, at 7 per cent, per annum, £12,035 6s. 9d.; dividend on the ordinary capital, at 30 per cent, per annum, £88,125 ; amount to be written off patents account, £2,500 ; amount to be placed to suspense ac- count, £20,000 ; balance to be carried forward, £20,337 9s. 3d. ; total, £142,997165.

, The directors propose again to place to suspense ac- count a sum of £20,000. Resolutions with regard to the mode and amount of the remuneration to be paid to Mr. Edward Milner, Dr. David Basil Hewitt, and Mr. Gustav Jarmay, who are directors of the company for services other than those of ordinary directors will be submitted to the general meet- ing for approval. The directors recommend to the shareholders that Mr. Thomas Hungerford Forgan, who has been secretary of the company since its formation in 1881, shall be elected a director, and, case of his election, a resolution, simi- lar to the foregoing, with regard to the mode and amount of his remuneration, will be submitted for ap- proval.

- Should Mr. Forgan be elected a director, the directors intend to appoint Mr. Frederick William Brock as secre- tary of the company. The auditors retire, but are eligible for re-election. JOHN CaosFIELD, Chairman. Winnington, Northwich, 7th August, 1890.
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday morning. Alderman Harrison presided, and there were also present— Messrs. Ratcliffe, T. Jones, Heaton, Davies, Aukland, Balliarry, Turton, W. Houghton, J. Houghton, Clarke, Eddows, D. Jones, Gill, Jolley, and Dignum, J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (workhouse master), and H. M. Mines (super- intendent of Padgate school.)

div.head: GIFTS.
div.p: GIFTS.

The Marriox of the Workhouse 'reported that a parcel of miscellaneous reading had been received from Mr. Page, of Aikin-st. Mr. J. Buckton, Fairfield Hall, had kindly promised a supply of papers and books every month. The Rev. S. Wilkinson had sent a basket of flowers for the sick wards.—Mr. RATCLIFFE proposed that the thanks of the Board be given to those who had sent gifts to the inmates, and this was agreed to.—Mr. HEATON said these gifts only showed, by making the matter known, how willing the public were to assist them.
SCHOOL rEES.
The School Fees Committee reported that they had allowed fees in 72 cases 65 of which were old and seven new cases.
THE INCREASE OF LUNACY.

The CLERK read a lete-i•---fi:orn C-h-e;CW.Asylum, stating that, owing to the increase in the number of patients ad- mitted therein, the spare beds at disposal were very few, and as this would probably continue to be the case until the completion of the enlargement of Macclesfield Asylum, the Asylum Committee would feel obliged if as much care as possible was exercised so that cases should not be sent which could be taken care of in the Workhouse, and in distinguishing between really pauper cases and those in which the patients' friends were able to send them to a private institution. The Clerk in referrinr, to some of the causes of the increasing number of lunatics in asylums, mentioned that one case—that of a man named Hobson who had been maintained since 1857—had cost the Union about £BOO. In another case—that of a man named Leatherbarrow—the Union had made payments of about £9OO extending over a period of about 39 years. —ln the course of some discussion it was stated that there were about 20 persons of unsound mind in War- rington Workhouse, and that the number in past years used to be larger than this.—Mr. SHEARER (relieving officer) said that Mr. Henley, the Government Inspector, had reported that while there was a decrease of 378 in the number of lunatics in workhouses in his district, there was an increase of 12,400 in asylums.—The WORK- ROUSE MASTER said that no person had been sent from there to an asylum if he could be done with at the Work- house —The matter then dropped. The relief cases were next taken.

div.head: TRANSFER OF HELIGOLAND. VISIT OF THE EMPEROR. _
div.p: THE TRANSFER OF HELIGOLAND. VISIT OF THE EMPEROR. _

• The " Reichsanzeior "of Saturday night contained the following order from the Emperor, signed on board his yacht the Hohenzollern: "We hereby order that un- til the proper constitutional measures can be taken, the Island of Heligoland shall be governed by an Imperial Chancellor under the Imperial laws, and with proper regard to the existing state of affairs in the island." This is followed by an order of the Chancellor appointing Captain Geissler, of the navy, Governor, and Herr Wermuth, Civil Commissioner. Herr von Boetticher arrived at the island at 2.20 p.m. Herr von Boetticher took formal possession of Heligoland. He delivered a speech in which he expressed a hope that the population of the island which, under the wise and just Govern- ment of Great Britain, had enjoyed such welfare, might be equally prosperous under the German rule. The Minister concluded by calling for three cheers in honour of Queen Victoria. A hearty "Hoch " was also given for the Emperor William. At the Casino, a kanquet was given to which about forty persons had been invited. Herr von Boetticher again spoke. He hoped that Germany and England would never be divided, and that the lofty wisdom which the Queen of England had shown on this occasion might always guide her. The Germans had a special sympathy for Queen Victoria as the mother of the Empress Frederick, and the grandmother of the Emperor. Mr. Barkly, who was evidently much moved, proposed a toast to the Emperor William in a short speech. In the meantime, the British sailors were busy removing the guns from the island. The British flag still fluttered beside that of Germany. After the formal 'transfer at the Government House, Mr. Barkly was escorted through the town to the harbour, where he em- barked on board the Admiralty yacht Enchantress, while a salute ot seventeen guns was fired from the British and German vessels. At sunset the Union Tack was slowly lowered, and henceforth Heligoland belonged to Germany. At noon on Sunday the Imperial yacht Hohenzollern appeared off Heligoland. She brought the Kaiser to view his newly-acquired possession. The Emperor after- wards reviewed the fleet and the 2nd Battalion of Marines. From the landing place his Majesty was es- corted to the upper part of the island. Here the Marines formed a square, and Herr von Boetticher read the pro- clamation already mentioned. The German flag was then hoisted, and the German vessels fired a salute. The Emperor made a short speech to the sailors and Marines. He said that a new and bloodless victory had been gained by the cession of Heligoland. The island in the future would serve as a formidable barrier to any enemy trying to invade the Fatherland from the German Ocean. At three o'clock the Emperor re-embarked and sailed for Wilhelmshaven. Nearly two thousand visitors were present to witness the ceremonies.
The Prince of Wales on Saturday, opened the new Portsmouth Town Hall, which has been erected at a cost of , £l5O 000.

PENKETII. THE HARVEST.

Harvesting is now in full swing in Penketh and neighbourhood. The farmers are sanguine of lair crops .if the rain does not interfere too much. Although the week has been so unpropitious, con- siderable quantities of corn is in the sheaf, and cut- ting is going on briskly. YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION. The usual weekly meeting of this association was held last evening week, there being present—Mrs. Coop (president), Mrs. Fildes, Mr. J. Simpson (sec- retary), and a good attendance of members. The Secretary having compiled a syllabus of lectures, essays, &c., for the coming session, Mr. J. T. Budden opeaed the session by reading a paper, entitled, "All sorts and conditions of men," being a general review of Walter Besant's book of this name. lie began by reading a short extract from the above book, and afterwards spoke on Mr. Besant as a novelist, also about his work among the artisans of London. After the essay, which was well received, an interesting -discussion took place, various questions being asked by the members, and replied to by the essayist, and the meeting closed with a vote of thanks to Mr. sudden.

div.head: POLITICS AT PENSETH.
div.p: POLITICS AT PENSETH.

- - Sir,—ln the report of Mr. John Atherton's annual trip, it was omitted to be stated that several widows of Liberals—who were left in the cold on the occasion of the Parochial trip to Southport—went to Chester at the expense of Mr. G. Broadhurst. Hitherto it has been the custom to provide for all the widows in Penketh without respect to the political creed of their departed husbands. But Mr. P. Pownall, who had the management of the widows' trip, evidently determined that the widows of Liberals should suffer for the sins of their husbands, and so, but for the kindness of Mr. Broadhurst, they would have been left entirely in the cold this summer. Yours, Sze.,
A 'LIBERAL.
THE NUISANCES AT HOWLEY..

- Sir,—What with the stench from Howley Intercepting Depot, the smell from the India Rubber Works, the Chemical Works, and the danger from the "death trap' (Howley brook), in which several children have been drowned, I think the inhabitants of Howley district have got their proportionate share of nuisances to put up with, without the slightest encroachment of any other. But, sir, we are now threatened with a most intolerable one in addition in the shape of the burning of a brick kiln, placed in the centre almost of the surrounding neighbmrhood, from which the whole of higher and lower Howley, Church-st., LatchfQrd side of the Mersey, the National boys' day school, in which some 500 or 600 scholars are taught, the Parish Church and Rectory grounds, and that important institution the Training and Clergy Schools, where a large number of ladies are being educated, will be seriously affected when the wind hap- pens to be in a particular direction. Now, lam well aware that the law says that a nuisance must ba committed before proceedings can be taken, but before this brick kiln is erected, and in order to prevent any future expensive proceedings, I would like to ask the Sanitary Committee whether there is no bye-law in existence to prevent, if erected, what everybody knows will be a great nuisance. If not, whtther it would not be better at once to acquaint those who are responsible for its erection, the great risk they are running of being summoned for creating a nuisance when the burning of these bricks in operation. A timely warning to those who, perhaps, may be acting innocently in the matter, might deter them from proceeding any further with the making of bricks in this locality. Will the Sanitary Committee kindly endeavour to protect us from this further nuisance.—Yours truly, D. Warrington, August 14, 1830.

div.head: NAVAL MANCEI7VRES.
div.p: NAVAL MANCEI7VRES.

So far as is known no general engagement has yet 'taken place between Sir George Tryon's fleet and the enemy," who are suspected to be cruising off Ushant. The " attack " has been confined almost exclusively to operations by torpedo boats, two of which were captured by the reserve fleet on Thursday morning, in the Dart. At Falmouth one torpedo boat was cut down almost to the water's edge by one of her own side, and has had to put into Plymouth for repairs.

div.head: CHEMICAL UNION.
div.p: THE CHEMICAL UNION.

A Glasgow correspondent says there is the best authority for stating that the Chemical Union, which has been so long talked about, is now an accomplished fact. With the exceptionof one small works inScotland and two in England, all the alkali works in the United Kingdom have given in their ad- hesion to the Union. The few remaining works above referred towill., it is expected, also ,join within a week or two. The capital of the Union will be about £8,000,000 sterling, of which a Mir proportion will be divided into debenture, preference, and ordinary shares. The Union will have a probable production of 150,009 tons ot bleaching powder per annum and 180,000 tons of caustic soda, and other forms of alkali about 300,000 tons. The Press Association is informed that the state- ment that the Chemical Union is an accomplished fact is incorrect. The formation of the proposed Chemical Union wonld be the signal for a combina- tion amongst the paper consumers with the object of re-opening on the co-operative principle some of the many chemical works now lying idle.

div.head: ALLEGED CHILD MURDER IN CHESHIRE. ARREST AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: ALLEGED CHILD MURDER IN CHESHIRE. ARREST AT WARRINGTON.

A young woman named Elizabeth Vernon,twenty- -two, fustian cutter, of Over, has been arrested at Warrington, on a charge of child murder. About .seven weeks ago, when she was an inmate of Left- ' ,wich Workhouse, she was delivered of a ckild, and 'left that institution,la.st Tuesday week,with the in- -tention of going to her father's house at Over, but her father declining to allow her to story in the louse, she stopped with a neighbour named Eger- -ton. At the time prisoner had two children with her, one about twelve •months old, and the baby about five weeks mid. Onthe following day she took -the youngest child away, saying she would leave it ort.the workhouse, and later on she was seen several miles away from Over. qn the afternoon she called /upon the persons at Over again, and informed them Chat -she had left the child at the workhouse. Pri- +Boner subsequently left Over hurriedly, and was /leen vzalking in the direction of Crewe on Wednes- day.. Detective-inspeetor Brittain instituted in- quiries respecting the mysterious disappearance of the chlid, and found it had not been left at the workhonse, and on Wednesday, in company with Sergeant Doyle, he arrested Vernon at Warrington. He afterwards found the body of in a ditch at Winsford. The child had been tied up in a night gown, and had evidently been thrown there. Vernon was beought up before the magistrates at Middle- wich, on Thursday,and remanded until the coroner's inquiry is NM.

THE SHIP CANAL.

LATCHFORD SECTION. On this section of the uanal there are engaged 1,500 men, 37 horses, 600 wagons, 20 locomotives, 10 steam navvies, 18 pumping stations,and 12 trains, with 30 miles of railroad. The men at the brickyard make nearly half a million bricks weekly. Of the tbtal excavation to be done, viz., 64 millions of cubic feet, nearly five millions have been accomplished. Nearly all the bridges have been completed. BLOWING UP A BBIDGE. On Sunday morning a party of Ship Canal and railway engineers were engaged in the operation of blowing up one of the bridges which crosses the London and North- Western main line near the village of Moore.. The em- . .

bankment for the railway deviation, which is to take place between Moore and Warrington, having been prac- tically completed up to this point, it became necessary to destroy a bridge, a portion of which came in the line of the new railway. To effect this object several charges of the new explosive, tonite, were inserted in different parts of the structure, and the bridge was literally blown to fragments. The noise of the explosion was like that of a battery of heavy artillery in action, and created some alarm amongst the inhabitants of Moore and the vicinity. VISIT OF SILK MANUFACTURERS.
