Gaddum and Co., and Kidd, Boden, and Co., Manchester; William Schmidt and Co., Bradford, Yorkshire ; George Watts and Sons, Manches- ter; R. J. Fergusson and Co., Brighouse; F. Sostier, Manchester; J. Bradwell and Co., London; W. B. Bar- chard, Manchester; Denis Bradwell, Congleton : and Andrew Cockroft, Halifax. WIDNES FERRY APPROACH. At Widnes Local Board, on Tuesday, the General Purposes Committee reported that they had been in correspondence with Mr. E. Leader Williams, of the Ship Canal Company, on this subject and they in- tended to consult the Board's solicitors, Messrs. Op- IDenheim and Company. The Chairman said as the Board were aware there had been a considerable excavation ot rock at the ferry approach at Widnes side of the river. That excavation would serve a very useful purpose in the navigation of the river and all interested in the trade and prosperity of the town, could only be glad that the excavation was being made. At the same time there were two things they wanted, and one was to have a proper approach to the ferry, which, no doubt, the Ship Canal Company would provide in due course, and the other was protection for the public. At the pre- sent time rock had been excavated to a depth of seven or eight feet close to the promenade,' and any person in the dark or at any other time, might easily fall, and be carried away by the tide and drowned. They asked the Ship Canal Company to take what steps might be neces- sary to render the place safe. The Committee had drawn attention to the dangar by placard, but as they were not responsible for the danger, they did not feel called upon to incur any further expense. The Committee's action was approved.
_ MEETING OE SHAREHOLDERS AT MAN- CHESTER.

The tenth ordinary general meeting of share- holders of the Manchester Ship Canal Company was held on Thursday, at the Concert Hall, Peter-street, Manchester, the Chairman of the Company, Lord Egerton of Tatton, presiding.

div.head: DIRECTOR'S REPORT.
div.p: THE DIRECTOR'S REPORT.

The report of the Directors stated that the amount received on capital account during the half year was £827,146 19s. Bd., and the amount expended £1,101,196 12s. 4c1., against the estimate of £1,230,745. The fol- lowing were the principal items of expenditure :—Con- struction of works, £896,020 Bs. 2d. ; land purchase and compensation, £36,593 18s. 2d. ; engineering and stir- veyin,g, £10,804 25.9 d. ; Parliamentary expenses, £5,816 6s. 7d. ; office and general expenses, £7,295 ss. ; interest en called-up capital, £87,699 19s. 4d. ; interest on calls In advance, £16,881 15s. 4d.; interest on mortgage debentures, £27,121 16s. 11d. The total capital expen- diture from the formation of the Company to the end of the half year amounted to £7,583,543 I7s. 10d. ; and the total receipts to £6,879,512 19s. 3d. The Directors' estimate of further expenditure on capi- tal account during the current half year is as fol- lows :—Purchase of land and compensation, £70,000 ; construction of works, £1,070,000; interest,engincering, and general expenses, £186,600. The net revenue of the Bridgewater Canals undertaking, after adding £l,OOO to the reserve fund and £5OO to the insurance fund to cover risks on the Mersey, was £30,227 195. 4d. Interest out of capital on the amounts called up on the shares was again paid in accordance with the Company's Acts of Parliament on the Ist July. A further call of £1 per share, making £7 per share called up, was made payable on the 31st July last. The Directors hope that it may not be necessary to make a further call before January next, as in the meantime they expect to be in a position to exercise the remainder of the Company's borrowing powers, for which the consent of the shareholders will be required. To enable the Company to exercise the re- mainder of the borrowing powers under the Act of 1885, £5 must have been paid up on each share. This renders necessary the forfeiture of those shares upon which the allottees have failed to pay the calls. The steps re- quired by law to enable the Company to forfeit such shares have been taken since the last meeting, and the Directors have, in accordance with the Acts which govern the Company, declared forfeited 2,331 ordinary shares and 20 preference shares. These shares were allotted to 785 persons, a large proportion of whom have left the district and their addresses are unknown. The Directors are glad to be able to report that since the last meeting £138,500 of ordinary share capital have been taken up at par by the Directors and friends of thei Company. The lower section of the canal between East- ham and the river Weaver is being prosecuted vigorously by the contractors day and night, so as to be ready to accommodate the Weaver and Ellesmere Port traffic at the beginning of next year. This will enable the works of the canal opposite the Weaver dock en- trances to be proceeded with without interfering with the Weaver traffic, and will free a large quantity of plant and a considerable number of men to assist in the com- pletion'of the upper sections of the canal. The lare' dredger constructed for the Company has been delivered , at Eastham, and the dredging of the entrance channel I will be at once proceeded with. The Directors are urging the employment of more men on the upper sections of the canal, and also greater progress with the construction of thetailway bridges. The Directors think that the muni- cipal and other local authorities should take measures at once to ensure the purification of the waters on: the upper reaches of the Mersey and Irwell. The Directors are considering a project for the enlargement and improvement of the port of Runcorn necessary to meet the wants of the gritwing trade, as well as to develop the valuable estate there owned by the Company. The Various Powers Bill was altered during its passage through the Upper House to meet the wishes of the Cheshire County Council, the London and North-Western Rdilway Company, the Daresbury Highway Board, and the Warrington Corporation, This necessitated an appli- cation for additional provisions, and caused some delay in its passage through that House, but it has passed the Lower 'House as an unopposed bill. The alterations so made will enable the Company to abandon another swing bridge, and the bill will now reduce the swing bridges over the Canal by three. This change will prove advantageous to the navigation of the Canal. Powers to make railways on the lands and quays of the Company (to be connected with the systems of certain of the great railway companies) and to levy tolls for the use of them have been granted on the terms proposed in the bill, and Parliament has also granted the power asked for to raise £600,000 of additional capital by mortgages or the crea- tion of debenture stock to rank after the borrowing I powers previously authorised, and also power to make the improvements proposed in the Bridgewater Canal at Runcorn, and to make by-laws for the regulation of that canal. The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the report, said lie was happy, in the first instance, to say that looking back over the last half year, he did not think there-was any reason for him to give a less favourable report than any he had given in any pre- vious half year. Although they were not yet em- ploying on the works as many as 20,000 men a number which, the late contractor, Mr. Wal- ker, estimated a the maximum, they had now in their employment 16,361 men. Those who visited the Canal would have seen that a con- siderable portion of it was .goractically finished. The Company had now 1,800 feet of openings into the Mersey placed In such a position as would be most favourable to the Canal and to the Weaver and other interests concerned in the river. (Applause.) They were glad to find that two of the leading rail- ways in the district—the Lancashire and Yorkshire and the Cheshire Lines—had obtained powers to put themselves in connection with the Canal railways in the docks. That, he thought, showed a very solid appreciation of their undertaking. (Hear, hear.) He trusted that public opinion might support that new body that had been formed of the two counties in bringing the Act for cleansing of rivers as early into operation as possible, (Hear, hear.) Sir 3. C. LEE, in seconding the motion, said the meet- ing would notice that the item of shares unissued now amounted to £305,430. Those shares were thecontrac- tor's shares. An amount of £138,000, which was un- issued at the last meeting in ordinary shares had since been taken up at par—(hear, hear)—many of the share- holders having come forward to assist the directors to get rid of that item. An amount, therefore, of £305,430 yet remained to be issued, and the board had made an arrangement with the executors of the late contractor to

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 16, 1890. A. VISIT TO TH ISLE OV MAN.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 16, 1890. A. VISIT TO TH ISLE OV MAN.

take up that amount on the 15th October and pay for them. That would enable the directors to issue mort- gage debentures to the amount of £453,000 yet unissued. A gentleman wanted to know whether they were going to complete the canal within the rarliamentary cost. He could not see into the middle of next week, but still he thought it was probable they should do so. The report was adopted unanimously. The CHAIRMAN proposed the following resolution, which was seconded by Sir JOSEPH LEE, and adopted : "That the directors' declaration of forfeiture contained in their resolution in that behalf of 2,311 ordinary and 20 preference shares in the company in consequence of the allottees therein named having failed to pay calls up, and the same is hereby confirmed except in any cases where the calls have been paid since the passing of the said resolution, and that the shares so forfeited be sold or otherwise disposed of as the directors think fit." After a vote of thanks had been passed to the chair- man and Directors, the meeting concluded.

BY WILKINS MICAWBER. T'other week, when th' Isle of Man fever wur so catchin', Ann Jane. who had bin rayther eawt o' sooarts fur sum toime, had getten it into hur yed at nowt wud put hur reet bu a trip across th' way- ter to th' Island. Aw tried t' perswayd hur at a walk reawnd Walton Arches or Hill Cliff, t' fust thing i' a mornin' an sum hot gruel wi' a bit ov gin-

germn 't just at bed toime, wud bi a lot cheaper—an' praps do hur as mich gud, bu i wur, no use fur "When a woman says she will, She will, depend on't ; And when she says she won't, She won't, and there's an end on't." At onyrate at's wot Willyam Shakespeer says, an' aw reckon he knew as mich abeawt th' fawts an'
Willis o' human nature as heere an' theere one.

" Theau would'nt bike to pay a heavy doctor's bill, would ta, Efrayh am ?" " Nawe," aw sed, " an' aw hope theau'll get aw reet ogen beaut sendin' fur ony o' thoose gentry." "Then aw mutt hay a change," hoo sed "an' th' . . . .

sooner it's brought abeaut th''better." Aw cud see—as the immortal Willyum varry for- siblee puts it—at hoo'd hay hur own way in th' end, soit wur decided at hoo shud try th' effeckts ov sea-voyage, an' wi' arranged fur hur t' sail fur Duglass on th' Tuesda an' return th' followin Frida.

_ Yo shud hey seen wot a comoshun ther wur amongst th' nayburs when it geet eawt at Ann Jane wur gooin to th' Island fur a tothree days. Wheay, wad yo beleeov it, we'd quoite a tea party th' day befoor hoo went (th' owd woman met nevvur hay' bin comin' bak ogen th' way tha went on), an fro' four o'clock i' th' afternoon to abeaut hauve past ten at neet th' taypot wur nevvur off th' hob, an' it wur as mich as aw cud do t' keep th' kettle boilin' an' mak fresh brews. WP had a kind ov an "At Home" wi' bread an' cheese an' pickells—weshed deawn wi' hot tay—fur refreshments, yo kno, an' aw con safely say at tha did justice to wot wur provided, speshally th' pickells, seem' at eawt or a middlin' sized jar aw cud ony find two little uns laft, which wurprobablee spared on ackeawnt o' theer yooath. Well, when aw coome deawnstairs th' next mornin' aw fund at hoo'd getten a large tin box fro somewheere an had ramna'd it full or clooas an other things, includin' two loaves at hoo'd baked th' day befooar, wrapped in sum owd "Examiners," a pot or presarves, one box of Beecham's pills, an Foxes Book o' 'garters. It wur th' fast time at ervur hoo'd bin away fro mi, an aw felt rayther deawn th' meawth when aw sed goodbye at th' central, an' as th' train steeumd eawt of th' stay- shun aw couldnt help sayin' to 'nisei "God bless thi, owd lass, wi aw thi faults aw luv thi still." Fooak may tawk as mich as:theyn amoind, bu aw'll tell yo wot, it's a poor heause at has no woman in it, an when aw gent whoam fro mi wark at neet, an fun th' fire eawt, an no tay reddy, an th' cat meawin' fur it's milk, aw begun t' wish at hoo wur bak ogen, aw did fur sure. Yo'd has, thowt at sum of th' nayburs wad praps has cum in an offered t' do a bit. Well, so did aw, bu aw wur sadly mistakken ; not one ov em even coome near, nor as mich as axt mi heaw aw wur gettin' on, which wur rayther shabby after wot tha'd sed an dun on th' neet at tha' made sich short wark o pickells. Well, aw didnt do amiss under th' cirkumkstances. Aw'd one or two misfortunes, at's true enuff. Aw oerslept misel one mornin; an when Ann Jane coome whoam ogen on the Frida an yerd heaw aw'd burnt a hole i th' kettle an brokken a cupple of puddin' dishes, hoo took it a deal better than aw thowt hoo wud bay dun. " It's just bike yo men;' boo sed, " bu aw'll for- gie thi this toime; it ony carves mi reet fur leavin' thi ;bu if ervur theau catches mi ga.livantin awe fro whoam ogen fur th' sake ov a change aw hope the'll not forget t' tell mi about it." " Wheay "aw sed, "theau doesnt mean t' say at theau feels no better fur thi trip, doesta ?" " Naythur better nor woss," boo replied, " bu awll tell thi aw abeaut it when aw get in th' heause, an aw've ead a cup o tay, fur aw feel rayther fainty. Awve had nowt t' eat sin aw left Duglass this mornin." "P'raps it wud be as well if aw wur t' explain here at awd had a letter fro bur sayin' at hoo'd bi at th' Central on th' Frida afternoon abeaut three or four o'clock, an at aw man meet hur theere which aw did, an this conversayshun took place as wi wur gooin whoam from th' stayshun. When wi geet in th' heawse,an' had had sum tay, an' at after ho'd tidyed up a bit, wi drew eawr cheors reawnd th' fire, an' boo commenced t' tell mi abeaut hur vizit to th' Isle o' Kan, an' wot boo thowt abeaut it. Aw'll giv' yo tit' story in hur own words : "Aw geet Liverpoo' aw reet,!an' wur deawn at th' landin' stage i' pratty gud toime, fur aw' didn't want t' goo i' ony crush if aw cud help it; but aw fun a grate monny fooak evidently wi th' same in- tenshun as misel, makkin ther way tooarts th' big booat, Which wur gettin' up steeum an lukkin as tho she'd bike t' bi makkin a start. Well, when awdlpaid th' mon at carry'd mi box on booard, a chap wanted t' sell mi " Tit Bits "fur three hauve- pence—as if aw wur soft—bu aw towd him t' tak it t' sumbry else at had mooare money than sense, cos aw'd made up mi moind at aw wouldn't be done bi anybuddy if aw cud help it. After lookin reawnd, aw oppen'd th' box fart' get mi Foxes Book o' Marters, so at aw cud her a bit or a read, bu it had getten so near th' bottom at aw had t' lift mi bread an' one or two mooare things eawt upo' th' deck, which caused a mon at stood by t' say at he wur glad t' see at ther wur corn i' Egpyt, an' axt mi if awd ervur tried th' experiment or castin' mi bread upo th' wayters an' lookin' fur it after monny days. Aw towd him aw hadn't; bu aw cud see at he wur tryin' t' bi funny. Aw took no further not is, so he left mi. When wi'd bin sailin' fur abeawt two beaurs, aw began t' feel raythur queer, as though awd etten summat at didn't agree wi mu; bu aw took four o Beecham's. an' had a walk reawnd th' booat fur t' see wet wur goin' on. Aw shud think ther wur abeaut eight hundert passingers abooard, aw fun sum or um varry sick, an' no wonder, when ev'ry other mon at coome near yo wur suckin a pipe as if his loife depended on't, an' makkin a chimbly or his meawth as though he're tryin' t' send eawt mooare smoke than wer even coomin' fro th' funnel o th' steamer itsel. Sum wur playin' at cards,an aw saw mooare than one shillin' change hands. One lot o' card-players at aw watched. after playing a short toime, went fur wot tha cawd a booze," an' feelin' rayther qurayus as to wot that meant, aw followed an watched em goo to th' refreshment place,wheer one or ern bowt th' tothers a bottle of beer, but befooar drinkin' tha made use o' th' followin' expresshuns : —"Well, here's mooare plus an' less parsons."— " Here's lookin' at yo."—" Here's luck ," whoile th' chap at had stood treat took off his hat an responded WI "Mooare fun." What tha did at after aw cawnt say, fur aw left em, bu awm sure tha wur up to no gud. Sum o'th passingers wur amusin' thersels wi' " Sailin an " Tha're aw varry foine an' large." whoile one or two tried t' makluv a bit, bu' aw think tha' didn't mak' mich progress, fur it had getten too rough fur that sooat o' thing. One poor woman at lay full length on a form wur wishin' th' booat ud sink, an when aw towd hur at wi shud aw bi dreawned hoo sed hoo didn't care wot hap- • pen't to hur. boo wur sartin or gooin' to a better place. Th' fackt o'th' matter wur,hoo didn't seeum care wheere hoo went to, so lung as hoo wur put eawt or bur misery. Well, we londed safely at Douglas in th' end, but aw nevvur seed such miserable looking' craythers as wi looked i' aw mi loife, bu' aw must say at con- siderin' it wurth fast toime 'at evvur awd bin on th' wavter aw stood it varry wee!. If aw cud ony hay' getten howd o' th' mon at pinned that papper to MI back which sed 1 big letters at aw wur "Lost "awd hay' pood his ears fur him. When aw geet off th' booat, aw thowt t' misel thers aw sooarts at coome to this place awst hay t' bi varry keerful. Aw lodged wi a Mrs. Kelly—not th' I Kelly at yo hear So mich abeawt—an ther wur abeawt fifteen mooare stoppin at th' same heause, an aw nevver coome across sich a crazy lot o' foo's ow mi travels, fur aw th' toime aw wur havin mi tay theere the wur at th' front dur yellin and sheawtin at ey'ryone at passed, an carryin on i' Melt a way at aw felt deawnreet ashawmed: Nay, the made th' heause into a propper bedlam, neet after neet, an aw nevver got t' sleep till tooarts one o'clock i' th' mornin ov aw th'toime aw wur theere. When awd finished mi tay, aw wur glad t' get eawt far a bit, so aw had a walk as far as th'prominhard, but aw hadn't bin eawt lung befooar aw began t' feel tired, so aw went back agen an had th' heause to 'nisei till late in th' evening, when aw went t' bed bu not to sleep. Oh dear, no! fur th' noise eawt- soide wur sumthin awful. Wet good onyboddy con see i' marchin up an deawn th' streets singin " Totty will yo go," an " Whoa killed Cock Robbin," neet after neet, is mooare than aw con say; bu when they're not satisfied wi dooin it eawtsoide, bu they mun repeat th' performance insoide as well, aw think at th' sooner they're sent Zululand an th' better. They'd bi a godsend to th' King o' that

country, speshally when he wur on th' war path Aw at they'd hay t' de wud bi t' make th' same row I at tha dun at Duglass, an th' enemy wed bi freetent eawt ov his wits. If onyone had towd mi afooar aw started at aw shud awye t' put up wi this, an hay prickles an other nasty things put i' nil bed, aw doant think aw shud hay bin so armous t' hay gone as aw wur. If aw cud only hay fund eawt whoa did it they wudn't hay put prickles in mi bed a second, toime, aw con tell thi, ba aw cudn't, an that's wot nettled mi. It seeums t' bi takken fur granted wi th' fooak at goo theere at tha con just do as they'n amoind. Well, when awd had mi breakfast th' next mornin', aw went .tooarts th' wayter, an' above one mon wanted t' tak mi a drive an' another even axt mi if awd bike V go out saraun fishin' ; but aw towd 'em t' moind ther own bisness, fur if tha made free wi' other wimmin at wur no rayson wheay' Ann Jane Edwards shad furget hersel'. Well, after awd had a look reawnd,an' went across to Douglas Head, an' watched 'em batbin' i' Port Skillyum, an' th' wayter bein' clear, ay" cud see 'em swimmin' bike yang fish, an' jolly fun tha wur havin'. Tiler's a splendid view o' th' sea fro' Douglas Head, while another attrackshun is th' Hotel, which aw'm towd is gen'rally creawded, speshally if it happens t' bi a fine day. In th' afternoon, aw went as far as Port' Erin, a varry pmtty place indeed, gettin' back to Douglass abeawt six o'clock—just in toime fur mi tay. At neet thee wur not quoite so mich noise i' th streets cos it turned eawt varry wet, an' aw thowt aw wur gooin' t' hay' a quiet toime ov it, bu' th' din at thooase fifteen made insoide wur so grate. at when aw went t' bed awreally didn't kno' whether aw wur on mi feet or on mi yed. Avern sure they did it on purpose V aggravate mu, fur directly aw left th' reawm tha burst eawt lafin', an' aw yerd one on 'em say—" Aw'm glad wi' hay shifted bar at last." Abeawt one o'clock i' th' mornin' aw wur wakkent eawt o' mi' fust sleep be th' mooast un- earthly yells at aw think it possible fur onyone t' mak', an' gooin' t' th' window aw seed six or seven yang men i' th' middle o' th' road. They'd formed a ring, bi howdin' one another bi th' honds, which tha kept swingin' up an' deawn in a varry wild manner, an' ev'ry neaw an' then aw managed V catch summat abeawt " owd ackquayntence hem' forgot." Awst not forgot 'era a hurry, an' they may thank ther lucky stars at they didn't get a wettin', fur awd getten a jug o' wayter th' reawm, which aw &Aid hay' thrown on 'em if tha hadn't gone away. Aw wur unable t' rattle fur sum toimela. fter this, but just as aw felt misel noicely dome thee a knock coome V th' bedreawm dur, Ayr sed " Whoa's theere ? "an' aw nevver felt so insulted i' aw mi loife when a mon's voice eawtsoide. sect—" Is Mr. Kelly i' this reawm?" Aw thowt aw shad hay faynted, bu pooin ;nisei t'gether agen aw sed— " Aw'll gie thi Mr. Kelly! wot do yo tak mi far?" An witheawt moore to do aw oppent t' dur, an I theer on th' londin' wur two poleesmen whoa towd mi tha'd fund th' front dur oppen, an' wur tryin' t' find eawt which reawm Mr. Kelly, th' londlord, slept in, so at he cud coome an' fasten it, but they'd not bin successful. "Awl soon find him fur yo even iv aw hay' t' wakken aw th' heawse," aw sect, an' aw wlnit thumpin' fast at one dur, then at another, followed bi th' poleesmen, nevyur fur one moment givin it a thowt at aw wur in mi dishabilly. Ay, theau wad hay si lit thi soides wi lafin, it theau'd seen heaw freetent they looked, when they oppen't th' dur an' saw mi' an th' two bobbies. Th' "Woman i' Whoite " wur a foo to it. Well, theau may judge fur thisel wot'a row they made when th' londlord, who had bin sleepin' i th' kitchen, wur wakkent bi th' screams, an' he coome runnin' up th' stairs as pale as deoth, an' wanted know wot wur th' matter. Whoile th' poleesmen wur explainin',aw went back to mi reawm, an' left 'em to it, bu befooar aw geet into bed aw made up mi moind at awd stond it no longer, bu goo whoam bi th' fast booat at aw cud catch. Wi this detar- minashun, aw lay mi yed once mooare upon' th" pillows, but aw slept so seaundly at it wur hauve- past ten befooar aw wakkent, an' when aw geet deawnstairs aw fund aw're not th' ony one at had oer slept thersels, fur th' breakfast wur ony bein' put on th' table. Well, as aw wur too late fur th' booat aw made th' best on't, an' aw went to a place cawd Castletown, wheere aw spent th' afternoon ramblin' abeaut, bu awm beginnin' t' feel sleepy, so aw'll tell thi mooare abeaut it another day." An' th' owd girl began t' malt tracks fur t' goo t' bed, an' as boo went upstairs, boo said—" They may say wot they bike abeaut, fooak goin' away fur a change ov air, bu in mi opinyun th' best place fur (Red fooaks is awhoam."
SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT SA.NKEY BRIDGES.

•Yesterday afternoon a man named Frederick Roberts (50), who lives at Mill-lane, met with a shocking accident. Re was billowing his employ- ment at Sankey Chemical Works, when he fell into a vat of nitrate acid. Lie was badly burned in various parts of the body, and was conveyed ta the Infirmary.
FRODSHAM.

OPEN-AIR CONCERT.—The Frodsham Military Band gave their third open-air concert on Saturday evening, in the presence of a large gathering of visitors and others, and the several items on the programme were much en- joyed. PAROCITIAL COMMITTEES.—At the monthly meeting of the Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship Parochial Com- mittees, held on last evening week, Air. H. E. Heywood in the chair, the Inspector of Nuisances reported on the dilapidated state of the sewage works, and pointed out the necessary works required to be done, when he was directed to attend to the same, and also to have the man- holes throughout the sewerage system cleansed. He also reported on a house situate at Netherton, which was un- lit for limmai habitation, and he was directed to call the attention'of the agent of the property thereto. • Plans in duplicate were produced from Messrs. Linaker and Davies, of proposed additions to a house in Overton, be- longing to the Rev. F. F. Edmunds, which were passed and recommended to the central authority for approval.
WIFE STABBING AT BOLTON.

An elderly man named James Cunningham, venetian blind maker, was on Thursday committed, at Bolton, to the Assizes, for stabbing his wife with intent to murder her. Mrs. Cunningham is well known to the police for her drinking habits, and her husband finding her drink- ing in a neighbour's house, threatened to take her life. He savagely stabbed her in the back. The prisoner, it is alleged, had to be prevented from carrying out his threat.

div.head: ANOTHER EARLESTOWN TRAGEDY.
div.p: ANOTHER EARLESTOWN TRAGEDY.
OPENING OF THE INQUEST.

—.— The inquiry as to the death of Alice Ann Dashwood, an Earlestown woman, was opened by Mr. Husband, deputy-coroner, in Warrington Workhouse, on Monday morning. As stated last week, the deceased had been admitted to Warrington Workhouse in a semi-conscious condition, and with bruises on her body, which, it was alleged, had been caused by her husband. Inspector Spinks, of Warrington, was present, and Sergeant Long- worth, of Newton, represented the county police. Inspector Spinks said the deceased had been admitted to the Workhouse on the 17th of June, suffering from bruises on the right side, the thighs, anal right leg. She was brought to the Workhouse on an order of the reliev- ing officer at Newton, Mr. Caldwell, and accompanied by her sister. She was in a semi-conscious condition while in the Workhouse hospital, and unable to give any intelligent account as to how she became injured, but it had been alleged that she received them by a series of abuses at the hands of her husband. The husband had absconded the day previous to the woman being brought to the Workhouse, and had not since been heard of. Deceased gave birth to a child in the Workhouse on the 12th July, and died on Wednesday, the Bth inst. The doctor refused to give a certificate as to the cause of death, and that was the first account the police received of her having sustained injuries. Sergeant Longworth said they had no hopes at present of getting deceased's husband. A warrant had been taken out on the 20th June for his apprehension for neglecting to maintain his wife, but that warrant had only been placed in the hands of the police on the 7th, the day after the woman died. They had no in- formation of anything being wrong with the woman till ' the Bth, when Inspector Spinks came over. Mary Jane White, a married sister of the deceased, living at Earlestown, said Alfred Dashwood, the husband of the deceased,worked mostly at the Vulcan Ironworks, Earlestown. She brought deceased to the Workhouse, but she was so ill she could not tell witness what her ailments were.—ln answer to Inspector Spinks, witness said her sister had been very queer since she became pregnant. She had heard it said that her sister had fallen downstairs. She had never told witness of her husband abusing her, and she had never seen Dashwood ill-use his wife. She had heard him threaten her, at the time be haci kicen summoned—about two years ago—for assaulting. her. Jessie Rose Davidson, a nurse at the Warrington Workhouse hospital, said deceased had three epileptic fits whilst in the Workhouse. She was semr-conscious all the time, and did not recognise her child. In answer to Inspector Spinks, witness said she did not think fall- ing downstairs or out of bed would cause the injuries. The bruises might be caused by kicks or by falling against the corner of anything. The Deputy Coroner thought that in cases of that kind the police should be informed of the condition of the in- jured person before death took place. IF. that had been done in that case the probability is that the husband would have been " shadowed." Inspector Spinks said the man went away three days before the woman was admitted to the Workhouse, and took with him a little boy seven years of age. It was then decided to adjourn the inquest for a fort- night.
"TOMMY BURNS 7-JUMPS INTO THE LIFFEY.

Tommy Bnrns surrendered at the Dublin Police Court on Thursday, and the police testified to his having jumped off the Bridge when the tide was only half in, a circumstance which startled the magistrate, owing to the well-known horrible stench of the river. Harry Montague, Burns's manager, deposed, amid great laughter, that Burns was the champion diver of the universe. Mr. Montague added that he bet Burns the price of a new hat that he would not jump into the Liffey. Witness could have bet ten to one he would not be allowed to do it. Air. Montague then produced a photograph representing Burn's encounter with a shark in the Mersey. The magistrate dismissed Burns on his undertaking not to dive in the Liffey again, and advised him for his own sake to confine his atten- tions to the Mersey in future. Mr. Montague said the police had treated Burns very kindly, and allowed him to take brandy after his arrest.—The magistrate : Indeed, I think he must have required it after been ten minutes in the Liffey. (Laughter.)

div.head: FA.TAL SWIM IN THE MERSEY.
div.p: FA.TAL SWIM IN THE MERSEY.

A WIPE'S SAD STORY. An inquest was held at the Devonshire Hotel, Runcorn, on Monday night, by the deputy-coroner, Mr. R. Dobson, on the body of Robert Moores, labourer, 32 years of age, of Surrey-st., who died on Saturday morning.—Emma Moores, the widow, said on Tuesday, the 6th inst., at noon, she took her husband's dinner to Weston Point. She was told he was in the Weaver Hotel, and she waited until one o'clock, when he came along the dock side. He said he wanted no dinner, as he was going to have a swim. A man then encouraged him to do so, and she told the man, whom she did not know, to go about his business as he could see that her husband had had too much beer. The man continued to challenge her husband, and the latter said he would swim to Runcorn, not for money, but for love. He pulled a pair of bathing drawers out of his pocket, and she went down on her knees and prayed him not to enter the water, but he pushed her away. undressed and jumped off the dock side into the water, shouting "Go en down to Runcorn; I shall be there as soon as you." She walked along the river side, carrying his clothes and his dinner. Opposite the pump- ing engine he went out of sight, and the men on board a packet shouted to the Ship Canal men to put a boat out, as a man was drowning, and they did so, rescued him, and brought him to Runcorn pierhead, where he put his clothes on. He was shivering all over, and she wrapped her shawl around him and brought him home. She fetched sixpeanyworth of whiskey, and gave it to him in some warm tea. She called in Dr. Mangan, who gave him some water and mustard, and prescribed for him. Her husband had been drinking for some weeks past. On Friday he was distracted with pain which he said would drive him out of his mind; and he made her fetch him a pennyworth of laudanum. She gave him six drops, and then he would have two pints of ale. At night she gave him the remaining three drops. On Saturday morning at four o'clock he was acting like a lunatic and at five o'clock he made her go out and fetch some laudanum. She went round to all the druggists, but they would not get up, and when she returned home without it her husband threatened to take her life with the poker if she did not at once fetch some laudanum. She fetched her brother Samuel hydrate, who afterwards brought twopennyworth of laudanum, and the deceased drank it in one dose, and went to sleep. Filen he ' wakened he was much worse and she went to Dr. Man- _ .

gan, but on her return he was dead.—Samuel Lvdrate deposed to buying the laudanum at Mr. Weston's shop, and said the deceased was in such agony he could not bear to watch him.—P.O. Woodrow said about 8 o'clock on Saturday morning he met the deceased, who said he was on his way to the Police Station to complain of his wife and Dr. Mangan, who, he said, had given him some mustard and water and he had never been well since. Witness smelled laudanum and the deceased said his wife had given it to him by Dr. Mangan's orders. The deceased then went towards home. Had witness known that the laudanum had not been ordered by the doctor, he would have taken some action that time.—Dr. Mangan said he was called in to the deceased on Tuesday afternoon. He was suffering from shock and waA also under the influence of amok. He assisted to place him in bed and prescribed for him. He had developed symptoms of congestion of the lungs, and he ordered treatment accordingly. He did not pre- scribe laudanum, and he did not know till after his death that he had had laudanum. He had made a post mortem examination of the body, which was wholly decomposed. Death had resulted from acute congestion of the lungs brought on.hy immersion in the water. I The deceased on Saturday would be delirious and not accountable for what he did.—By a Juryman : The laudanum might have accelerated his death.—The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical testi- mony, and asked the coroner to caution the wile for ad- ministering laudanum.

div.head: REASON WHY.
div.p: THE REASON WHY.

Why is it that some people can scarcely venture out of doors during damp and foggy weather ? It is because that owing either to a naturally delicate constitution or the neglect of proper precaution in time, they are liable at the least exposure to draughts, winds, or damp, to catch a cold which will develope into a cough. Influenza, Asthma, Bronchitis, Inflammation, or even Consumption! Why is it that others either can not or dare not enjoy the pleasures on the table, that partaking of necessary food is impossible, or the free indulgence of their taste results in horror which the bravest shrink from ? It is because they are troubled with Indigestion iu some form or other, whether it goes under the name of Dyspepsia, Flatulence, Bilious, Head-ache, Loss of Appetite, or any other form of that malady. div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

RYDE REGATTA. Lethe won the Commodore's Prize in the Royal Victoria Regatta at Rvde yesterday. FATAL COLLISION AT SEA. A Lloyd's telegram says that the steamer Rennik, of Shields, sank the Sarah Jane, of Whitby, on Thursday evening, off Whitby. Two of the crew were drowned.
LATEST CRICKET. Yesterday Surrey beat Middlesex by one innings and 162 runs. Gloster closed second innings for 170; Notts 123 for eight wickets; Australians second innings 118 for one wicket.
NEW OFFICIALS AT OSBORNE. The Earl of Jersey went down to Osborne yesterday to kiss hands on his appointment as Governor of New South
Wales ; and Sir E.Y. Monson, British Minister at Athens,
also went to have audience of the Queen. THE "MATRIMONIAL NEWS" CASE.

The young lady who has been awarded £lO,OOO damages for breach of promise of marriage by the editor of the • Matrimonial News" is reported to have received several offers of marriage from unknown sympathisers.
FATAL BURNING ACCIDENT.

The wife Of—a-ii77;st-H-a-n-;"elnita-f3l-enin-led-favitt died at the Hospital there yesterday morning from burns. Her husband was boiling tar on Thursday to coat a fowl house when it boiled over and took fire, burning them both. The husband is badly injured.
THE SOUTH WALES STRIKE. TRAFFIC RESUMED.

Traffic was resumed On-th-e—B-airWithymney, and Taff Vale Railway, early yesterday morning. Pilot engines preceded the first trains in order to see that the lines were clear and all the points in working order. As the whole trade of the district has . been upset by the eight days' strike very few goods and mineral trains will run, and it will be several weeks before the traffic gets back to its normal condition. THE CHESHIRE MURDER CONFESSION. ANOTHER LETTER OF CORROBORATION.
Referring to the extraordinary confession of murder, detailed on page 6, we have to add that yesterday morn- ing Mr. Churton. South Cheshire coroner, received the

following letter from a medical gentlema'n in the Bun- bury district, in reply to an inquiry as to whether 'Mrs. Blagg, widow of the hanged man, was still alive "Dear Sir,—l have seen poor old Mrs. Stagg, and I have promised her I would write to you, as you could help her very much by placing the letter before the Home Secretary. Several of the jurymen are now living, and they informed me your words at the inquest were, • There is no direct evidence against Blagg.' Mrs. Blagg remembers distinctly James Jones coming the night before to their house and borrowing her husband's shoes and leaving his clogs. Mrs. Blagg is at present, and has been for a great many years, in receipt of parish relief." The coroner will not, of course, place the matter before the Home Secretary until he has ascertained the full particulars from New Orleans.

div.head: GALE ON THE COAST &c. BREAKDOWN OF A STEAMER.
div.p: GALE ON THE COAST &c. BREAKDOWN OF A STEAMER.

The pleasure steamer Victoria, from Torquay for Wey- mouth, broke down on Thursday evening off Portland, but the captaiik brought his vessel round Weymouth without mishap. The schooner Annie, belonging to the port of Hagle, bound from Cardiff to Hastings with coal, went ashore at Hastings and became a wreck. The lifeboat rescued the crew. H.M.S. Hecate, Cyclops, and Belle'sle, and torpedo boats 74 and 85, of the reserve squadron, returned to Portsmouth from Portland yesterday through stress of weather, the ironclads taking shelter under the lee of the Isle of Wight, and the torpedo boats being driven by the gale into the harbour. A gale of extraordinary violence was blowing at Blackpool yesterday morning. At high-water the waves washed over the promenade, and the electric tramcar traffic had to be suspended. A terrible gale burst over Cheadle, yesterday morning, levelling two of the large tents in which the twenty- third annual show of the Cheadle Floral and Horcicul- . _ _ _ _ _
- tural Society as being held. Considerable damage was done to the plants, flowers, and fruit which was staged.
TFIE ACTION AGAINST CAPTAIN LYON.

The hearing was resumed at Lewes Assizes, on Thurs- day, of the action by the costumier named Picket to re- cover nearly £9OO for goods supplied to Mrs. Lyon, wife of Captain Lyon, of Worthing.—Mrs. Lyon gave evi- dence that after marrying Captain Lyon she received visits from Captain Warner and large sums of money with her husband's knowledge.—The Solicitor-General, for Captain Lyon, submitted there was no case, and that there was a scandalous conspiracy against Captain Lyon. —For the defence Captain Lyon said when he married he did not consent to his wife continuing a life of im- morality, and he never heard of Captain Warner until February, 1889. He aid not know of Warner's periodical visits. Yesterday the hearing was resumed at Lewes Assizes. Mr. Dutton, solicitor to the defendant, denied the statement of Captain Warner's soliciior that he had, on behalf of Captain Lyon, threatened divorce proceedings against Captain Warner unless the latter paid Mrs. Lyon's debts.—The Solicitor-General, addressing the jury, said it was clear that the plaintiff entirely rested his case on the imputation that Captain Lyon was a party to his wife's adultery, and this argument had been swept away. Baron Huddleston, in' summing up, said he would have stopped the case on the previous day if it had been merely a question of the husband's liability,but he felt that Captain Lyon had a right to ask his country- men to free him from the abominable accusation, which, if true, would render him unfit to enter respectable society.. The jury failed to agree. After an interview with the judge, they were again locked up.

YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. SIR J. LINTORN SIMMONS' MISSION.—Mr. STANnovE, answering Mr. Healy, said Major Ross, of Bladensburg, who now belonged to the Coldstream Guards, was granted leave of absence that he might accompany Sir Lintorn Simmons to Rome, in the capacity of secretary. It happened that during his absence his turn for promo- tion came and he was promoted. There was nothing beyond that to account for his advance in rank. THE POTATO CROP I IRELAND.—Replying to various questions, Mr. A. J. 13ALvotra said the reports he had re- ceived showed that there had been a serious failure of the potato crop, but they did not justify the anticipation of famine. _ _

THE ANGLO-PORTUGUESE CONVENTION.—Sir. J. PER- GUSSON, answering Dr. Cameron, said the convention between Great Britain and Portugal had not yet been signed, and therefore, he could not state its terms. He could only say that we were on the eve of a satisfactory and amicable settlement. NEXT SESSION.—MT. GOSCHEN said it had been abso- lutely decided that the House should meet in the middle of No_vember. LICENSING IN IREI.AND.—On the motion of Mr. HEALY the order for the Licensing (Ireland) Bill was dis- charged and the Bill withdrawn. He charged Mr. T. W. Russell with persistent opposition to the measure. THE APPROPRIATION BILL.—Upon the second reading of the Appropriation Bill, Mr. JENNINGS, (Conservative), complained of the mismanagement of business. He condemned the postponing of Supply until there was really no time to consider the estimates. Mr. BUCHA- NAN complained of the neglect of Scotch Supply, and Mr. LABOUCHERE wished the Government to adhere to the ar- rangeinents of former administrations. The House adjourned at five minutes to eight.

div.head: SUICIDE IN A LUNATIC ASYLUM.
div.p: SUICIDE IN A LUNATIC ASYLUM.

George Dawson, thirty-one years of age, who was tried at Lincoln Assizes last month on the charge of murdering his wife and mother-in-law, and afterwards attempting to commit suicide, has committed suicide in Broad moor Asylum, where he was removed, having been found insane. Dawson was found cutting his throat with a piece of tin, part of a tobacco box, which he must have picked up. The windpipe was severed, and the patient succumbed to the injuries. "Suicide while insane " was the verdict returned at the inquest.
--o-- SHOEBURYNESS CAMP.

The Shoeburyness Volunteer Artillery meeting was continued on Thursday. In the competition with the 10-inch gun the first and second detachments of the 3rd Kent won the first prize, scoring 30 points. The Ist City of London first and second detachments were second, and the first Cinque Ports (Sandgate and Dover) third. Between five and six on Thursday morning, firing at Shoeburyness commenced with the 10-inch gun by selec- ted brigade detachments at twelve, fourteen, and sixteen hundred yards The 3rd Kent took the first prize with 30 points, the Ist City of London the second with 30, the Ist Cinque Ports third with 28. No detachment failed to hit the target. In the officers' competition with the same gun only one hit was made, and that at a ricochet. For this weeks' fire discipline, the Ist Cinque Ports, under Major Mate, have made the best record. Yesterday the artillery volunteers returned to their homes. The Kent and Cinque Ports detachments were first to depart, marching to the railway station headed by the Ist Kent Band, playing "Auld Lang Sync." Other detachments followed in special trains. To-day (Saturday) the second division will encamp and com- mence their competitions on Monday.

Two mew, Patrick Davey and Michael Fox. were killed on Wednesday evening at Spanish Point, Miltown Mal- bay, by a sandslip. The tug Flying Dart has been sunk in collision with the London and North-Western pompany's steamer, bound from Holyhead for Dublin. The Emperor of Germany left Berlin for Kiel yester- day, en route for Russia, in order to visit the Emperor and witness the naval manceuvres. The Postmaster-General, in a letter to Mr. W. S. Caine, expresses the hope that he may be able to rein- state nearly fifty of the postmen who were dismissed for the part they took in the recent agitation.

NOTICE. is Hereby Given, that at a Quarterly Meeting of the Cheshire County Council, held at the Town Hall, -123. the City of Chester, on Thursday, the seventh day of Augur:, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred amid ninety, IT WAS ORDERED that the following BYE-LAW made by the Court of General Quarter Sessions of the Peaces Bolden at Nether Knutsiord, on the 3rd day of April, 1882, be repealed, viz. : " A Locomotive shall not pass over any Turnpike Road, "Main Road, or other Highway, during the hours " betwen 7 p.m. and 3 a.m." and that.thedollowing be substituted therefor as the third Bye-Law, in part VI. of the Bye-laws, made pursuant to the Highways and Locomotives (Amendment) Act, 1878. by the Court of Quarter Sessions for this County, and confirmed by the Local Government Board on the 13th August, 1881, such new Bye-law being the same as that originally made and con- ' firmed as lastly aforesaid, that is to say— During the period from the first day of May to the 31st " day of October, both days inclusive, in any year, a " Locomotive shall not, during the hours between 8 " p.m...and 4 a.m., pass over any Turnpike Road, Main " Road, or other Highway, and during the period from "the ;first day of November to the 30th day of April, " both days inclusive.
